10077-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-:
This October 1862 Atlantic Monthly leads with Autumnal Tints, an essay on the brilliancy of American autumn foliage that surprises Europeans. English poetry, the writer notes, has no account of such color, since English trees take few bright hues, and Thomson's Autumn says little more than that woods grow dusk and dun.

Later sections praise the purple grasses, the red maple, fallen leaves, the sugar-maple, and the scarlet oak, tree by tree. The essay, now known as Thoreau's, remains a classic of nature writing. Readers get autumn in New England at its most vivid, observed leaf by leaf.
10314-the-sonnets-of-michael-angelo-buon:
John Addington Symonds translated these sonnets into rhymed English in 1878, the first such rendering of both poets together. Michelangelo, the Renaissance artist, and Tommaso Campanella, the later philosopher-priest, speak here as poets of faith, love, and inward struggle. Symonds kept the old English spelling of Michelangelo's name on purpose.

His preface and notes explain hard passages, with help from Italian scholars, and some pieces had first appeared in magazines. The sonnets range from art and beauty to prison, God, and the soul's longing. Readers get two strong, linked voices of Italian poetry in graceful, readable English verse.
10338-with-the-turks-in-palestine:
Alexander Aaronsohn published this memoir in 1916, after serving under the Ottoman Turks in Palestine during the First World War. Aaronsohn, a Jewish settler at Zicron-Jacob, was pressed into Turkish service and saw the war from inside a crumbling empire. He dedicated the book to his mother, who lived and died for a renewed Palestine.

Chapters cover road-making, hidden arms, the Suez campaign, a plague of locusts, Lebanon, and a robber baron, ending in a rash adventure and escape. German propaganda and Turkish rule frame the tale. Readers get a vivid, personal account of Palestine at war, told by a man caught between empires.
10410-the-powers-and-maxine:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson published this romance in 1907, with pictures by Frank T. Merrill. The Williamsons, authors of many motor and society romances, center this tale on Maxine, a woman of stage and secrets, and on Ivor, Lisa, and Diana, whose lives cross hers. Paris, diamonds, and midnight drives frame the plot.

Lisa listens and makes mischief, Ivor travels to Paris and does what he can for Maxine, and Maxine gives back diamonds, drives with the enemy, and makes a bargain. Diana takes a midnight drive and a strange errand. Readers get a stylish, romantic thriller of Edwardian society and intrigue.
10435-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-:
Issued in October 1858, this number of The Atlantic Monthly belongs to volume two, number twelve, when the magazine was still young. The Atlantic mixed literature, art, and politics for educated American readers, with essays, poems, and stories in each number. Many hands wrote it, under an editor who shaped its liberal voice.

The lead essay, The New World and the New Man, compares rivulets joining into the Missouri with human streams joining into history. Other pieces treat books, art, and public life in the same thoughtful style. Readers get a rich, mid-century magazine number, full of ideas that shaped pre-Civil War America.
10460-when-day-is-done:
Edgar A. Guest published this poetry book in 1921, dedicating it to a real friend who never knows when day is done. Guest, America's beloved newspaper poet, writes short, plain verses on home, work, children, and faith. The index alone shows his range, from autumn evenings to a boy and his dog.

Poems treat a boy and his dad, a boy and the flag, Christmas gifts for mother, cleaning the furnace, and committee meetings, all with humor and warmth. Guest's rhymes are simple, direct, and meant for daily reading. Readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned collection of verse for family and fireside.
10495-under-king-constantine:
Katrina Trask published these verse tales in 1893, set in the obscure time just after King Arthur's death, when Sir Constantine, son of Cador of Cornwall, was chosen king. Trask admits the tales have no legendary warrant; she invents them in Malory's spirit. The book is poetry, not history.

Sanpeur opens the set, with Constantine at the hunt, knights and dames in gold and purple, and Gwendolaine, whose moods shift like wind. Love, pride, and chivalry drive the verse. Readers get a romantic, late Victorian Arthurian book, graceful in language and rich in courtly color.
10626-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly, founded in Boston, was a leading American magazine of literature, art, and politics, and this entry holds its issue of August 1858. Many writers contributed, so no single author speaks for the whole number. Its pages mix essays, poems, and stories aimed at educated readers in the years before the Civil War.

The issue opens with "Daphnaides," an essay tracing the English laurel, or poet's crown, from Chaucer down to Tennyson. Other pieces range across books, history, and public life in the same serious, lively style. For modern readers, the number offers a clear sample of what thoughtful Americans were reading and arguing about in 1858.
10695-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly's issue of January 1859 shows the Boston magazine at its mid-century height, mixing essays, stories, and poems by many hands. Its contents range from "Agrarianism" and "Bulls and Bears" to travel pieces, a plea for the Fijians, and a debate titled "Ought Women to Learn the Alphabet?" Poems and serial fiction fill the remaining pages.

Readers of the time would have found the Professor at the Breakfast-Table and the opening of The Minister's Wooing among its attractions. The number captures American letters on the eve of the Civil War, serious, curious, and wide-ranging. Modern readers can sample the magazine exactly as its first subscribers did.
10763-it-can-be-done:
Joseph Morris and St. Clair Adams collected It Can Be Done as a book of poems of inspiration for readers needing courage. Its pages mix famous names with lesser-known writers: Leigh Hunt, Longfellow, Shakespeare, and Burns stand beside Grantland Rice, Douglas Malloch, and Ellen Gates. Titles promise grit, hope, and cheerful effort.

The anthology is meant to be dipped into in hard moments, with short poems that urge persistence and a brave life. Its editors chose verse that lifts rather than puzzles. Readers get a hearty, old-fashioned book of encouragement, typical of the inspiration anthologies popular in early twentieth-century America.
10804-the-fortunate-foundlings-being-the:
The Fortunate Foundlings, printed in London in 1744, tells the supposed true history of Colonel M----rs and his sister Madam Du P----y, children of a duke's son. Their travels carry them through wonderful accidents and the polite courts of Europe, meeting persons of condition and adventure at every stop. The book claims to be genuine history, not fiction.

Its preface defends that claim against a flood of false memoirs, promising entertainment and improvement for youth of both sexes. The tale mixes romance, travel, and court life in eighteenth-century style. Readers get a period novel of foundlings, fortune, and European courts, in the manner of its age.
10854-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1860 opens with "Some of the Haunts of Burns," by a tourist without imagination or enthusiasm. The writer leaves Carlisle, hurries through Gretna Green and flat, boggy country once haunted by moss-troopers, and reaches Dumfries on a hot day, seeking Burns's haunts in town. Hills rise as the journey goes on.

The number mixes travel, essays, stories, and poems, as the Boston magazine always did. Its pieces reflect American letters on the eve of civil war. Modern readers can open the issue as subscribers did, and follow a wry pilgrimage to Scotland's national poet.
10998-a-catechism-of-the-steam-engine:
John Bourne, civil engineer, wrote this question-and-answer manual on the steam engine, revised for a new edition. Chapters cover estimating power and performance, boiler proportions, engine proportions, and constructive details for land, marine, and locomotive engines. Later chapters treat steam navigation, paddle wheels versus screws, and recent engines of every class.

Questions such as whether a pump could work without valves get careful, practical answers, with explanations of indicators, gauges, and centrifugal pumps. Bourne addresses mines, mills, railways, and agriculture, giving builders and managers rules they could use. The book remains a detailed record of Victorian engineering practice at the height of steam power.
11061-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1860 opens with The Carnival of the Romantic, in which the nine Muses, driven from Helicon and Parnassus. The essay surveys romantic literature, from troubadours to Haworth and Stratford, and holds a council on modern letters.

Other pieces in the issue mix literature, art, and politics, including a scientific discussion of starch digestion, saliva, and tobacco's effect on the stomach. The magazine, founded in Boston, gathered leading American writers of its day. This number shows the Atlantic just before the Civil War, learned, literary, and engaged with science and society.
11118-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for January 1861 opens with Washington City, a portrait of the capital as a paradise of paradoxes, a city of magnificent distances and still more magnificent discrepancies. Washington, the essay says, is alternately populous and uninhabited, a hibernating place of fashion, intelligence, and vice, and a Sevastopol besieged by contractors and claim agents.

Streets cut into scalene triangles vex strangers, who must learn to avoid the hypotenuse of street triangulation. Other pieces include a study of Caspar Hauser, the mysterious youth who knew only man and beast, bua and ross, and who sensed animals and metals strangely. The issue, published as secession began, shows the Atlantic at a moment of national crisis, witty, learned, and alarmed.
11157-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1861 opens with Trees in Assemblages, an essay on how trees please us in groups rather than alone. A solitary fir by a roadside is stiff and disagreeable, but a deep forest of firs rivals any species in grandeur, while elm and oak are grand standing alone. The Romans used silva for timber wood, saltus for wild mountain wood, nemus for a grove, and lucus for a sacred wood.

English makes these distinctions only with adjectives: forest, grove, copse, and thicket. An unbroken forest, the writer warns, makes a dreary picture and an unattractive trip through gloomy uniformity. Another piece mocks affected language, calling mine affections, wife mine, and sylvan grove Veal. The issue shows the Atlantic's range, from natural history to the policing of good English.
11158-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1862 opens with Wild Apples, a history of the apple-tree. The geologist tells us the rose order, true grasses, and mints appeared only shortly before man, and apples fed an unknown primitive people whose traces lie at the bottom of Swiss lakes. Tacitus says ancient Germans satisfied hunger with wild apples.

Niebuhr notes that Latin and Greek agree in words for house, field, plough, wine, oil, milk, sheep, and apples, while war words differ utterly. Goddesses contended for it, dragons watched it, heroes plucked it, and Solomon sang of the apple-tree among the trees of the wood. Later pages follow Tom, a deaf musical boy whose soul witnesses faithfully to music's meaning.
11173-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for January 1860 opens with Our Artists in Italy, on the sculptor Hiram Powers. Antique art, the writer argues, tests the genuineness of the art-impulse: even to genius, a true art-life is difficult, full of surprises at new necessities, like a commander bearing sealed instructions. Thorwaldsen waited wandering by the Tiber a thousand days, then in one day uttered his immortal Night.

The artist's first duty is possession of himself in the highest, making his habitual consciousness from the noblest revealed to it. Later pages take readers through a Roman church door, past hawkers crying coloured portraits, medals, and wax children for one baiocco, into incense and crowds of priests, beggars, soldiers, and villagers. The issue joins art theory with vivid Italian travel writing.
11298-wanderings-by-southern-waters-east:
Edward Harrison Barker's 1893 travel book, Wanderings by Southern Waters: Eastern Aquitaine, follows rivers and valleys in southwest France, from Martel in Guyenne south to the Dordogne. Chapters cover the valley of the Ouysse and Roc-Amadour, the Alzou to the Dordogne, underground wayfaring in the Célé valley. the Albigensian country, the Rouergue, the black Causse, the cañon of the Tarn, and the valley of the Lot. Illustrations include the Pont Valentré at Cahors.

Barker, author of Wayfaring in France, walks slowly, noting fruit valleys, nightingales, tiled roofs, and old towns like Figeac. His prose favors landscape and history over practical guidance. The book suits armchair travelers and readers planning walks in the Dordogne and Lot country.
1133-cymbeline:
Imogen, daughter of King Cymbeline of Britain, defies her father to marry the poor but worthy Posthumus, who is banished to Rome. There a villain wagers that Imogen can be seduced, and the plot tangles with lost princes, a wicked queen, and a Roman invasion. William Shakespeare's late romance ends in a flood of reunions.

Imogen, disguised as a boy, survives dangers and a false report of death to reach her husband. The play mixes comedy, tragedy, and fairy tale, with a famous sleep scene in the wilds. Its warmth and its twists make it a favorite of those who love Shakespeare's late, forgiving mood.
11358-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1861 opens Near Oxford, an excursion narrative in which a party rides a four-horse carriage with postilions in scarlet jackets toward Blenheim. The narrator notes Oxfordshire's level country, a gabled house at a turnpike gate, and Woodstock's Black Bear inn, ancient and respectable, with balustraded staircases and queer old pictures. The day is perfect English weather, warm with a spice of austerity.

The piece is travel writing as leisure, published while the Civil War raged at home, and it shows the Atlantic's range beyond American politics. Its pleasures are observational: horses, inns, and landscape. Readers interested in Victorian travel prose will enjoy its unhurried, companionable tone.
11624-the-reflections-of-ambrosine:
Elinor Glyn's novel opens with Ambrosine wondering whether blue blood brings disadvantages, such as pretending to like well-aired rooms without fires in December. Her grandmother says economies must be accepted with calmness, and rebellion is worthwhile only if it improves matters.

Papa's tiresome speculation in South America has cut the family's means, and Ambrosine must learn to live with less. Later she turns from novels, which seem untrue and mawkish, to philosophy and to mystery stories that make her forget rain. The book is a society novel told in a young woman's sharp voice.
11801-u-s-copyright-renewals-1950-januar:
Renewal registrations for literature, art, and film in the first half of 1950 fill this catalogue with an alphabetical list under title. Cross references lead from every essential name and variant form to the main entry, and musical works are left out.

Entries give original and renewal dates with R numbers, as in Abbott's Digest of New York reports, renewed in April 1950, and Sinclair Lewis's Babbitt, cross-referenced in the same list. Claimant codes in parentheses name authors, widows, children, and publishers. The volume is a finding tool for copyright history, not a reading book, and it rewards a patient searcher.
11803-u-s-copyright-renewals-1951-januar:
For the first half of 1951, this renewal catalogue lists Class A works alphabetically under author, editor, compiler, or title. Joint authors and editors appear as references to main headings, and each entry states both original and renewal registration.

Austin Abbott's digest of New York reports, renewed in April 1951, opens the A sequence, followed by Achmed Abdullah, Phyllis Ackerman on wallpaper, and Aeschylus in Gilbert Murray's rhyming verse. Rudyard Kipling's Dundee address of 1923 appears renewed in January 1951. The list is a legal record, dense with names, dates, and R numbers, made for checking a single title at a time.
11805-u-s-copyright-renewals-1952-januar:
January to June 1952 brings another Class A renewal list, arranged under main headings with cross references from joint authors and variant names. Original and renewal facts sit together in every entry, so a reader can trace a work from first registration to its renewal.

Austin Abbott's brief for criminal cases, third edition by James J. Barbour, renewed in June 1952, and his digest of New York reports, renewed in April, head the list. George M. L. La Branche's salmon and dry fly, renewed in June, shows the range beyond law books. The volume is a working index for publishers, libraries, and heirs checking rights.
11807-u-s-copyright-renewals-1953-januar:
This 1953 renewal volume lists Class A works for January to June, alphabetical under author, editor, compiler, or title, with references from joint names and variants. Each entry carries original copyright and renewal registration together.

George William Russell, under his pseudonym A. E., and Pierre Abailard's letters of Abelard and Heloise, translated by C. K. Scott Moncrieff, appear early, with renewals in May 1953. Charles G. Abbot on the earth and stars follows. The catalogue runs through the alphabet in the same steady pattern, a reference shelf for rights holders rather than a book to read straight through.
11809-u-s-copyright-renewals-1954-januar:
For January to June 1954, the renewal list covers books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions, arranged under author, issuing body, or title. Cross references from claimants, joint authors, and variant forms are interfiled, so a search under any name leads to the main entry.

Austin Abbott's digest of New York reports for 1925, renewed in April 1954, opens the sequence, with Lawrence F. Abbott's Twelve Great Modernists renewed the same month. Achmed Abdullah's Ruth's Rebellion follows in March. The volume is a dense, alphabetical record of who renewed what, and when, in the first half of 1954.
11811-u-s-copyright-renewals-1955-januar:
January to June 1955 renewals are listed here under author, issuing body, or title, with cross references from claimants and joint authors interfiled. Books, pamphlets, serials, and contributions to periodicals all appear, each with original and renewal dates.

An orchestra folio from ABC Music Corporation and Austin Abbott's digest for 1926, renewed in April 1955, open the list. Louis Adamic on California facts follows. Midway through, translations appear, from Gide's Counterfeiters and Mann's Magic Mountain to Hamsun's Mysteries and Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights. The volume maps a half year of renewed rights.
11813-u-s-copyright-renewals-1956-januar:
This catalogue records renewal registrations for January to June 1956, arranged by author or issuing body, or by title for serials and compendia. Original and renewal information sit in each entry, with references from claimants and joint authors interfiled.

George Abbott and Anne Preston Bridgers's Coquette, renewed in May 1956, and Lucy Thurston Abbott's Rusty-cats, renewed in January, show the mix of plays and children's books. Abbott's Digest for 1927 to 1928 follows in April. Midway, Ring Lardner stories from Collier's appear, renewed by his widow. The list is a half-year snapshot of American publishing rights.
11815-u-s-copyright-renewals-1957-januar:
For the first half of 1957, renewal registrations are listed alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title for serials and certain works. Each entry gives both original and renewal registration, with references from claimants, joint authors, and variant names interfiled.

Kenyon Taylor Abbott's Thirteen, renewed in February 1957, and Wilbur C. Abbott's New York in the American Revolution, renewed the same month, open the A sequence. Stephen Leacock's Iron Man and Tin Woman, renewed in February, appears later. The volume is a reference list, best used to verify one work, one author, or one renewal date at a time.
11817-u-s-copyright-renewals-1958-januar:
January to June 1958 renewals fill this list, alphabetical under author or issuing body, or under title for serials and compendia. Original and renewal facts appear together, with references from claimants and joint authors interfiled throughout.

A cumulative index to the American Law Reports for 1929 to 1930, renewed in April 1958, opens the volume, followed by Elisabeth Abbott's French novel, renewed in June. Harold Lamb's work, renewed in April, and a guide to histology by Avery Lambert appear later. The catalogue is a legal and publishing reference, recording a half year of renewed copyrights in order.
11819-u-s-copyright-renewals-1959-januar:
This 1959 renewal list, for January to June, arranges books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions under author or issuing body, or under title. References from claimants, joint authors, and variant forms are interfiled, and each entry states original and renewal registration.

Jane Abbott's Silver Fountain, renewed in May 1959, and Abbott's New York Digest pocket parts for 1931, renewed in January and April, open the volume. Oliver LaFarge's Sparks Fly Upward, renewed in April, appears later. The catalogue is a half-year record of rights renewed, useful to libraries, publishers, and heirs tracing a title.
11821-u-s-copyright-renewals-1960-januar:
January to June 1960 renewals are recorded here under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and joint authors interfiled. Each entry gives original copyright and renewal registration, so a title can be traced across the renewal term.

Abbott's New York Digest pamphlets for 1932 and 1933, renewed in April and July 1960, open the list, with Elisabeth Abbott's translation of The King of Rome cross-referenced nearby. Later entries cover law reports, motor vehicle law, and pleading practice. The volume is a reference catalogue, not a narrative, and it serves rights research first.
11823-u-s-copyright-renewals-1961-januar:
This 1961 renewal list covers January to June, with a special case at the start. Austrian citizens whose works became eligible for renewal between March 1938 and July 1956 could register within a year. That rule came from the Austrian Copyright Extension Proclamation of June 1960.

Ordinary entries follow in alphabetical order after that note. Jane Abbott's Fiddler's Coin was renewed in June 1961. William H Leach's Cokesbury marriage manual was renewed in January. Stephen Leacock's Dickens life was renewed in January as well. His Lincoln Frees the Slaves was renewed in June. The volume is a rights record with a wartime footnote.
11825-u-s-copyright-renewals-1962-januar:
January to June 1962 renewals are listed alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and joint authors interfiled. Original and renewal registration appear in each entry, with R numbers for checking.

Abbott's New York Digest pamphlets for 1934 and 1935, renewed in January and April 1962, open the volume. Karl Adam's Son of God, in Philip Hereford's translation, follows. Later entries include Jonathan Latimer's Murder in the Madhouse, renewed in April, and Owen Lattimore's Mongols of Manchuria, renewed in February. The list is a half-year rights index.
11827-u-s-copyright-renewals-1963-januar:
This 1963 renewal volume, for January to June, lists books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Each entry states original and renewal registration.

Hans Aanrud's Sidsel Longskirt and Solve Suntrap, in translation by Dagny Mortenson and Margery Bianco, renewed in February 1963, opens the A sequence. Abbott and Walker advertising helps follow in March. Later, John Lair's barn dance songs from 100 WLS Barn Dance Favorites, renewed in January, show the musical side of the list. The catalogue is a rights tool.
11829-u-s-copyright-renewals-1964-januar:
January to June 1964 renewals are arranged alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Original and renewal dates appear in every entry, with R numbers.

John Abbe's Around the World in Eleven Years, renewed in March 1964, and Abbott's promotional advertising pamphlets, renewed in May, open the volume. Abbott's New York Digest cumulative pamphlets follow. Later, Dorothy H. Jenkins's Vines for Every Garden, renewed in February, and Rowland Johns's dog books, renewed the same month, show the list's everyday range. The volume is a rights index.
11831-u-s-copyright-renewals-1965-januar:
This 1965 renewal catalogue, for January to June, lists works alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Original and renewal registration appear together in each entry.

The A. L. A. Green Book, renewed in February 1965, and Arthur L. Abbott's National Electrical Code Handbook, fourth edition, renewed in January, open the list. Austin Abbott's Abbott on Facts, fifth edition, renewed in April, follows. Later pages run through long series of pamphlets and parts, each with its own R number. The volume is a dense rights record for a single half year.
11833-u-s-copyright-renewals-1966-januar:
January to June 1966 renewals are listed alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants, joint authors, and variant forms interfiled. Each entry gives original and renewal registration, with R numbers.

Michael Aaron's piano course book, cross-referenced to MacLachlan, and Austin Abbott's forms of pleading supplement, renewed in March 1966, open the volume. Daisy T. Abbott's Northern Garden Week by Week, renewed in April, follows. Later, E. C. Abbott's We Pointed Them North, renewed in April, and Polly Kempton's poetry of circumstance appear. The list is a half-year rights catalogue.
11835-u-s-copyright-renewals-1967-januar:
This 1967 renewal list, for January to June, arranges works alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Original and renewal facts appear in each entry.

Patience Abbe's No Place Like Home, by Patience, Richard, and John Abbe, renewed in April 1967, opens the sequence, with Berenice Abbott's Changing New York cross-referenced nearby. Daisy T. Abbott's Indoor Gardener, renewed in June, follows. Later, Osa Johnson's I Married Adventure and Jungle Friends, renewed in March, show the list's range from gardening to travel. The volume is a rights index.
11837-u-s-copyright-renewals-1968-januar:
January to June 1968 renewals are listed alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Original and renewal registration appear together, with R numbers for each work.

Lawrence Abbot's Approach to Music, renewed in May 1968, and Arthur L. Abbott's National Electrical Code Handbook, fifth edition, renewed in April, open the volume. Jane Abbott's Clo, illustrated by Herman Fay, follows. Later, Michael Innes, under his own name Stewart, and Engels and Marx from International Publishers appear. The catalogue is a half-year record of renewed rights.
11839-u-s-copyright-renewals-1969-januar:
This 1969 renewal catalogue, for January to June, lists works alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Original and renewal registration appear in each entry, with R numbers.

Kathryn Trimmer Abbey, cross-referenced to Hanna, and Abbott's New York Digest volumes 39 and 42, renewed in December 1968, open the list, with cumulative pamphlets following in January and April 1969. Later, Kirsopp Lake's Family 13, a study of the Ferrar group of Mark, renewed in March, shows the scholarly side. The volume is a rights record for a half year.
11841-u-s-copyright-renewals-1970-januar:
January to June 1970 renewals close this run of catalogues, listed alphabetically under author or issuing body, or under title, with references from claimants and variant forms interfiled. Original and renewal registration appear together, with R numbers.

Anthony Abbott's Shudders, a Thatcher Colt police mystery, renewed in February 1970, and Abbott's New York Digest cumulative pamphlets open the list. Rose Wilder Lane's Discovery of Freedom, renewed in January, and James W. Lane's Whistler, renewed the same month, appear later. The volume is a half-year rights index, ending a twenty-year run of renewal lists in this slice.
11843-u-s-copyright-renewals-1971-januar:
Issued by the United States Copyright Office, this half-year catalog records renewal registrations made from January through June 1971. Entries run alphabetically by author or issuing body, with cross-references from claimants, joint authors, and variant names interfiled throughout the list.

Most renewals concern works first registered in 1943 and 1944, from books and pamphlets to serials and magazine contributions. For each title the entry gives both the original registration and the renewal date, number. Claimant, making the volume a compact record of which mid-century works stayed under copyright protection. Early entries include Academy of Political Science proceedings and accordion methods, showing the catalog's range.
11845-u-s-copyright-renewals-1972-januar:
Covering renewals registered in the first half of 1972, this Copyright Office catalog lists books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions in alphabetical order by author or issuing body. Cross-references from renewal claimants, editors, and variant forms of names are woven into the main sequence.

The bulk of the entries renew works first copyrighted in 1944 and 1945. Each gives the original date and number beside the new renewal number and claimant. Researchers tracing a title's ownership, or checking whether a mid-1940s work remained protected, will find the essential facts stated in a single line per work.
11847-u-s-copyright-renewals-1973-januar:
Renewal registrations from January to June 1973 fill this Copyright Office volume, arranged alphabetically by author, issuing body, or title for serials. Each entry pairs an original registration from the mid-1940s with its renewal claim, and references from claimants and joint authors are interfiled.

The range runs wide, from piano courses and school texts to novels, legal digests, and magazine stories first published in 1945 and 1946. Because every line names the claimant and the renewal date, the catalog serves as a dated snapshot of who still held rights in those works nearly three decades after first publication.
11849-u-s-copyright-renewals-1974-januar:
Unlike its alphabetical predecessors, this 1974 Copyright Office volume arranges renewals by registration number, in continuous sequence across all classes of material. The shift means books, films, and periodical contributions sit side by side in number order, with breaks where other classes intervene.

Entries cover renewals filed in the first half of 1974, many for works first registered in 1945 and 1946. Comic-strip installments stand out in the run, with repeated Superman and Batman entries beside novels, textbooks. Songs, each line tying an original registration to its renewal claimant and date. Entries for comic strips, novels, textbooks, and songs sit side by side in that number order.
11851-u-s-copyright-renewals-1975-januar:
Opening with books and pamphlets, this 1975 Copyright Office catalog records renewals registered from January through June of that year. Entries are numbered in sequence and give the original copyright date and number, the renewal number, the claimant, and the renewal date for each work.

Most of the titles were first published in 1947, including novels, histories, textbooks, and magazine stories later issued in book form. Tarzan comic-strip installments, Loyola University Press ethics texts. Popular fiction all appear in the same run, showing how broad the renewal system reached in a single half-year.
11853-u-s-copyright-renewals-1976-januar:
This Copyright Office volume lists book and pamphlet renewals registered in the first half of 1976, again in registration-number order. Each entry states the work's original registration, usually from 1947 or 1948, and then the renewal claimant, date, and number.

The catalog moves from histories of medicine and New Yorker stories to school texts, hymn collections, and an Oxford companion to American literature. Cross-references to related renewal entries appear in parentheses, helping a reader follow a title that was renewed more than once or under more than one claimant. Among the magazine pieces renewed in this run are Christopher Cluett's Take a Letter columns in Collier's. William Thomas Walsh's Saint Peter, the Apostle is also renewed, each with its original and renewal dates.
11855-u-s-copyright-renewals-1977-januar:
Books and pamphlets renewed in the first half of 1977 make up this Copyright Office catalog, arranged by registration number with a handful of non-renewal entries noted. For every title the entry records the original copyright, the renewal claimant, and the renewal date.

Works first published in 1948 and 1949 dominate. They range from Winston Graham's novel Cordelia and Jean Stafford's New Yorker letter from Germany to chemistry workbooks, a Francis Bacon study, and syndicated King Features weeklies. Together they document the last years of the old twenty-eight-year renewal cycle for mid-century publishing.
11880-ronicky-doone:
Max Brand's 1921 western Ronicky Doone opens with its hero arriving in town as a solid, swiftly moving dust cloud, the wind keeping pace with his galloping horse. Only when he halts before the hotel and swings down does horse or rider become distinctly visible, and the animal is seen to be in need.

The first chapter, A Horse in Need, sets Brand's pattern: fast action, terse dialogue, and a hero judged by how he treats his mount. Later scenes turn on pride and love, as Ronicky tells Caroline Smith that Bill Gregg loves her as she loves him, and she protests that it is not true. The novel moves between gunplay and romance with the brisk confidence of a pulp western at its best.
11898-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-:
Volume 4 of Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, the second of two parts on France and the Netherlands, gathers travel writing by well-known authors, selected and edited with introductions. It belongs to a ten-volume series that moves from Great Britain and Ireland through Germany, Austria, and Switzerland to Italy and Greece.

Its pages linger on French coastal towns, where a dinner waits below while Madame Poulard shows visitors the view from the ramparts. On shattered ridges and rocky coasts described by earlier travellers. Read as a whole, the volume lets famous writers do the guiding, so France appears through many eyes rather than a single guidebook voice.
12099-memories-of-jane-cunningham-croly-:
Memories of Jane Cunningham Croly, known as Jenny June, edited by Caroline M. Morse and published in 1904, opens with a portrait and a facsimile signature reading, with sincere affection yours ever, J. C. Croly. The volume is affectionately dedicated by the Woman's Press Club of New York City to the General Federation of Women's Clubs in America.

Contents include Jenny June by Ethel Morse and a brother's memory, among other tributes to Croly, a pioneering woman journalist who founded the women's club movement's press networks. The memories together form a group portrait: colleagues, family, and clubwomen recalling a woman who made journalism a profession open to women.
12142-sterne:
H. D. Traill wrote this short life of Laurence Sterne in 1882, drawing on the brief memoir Sterne left for his daughter and on letters that run to his death in 1768. Sterne was a Yorkshire clergyman who became famous late, at forty-six, with the first volumes of Tristram Shandy.

Traill follows Sterne from Cambridge and parish work through sudden literary fame, travel in France and Italy, and the writing of A Sentimental Journey. He weighs the charges of borrowing and loose living against the warmth and wit readers loved. The book also explains why so little solid record survives: friends who might have written his life never did, leaving letters and anecdote to fill the gaps.
12257-the-go-getter-a-story-that-tells-y:
Peter B. Kyne published The Go-Getter as a business fable, dedicated to Brigadier-General Leroy S. Lyon, who practiced a religion of loyalty to country and appointed task. Kyne, a California writer, wrote the story for managers and salesmen.

The plot follows Cappy Ricks, a lumber and shipping magnate with more troubles than a hen with ducklings, and his young aide, who must carry out a seemingly impossible errand. A mid-book dispute turns on whether an appointment was temporary, and who must find a successor. Kyne moral is plain: take the task, do not make excuses, and deliver. The story became a byword in American business, quoted by bosses who wanted initiative without complaint.
12264-father-payne:
Arthur Christopher Benson published Father Payne in 1915, a book of talks and portraits centered on a fictional wise host. Benson, a Cambridge don and author of the words to Land of Hope and Glory, shapes the book as a series of short chapters on life.

Father Payne, Aveley, the society, and the system introduce a household where men gather to talk. Later chapters treat going to church, newspapers, hate, writing, marriage, loving God, friendship, beauty, war, cads and Pharisees, and fear. The tone is reflective and humane, with aphorism rather than argument. The book suits readers who like moral essays in story form, where character teaches more than doctrine.
12293-old-cookery-books-and-ancient-cuis:
W. Carew Hazlitt published Old Cookery Books and Ancient Cuisine in London in 1902, as part of the Book-Lover Library edited by Henry B. Wheatley. Hazlitt, a bibliographer and antiquary, surveys English cookery writing from medieval manuscripts to his own day.

The book describes early receipt books, their authors, and their dishes. A mid-book receipt calls for a quart of strong green tea poured into a skillet, mixed with egg yolks, white wine, nutmeg, and sugar, stirred over fire. Hazlitt treats cookbooks as history: what people ate reveals trade, manners, and wealth. The volume is a delight for book lovers and food historians, learned, anecdotal, and fond of old kitchens.
12307-giorgione:
Herbert Cook published this monograph on Giorgione in 1904, a second edition revised with a new appendix, first published in November 1900. Cook, a barrister and art historian, studies the Venetian painter born halfway between mountains and sea at Castelfranco.

Ruskin called him young George of Castelfranco, of the Brave Castle, Stout George, George of Georges. Cook weighs attributions, documents, and pictures, including the Madonna and Child with two saints at Castelfranco. A mid-book note admits that documents quoted by Venturi go back only to 1640, so identity from life cannot be proved. The book is a careful early study of a painter whose short life left few certain works.
12371-the-experiences-of-a-barrister-and:
Samuel Warren published The Experiences of a Barrister and Confessions of an Attorney in 1880, a book of legal stories drawn from circuit life. Warren, a Victorian lawyer and novelist, writes from the bar and the attorney office alike.

Contents include the March assize, the northern circuit, a contested marriage, mother and son, the writ of habeas corpus, Esther Mason, marriage settlements, and circumstantial evidence. Later tales cover accommodation bills, refugees, life policies, and bigamy or no bigamy. A mid-book scene has Eugenie denounced as an artful intrigante who entrapped Mr. Arthur Rushton. Warren stories mix law with melodrama, showing how cases turn on character as much as evidence.
12412-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-:
The January 1863 Atlantic Monthly, volume eleven, number sixty-three, opens with Happiest Days, a nostalgic essay on childhood visits. The writer asks whether readers were never interrupted in play to have faces washed, hair combed, and soiled aprons exchanged for clean ones before meeting a mother early friend.

Other pieces in the number address the Civil War and Anglo-French tension, with a reported remark of Louis Napoleon asking why the English try to provoke war with him. The mix of memory and politics is typical of the Atlantic in wartime. The issue shows a literary magazine balancing private feeling with public crisis, as the war entered its third year.
1261-betty-zane:
Zane Grey tells of Betty Zane, a young woman at Fort Henry on the Ohio frontier, who, during an Indian siege, runs through enemy fire to fetch gunpowder from a cabin store. The tale follows her courage, her love for a young officer, and the fort's fight for life.

Grey draws on the true story of his own ancestor, and the novel mixes siege action with frontier romance. The book, one of his earliest, shows his gift for stirring tales. It suits readers who like American frontier history told as adventure.
12683-christine:
Alice Cholmondeley's 1917 book prints the letters of her daughter Christine, a young Englishwoman studying music in Germany just before the First World War. Christine arrived eager to like Germans and German life, and wrote home with warmth about teachers, friends, and daily scenes. Her mother's preface frames the letters after Christine's death in Stuttgart in August 1914.

As the months pass, the letters grow sharper about German pride, militarism, and public temper, and the mother argues they show the mood that led to war. Read today, the book is both a family memorial and a wartime document. Its power lies in one bright, frank voice changing its mind.
12811-the-human-machine:
Arnold Bennett's Human Machine, first published in 1908, treats the mind as a machine we mostly neglect. Chapters on habit, concentration, daily friction, overwork, and interest argue that we take ourselves for granted and then blame fate for the breakdown. Bennett opens with men who love a machine more than a woman, and calls them blessed.

His counsel is practical: use the machine well, or it will use you badly, as when we curse a shower instead of putting up an umbrella. Reason, habit, and a steady interest in life form his cure. The book reads as a brisk early self-help classic from a novelist who knew work.
1308-a-florentine-tragedy-la-sainte-cour:
Oscar Wilde's unfinished play A Florentine Tragedy tells of a merchant who returns home to find his wife with a prince, and of the duel of words and swords that follows. Beside it stands La Sainte Courtisane, a fragment in which a courtesan seeks a holy man in the desert.

Both pieces show Wilde's late style: rich verse, paradox, and a taste for sin and sanctity side by side. The volume gathers what he left undone, with notes on their state. It draws readers who want Wilde's last dramatic experiments, brilliant even unfinished.
13152-the-firm-of-girdlestone:
Arthur Conan Doyle's early novel The Firm of Girdlestone, dedicated to Professor William K. Burton of Tokyo, follows a London trading house built on African trade. Its chapters run from John Harston's appointment to a corner in diamonds, a land of diamonds, and news from the Urals. The firm, rich in ivory, skins, and strange goods, hides a darker trade beneath respect.

After her father's death, Kate Harston is taken from Fulham to live in Girdlestone's great house, free to roam from garret to cellar and garden. Sailors such as Captain Miggs of the Black Eagle, glass in hand, mix with clerks and schemers in the firm's orbit. Doyle's tale is a melodrama of greed, diamonds, and murder, written before Sherlock Holmes made his name.
13161-sane-sex-life-and-sane-sex-living-:
H. W. Long, a doctor, published Sane Sex Life and Sane Sex Living in 1919 as a frank guide for married readers, under medical direction. Long dedicates it to fellow doctors and to all who read it under their care, and he insists it be read from start to finish without skipping. His aim is to replace ignorance and shame with plain anatomy and moral counsel.

Long explains the prostate gland, its fluid, and its role as a carrying medium for sperm, in careful, clinical terms. He then argues that married couples may choose the number of children by will, not blind instinct, and that such choice is reasonable. The book is a period piece of sex education, earnest, clinical, and shaped by the eugenics publishing of its day.
13260-droll-stories-complete-collected-f:
Honoré de Balzac's Droll Stories, collected from the abbeys of Touraine, first appeared in March 1832 from Gosselin of Paris. A translator's preface defends the book as a work of art in the highest sense, likening Balzac to Boccaccio, Rabelais, and Ariosto. Balzac paints French life in the sixteenth century in the language of the merry vicar of Meudon.

Tales turn on wives, constables, and priests, with one constable striking a table and marching to attack Poissy, and another petition signed in 1271 on All Saints' Day. Master Tournebouche reads a charge, and all but Jehan Rabelais persist in their claims. The stories are bawdy, witty, and archaic in style, a deliberate throwback to Renaissance tale-telling.
13395-since-ce-zanne:
Clive Bell gathers essays on painting after Cézanne, written when the new French movement was still fresh and fiercely argued. He pairs theory with portraits of working artists: Cézanne himself, Renoir, Matisse, Picasso, Bonnard, Duncan Grant, Marquet, Othon Friesz, and Derain, with a chapter on Negro sculpture.

Bell keeps returning to one claim: form, order, and feeling matter more than story or likeness. He defends bold simplification and distortion, judges Marquet against Matisse, and takes up criticism, standards, art and politics, and the authority of the artist. The book reads as both a guide to modern painting and a defence of its hardest new ideas.
13530-halcyone:
Elinor Glyn's 1912 novel Halcyone takes its name from the fairy maiden, daughter of beach and wind, who loved sailor boy Ceyx. Married him, and, after his wreck, built a nest in halcyon days when no storms ruffle the summer sea. Glyn dedicates the book to Lord St. Helier, friend of her classical studies.

Mrs. Cricklander, facing scandal, finds Arabella Clinker, a plain, highly cultivated English gentlewoman of forty-two, once governess to a foreign royal family, now supporting an aged mother by lessons. Sir Benjamin, pressed tenderly by Mrs. Cricklander, assures her a patient will get quite well. Glyn mixes myth, society, and a heroine's search for a calm sea after wreck.
13756-story-of-chester-lawrence-being-th:
Nephi Anderson wrote this 1913 novel as a sequel to Piney Ridge Cottage. Chester Lawrence, who played a large part in that earlier story, now takes centre stage. The book follows his life, faith, and love in a Mormon community in Utah. Anderson presents it as the completed account of one man's course.

Chester faces illness, empty seats at breakfast, and the strain of communal life. Friends, family, and church duties shape his choices. Anderson writes with plain sympathy for Latter-day Saint belief and practice. Romance and moral testing carry the plot forward. The novel suits readers interested in Mormon fiction and early Utah life.
13783-the-boy-inventors-radio-telephone:
Richard Bonner wrote this boys' adventure novel around a new invention, the radio telephone. Jack and his friends help Professor Chadwick and young inventor Chester Chadwick test speech sent through the air. An airship trial forms the centrepiece: the first spoken words exchanged between airship and land. Rivalry, accidents, and mystery surround the tests.

Bonner explains wireless ideas in simple terms between thrills. The boys face a strange character, a missing professor, and a race to prove the device. Illustrations by Charles L. Wrenn add to the excitement. The book belongs to a series that mixed invention with adventure. Young readers get both a story and a glimpse of early radio.
13924-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for January 1862, volume nine, number fifty-one, shows a magazine at war. Contents list Agnes of Sorrento, Fremont's Hundred Days in Missouri, and essays on American civilisation. Autobiographical sketches of a strength-seeker and pieces on childhood sorrows appear. Health of girls and fruits of free labour follow.

A scientific piece discusses Linnæus and classification among naturalists, leading to clearer views of animal relations. The Atlantic mixed literature, art, and politics for a Northern readership. Its Civil War numbers shaped public debate. This issue captures Boston literary culture under strain. It rewards readers of nineteenth-century magazines.
1408-the-natural-history-of-selborne:
Gilbert White's classic, written as letters from his Hampshire village of Selborne, records birds, beasts, weather, and country life with patient care. Swallows and swifts, tortoises and field mice, rings of crops and quirks of soil all find a place, noted over years of walks and watchful mornings.

The letters mix observation with questions, and White is quick to admit what he does not know. His parish becomes a small world studied whole. The book helped found natural history in English, and it still charms readers who love a close, unhurried look at one patch of ground.
14393-the-inner-shrine:
Basil King wrote The Inner Shrine in 1909, a novel of today about love, pride, and hidden pasts. Diane, a French widow of charm and sorrow, stands at its center. A banker, a child named Dorothea, and a circle of guests move round her. The tale follows letters, cablegrams, and drawing room talk. King writes of society folk whose polished manners hide deep feeling.

A man hurries back from luncheon hoping for one last glimpse of Diane before her train. He finds her on foot in the sun, under a black parasol, since stable mishaps kept the horses in. Later her ways sink into Dorothea, who copies her French and Irish tones and gestures without knowing it. The father watches this copy grow and feels his patience wear thin. The novel turns on how one strong soul shapes a child and a household.
14405-patriarchal-palestine:
The Reverend A. H. Sayce, Oxford professor of Assyriology, wrote this study of Palestine in the age of the patriarchs, drawing on Egyptian monuments and cuneiform tablets as well as Genesis and Exodus. A map marks the chief places named in those books.

Sayce sets Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in a world of Egyptian pharaohs, Canaanite cities, and trading routes, and he discusses dynasties, conquests, and the coming of the Israelites. The scholarship is Victorian, and later finds have revised much of it, but the book shows how archaeology first began to test the biblical narrative against outside evidence.
14459-proportional-representation-applie:
T. R. Ashworth and H. P. C. Ashworth published this 1901 London treatise on how to make votes count fairly under party government. They argued that winner-take-all elections distort the people's will and entrench party machines.

The authors compare the Hare system, the free list, preferential voting, and the block vote, then apply their preferred reform to Australian legislatures. A final chapter links fair representation to social progress. The authors hoped fairer voting would calm party bitterness and widen public trust. The book is a clear Edwardian case for proportional voting, written before most democracies had tried it at scale.
14475-mary-erskine:
Mary Erskine, a Franconia story by the author of the Rollo books, appeared in 1850 from Harper and Brothers. It follows a young farm wife in rural New Hampshire after calamity strikes her household.

Mary faces debt, visitors, and hard choices about money and work, guided less by preaching than by sympathy and example, as the preface stresses. Albert, her husband, weighs an offer of credit and what it means for his standing. The tale is gentle moral fiction for young readers, teaching character through daily farm life rather than formal lessons.
14493-the-nursery-no-165-september-1880-:
The Nursery, a Boston monthly for youngest readers, reached number 165 in September 1880, priced at fifteen cents a copy. Its contents mix short tales, verses, and pictures for small children.

Items include a sketch of the painter Rosa Bonheur, Pip and Pop, a story of a dirty face, watering flowers, a child fascinating birds, and Daddy Frog. The tales are short, moral, and gentle, with birds returning to a kind girl through winter. The issue shows Victorian children's publishing at its most tender, made for reading aloud at bedtime. The Nursery ran for decades as a favorite of young families.
14907-living-alone:
Stella Benson's 1920 novel, first published in 1919, warns that it is not a real book, does not deal with real people and should not be read by real people. Written for the magically inclined minority, it claims a place among the many real books already written for real people, as a little alien trespasser.

Benson thanks editors of the Athenaeum and Pall Mall Gazette for reprinting a poem, Detachment, and early chapters. What follows is fantasy of a London woman living alone, with witches, lodgers and a world that slips between real and unreal. Benson writes with wit and strangeness, and the novel now reads as an early modernist fable about independence, solitude and magic.
14998-the-go-ahead-boys-and-simon-s-mine:
Ross Kay's Go Ahead Boys and Simon's Mine, illustrated by R. Emmett Owen and published by Barse and Hopkins, follows Davy Crockett's motto: be always sure you are right, then go ahead. Kay's series for young men includes Smugglers' Island, the Treasure Cave, the Mysterious Old House, the Island Camp and the Racing Motor Boat.

Simon's mine adds a new adventure to that list, with boys, a mine and the dangers that come with digging for wealth. Kay, author of Dodging the North Sea Mines and With Joffre on the Battle Line, writes brisk schoolboy adventure at seventy-five cents a volume. The book suits readers who like pluck, friendship and a mystery solved by going ahead, carefully.
15035-fishing-grounds-of-the-gulf-of-mai:
Walter H. Rich, agent of the United States Bureau of Fisheries, surveys fishing grounds of the Gulf of Maine, with tables and maps in the HTML version. Its opening asks what the Gulf of Maine is, geographically and historically, noting the earliest mention on old Icelandic charts.

Those charts show Cape Cod Bay roughly in southern areas and the Bay of Fundy in northern ones, giving the gulf its shape before modern surveys. Rich then describes grounds, depths, currents and catches ground by ground, for fishermen and students of marine life. The volume remains a standard reference for New England fisheries, precise about place and practical about fish.
15177-nocturne:
Frank Swinnerton's 1917 novel follows Jenny through one night in London, in three parts: evening, night, and morning. It opens at six o'clock by Westminster Bridge, where Jenny, on a tram from the Embankment, stares at Thames water glistening with reflected lights and feels a sudden, sinister terror. Uneventful life, not danger, threatens her.

Chapters trace a treat, rows, a wish, an adventure, a yacht, and consequences after the theatre, with a Cinderella turn near the end. Swinnerton writes in a realistic, psychological style, close to Jenny's inner life. Readers who like quiet, character-led novels will find Nocturne subtle, atmospheric, and humane.
15192-salomy-jane:
Bret Harte's Salomy Jane, in book form in 1910, opens with a single shot gone wide of a vigilante ringleader. Red Pete, his hand cramped by hard riding, surrenders to his captors, while his fellow fugitive gives up the chase with relief. The vigilantes, hot for revenge, are content to take their men alive.

Salomy Jane herself, a California girl of spirit and charm, soon shapes the tale of kisses, escapes, and reflections that follow. Harte writes in his familiar Gold Rush style, with local color and dry humor. Fans of Western short novels will find the book brisk, romantic, and full of frontier feeling.
15251-the-biography-of-robert-murray-m-c:
Andrew Bonar's biography of Robert Murray McCheyne tells of the young minister of St. Peter's Church in Dundee, who died in 1843 at thirty. A publisher's preface calls the life deeply spiritual, used by God to challenge and bless hundreds of thousands. The book reprints memoirs from a larger work, without letters and sermons.

McCheyne's short ministry, marked by prayer, preaching, and pastoral care, made him a prince among men in Bonar's phrase. The biography became the standard life of its subject. Christian readers will find it inspiring, tender, and focused on a life given wholly to faith.
1538-cymbeline:
Cymbeline, king of Britain, banishes Posthumus, the poor gentleman who secretly wed his daughter Imogen, and the play follows Imogen's trials across Britain and Rome. A villain, Iachimo, wagers on her chastity, steals into her bedchamber, and lies to Posthumus, who orders her death in a jealous rage.

Disguised as a boy, Imogen wanders to Wales, where lost princes live in hiding, and the tangled plot resolves in a famous final scene of recognition. The play blends romance, history, and comedy. It is a late Shakespeare work of forgiveness, patience, and families restored.
1548-locrine:
The Lamentable Tragedy of Locrine, an anonymous Elizabethan play once linked to Shakespeare, tells of Locrine, eldest son of the legendary King Brutus. After Brutus divides Britain among his sons, Locrine must face the invading Huns, the death of his brother Albanact, and a war for the island's rule.

Through camps, courts, and battlefields, the play follows Locrine's victories and his fatal love for the Hun queen Estrild, which undoes his marriage and his reign. Its verse is rough and its action is bloody. The play is a curiosity of early English drama, valued for its place in the Shakespeare Apocrypha.
15485-catharine:
Nehemiah Adams wrote this memorial book in Boston in 1859, inscribed to the young ladies of his congregation, to friends of Catharine, and to every father with a daughter in heaven. It tells of a daughter of nineteen, led by the Saviour through long sickness and death, so that she and those who watched her could say they were more than conquerors. A Coleridge couplet heads the first chapter.

Five chapters carry the meditation: more than conqueror, fear of death eased, the search for the departed, the silence of the dead, and the redemption of the body. Adams writes to commend his child's faith to other hearts, not to indulge parental grief. The book is a Victorian work of consolation, earnest and scriptural, meant for bereaved families seeking hope beyond the grave.
155-the-moonstone:
A great yellow diamond, stolen from an Indian shrine, brings ruin to an English house. Wilkie Collins's Moonstone, told in eight narratives, opens with the storming of Seringapatam in 1799 and the gem's curse. Rachel Verinder receives the stone on her birthday, then it vanishes in the night.

Betteredge the steward, Sergeant Cuff, and lovers Franklin Blake and Rachel each tell part of the tale. Opium, a painted door, and a second theft twist the plot toward truth. Collins builds suspense from conflicting views rather than one voice. The novel founded the modern detective story.
15654-the-firing-line:
Robert W. Chambers, author of The Fighting Chance and The Younger Set, published this novel in New York in 1908, with D. Appleton and Company. It is dedicated to Margery Chambers, and a frontispiece shows a woman facing a man, white as death, looking at him blindly. Twenty-nine chapters carry military titles through a society novel's campaign of love and pride.

Chapters run from a skirmish, a landing, and an advance through reconnaissance, a flank movement, and an armistice to an invasion and terra incognita. Pathfinders, allied forces, silent partners, and strategy lead to fire, an ultimatum, echoes, and peril. The line of battle, a new enemy, reinforcements, and a roll call end in capitulation. Chambers uses war's language for courtship, where every move is a maneuver and surrender is the price of love.
15760-the-forest-of-swords-a-story-of-pa:
A war novel by Joseph A. Altsheler, author of the Texan and Civil War series, set in Paris and at the Marne. Altsheler writes for young readers who liked history with adventure. The Great War opens with Paris in alarm and armies marching. His heroes, an American youth and his French friend, are caught in the storm.

Paris streets, spies, and marching columns fill the early chapters, before the battle of the Marne decides France's fate. Swords, rifles, and aeroplanes share the field in Altsheler's telling. Friendship and courage carry the boys through danger. The novel works as rousing history: a famous battle seen through young eyes, with pace and patriotic fire.
15838-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1863, volume twelve, number seventy-two, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston. In the Civil War years the Atlantic mixed literature with politics for a Northern audience. Essays, tales, and poems shared pages with war reporting. This number opens with a literary study, not a battle piece.

Charles Lamb's uncollected writings take the lead in a second paper, recalling Mr. H. and Godwin's Antonio at Drury Lane. Elia's life and letters frame the discussion. Other contributions treat art, letters, and the war's moral questions. The issue gives a fine sense of wartime reading: even amid crisis, readers sought essays, history, and good prose.
15972-the-record-of-a-regiment-of-the-li:
A regimental history by Colonel M. Jacson, of the First Battalion Devonshire Regiment during the Boer War, 1899 to 1902. Hutchinson and Company issued it in London in 1908. A frontispiece shows the monument to officers and men of the regiment who fell on January 6th on Wagon Hill, during the siege of Ladysmith. Jacson writes as a soldier-historian.

Chapters follow events leading to the siege of Ladysmith, the siege itself, and the advance north under Sir Redvers Buller. Lydenburg and trekking in the north-east Transvaal close the campaign. Maps and pictures join the narrative. The record stands as a battalion's own history: hard marching, hard fighting, and comrades remembered by name.
16001-willy-reilly-the-works-of-william-:
William Carleton's Irish novel opens with Willy Reilly, a humble Catholic man, bringing an old Protestant squire safely home after rescuing him from danger. The squire, grateful and blunt, declares that a Catholic can still be a gentleman, a brave man, and a man of honor. Reilly answers with a smile, saying nothing in his faith makes a man dishonorable or cowardly.

From that meeting grows a story of gratitude, prejudice, and rank in rural Ireland, where religion could divide neighbor from neighbor. Carleton, himself Irish, writes with local knowledge and a storyteller's pace. The novel offers modern readers a vivid, old-style look at Irish life, pride, and the cost of bigotry.
16033-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-:
Ticknor and Fields issued this August 1863 number of The Atlantic Monthly, volume twelve, number seventy, in the middle of the Civil War. The magazine billed itself as a journal of literature, art, and politics, and its lead piece, An American in the House of Lords, follows an earlier sketch of the House of Commons. The writer guides readers into the Lords' hall at Westminster, praised as a fine specimen of Gothic civil building.

Other pages would have mixed essays, stories, and poems in the Atlantic's high, serious style. This number shows American readers looking abroad even while war raged at home, studying British government with a curious, critical eye. It remains a fine sample of the magazine that shaped American letters.
16039-the-lost-lady-of-lone:
A novel by Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth, author of The Hidden Hand and Nearest and Dearest, issued in 1876. A publishers' notice calls it different from any of Southworth's other novels. Its plot, unusually provocative of conjecture and interest, rests on thrilling and tragic events in the domestic history of a distinguished Highland family of Scotland.

Southworth's skill in character and plot finds full scope in the tragic annals. Love, rank, and hidden wrongs drive the tale through Highland scenes. Her prose stays swift and feeling, never letting the reader rest. The novel charms as high melodrama: a lost lady, a proud family, and a fate woven from old sins.
16057-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
Ticknor and Fields issued this August 1864 Atlantic Monthly, volume fourteen, number eighty-two, while the Civil War entered its fourth year. Its lead essay defends Charles Reade as a great novelist, not merely a clever one, refusing to rank him between Trollope and Collins on gossip and tangled plots. The writer argues that only a full survey of Reade's books can show his true stature.

Other pages in the Atlantic manner would mix fiction, poetry, and political essays for a serious Northern readership. The number captures literary debate at a moment when American letters sought leaders to replace voices lost to the age. It remains a strong sample of the magazine's mid-war criticism.
16087-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
Volume fourteen, number eighty-four of The Atlantic Monthly, dated October 1864, leads with a Civil War sketch called A Night in the Water. Its narrator recalls picket duty in the delicious early summer of the South, among flowery forests on a blossoming island, galloping between outposts within a five-mile radius. Moonlit nights alternate with dense darkness, and a Rebel scout once fires at one of his officers.

The Atlantic's mix of literature, art, and politics gave Northern readers war reporting in literary dress, alongside essays, stories, and poems. This number captures the strange beauty and sudden danger of campaign life as a soldier remembered it. It remains a vivid primary source on the Civil War's Southern theater.
16119-doctrina-christiana-the-first-book:
Manila, 1593: the Doctrina Christiana is the first book printed in the Philippines, and this volume gives a facsimile of the copy in the Lessing J. Rosenwald Collection at the Library of Congress. Edwin Wolf 2nd supplies an introductory essay on the book's long, tangled hunt, traced from Manila to Berlin and from Italy to Chile through scraps in books and archives. Bibliographers pieced its story together clue by clue.

The facsimile itself lets readers see the early printed pages as they survive, with their Spanish and local-language text for teaching the faith. Wolf's essay reads like a detective story, full of false scents and careful guesses. The book matters to students of printing, missions, and the early Philippines alike.
16200-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
Volume thirteen, number seventy-five of The Atlantic Monthly, published in Boston by Ticknor and Fields in January 1864, shows the magazine's Civil War range. Contents list Ambassadors in Bonds by Caroline Chesebro, Annesley Hall and Newstead Abbey, and The Beginning of the End. A piece on Bryant and California as a Vineland follow. Robert Dale Owen writes on the Convulsionists of St. Medard. Bayard Taylor cruises Lake Ladoga, and J. T. Trowbridge recalls a first visit to Washington.

Fouquet the Magnificent, Genius, a glacial period essay, and fast-day and fighting pieces fill out a rich number. The Atlantic mixed literature, science, and politics for serious Northern readers. This issue offers a vivid table of contents from the war's third winter.
16414-quincy-adams-sawyer-and-mason-s-co:
Charles Felton Pidgin paints New England home life in this 1905 novel, revised from an earlier edition. Quincy Adams Sawyer, plain Mister despite ancestors who were merchants, lawyers, and presidents, aims to live up to a high standard of gentlemanly conduct. Village gossips wonder who he is, what he came for, and how long he means to stay.

Pidgin dedicates the book to James Russell Lowell, whose poem The Courtin' inspired it. The tone is warm and humorous, with country characters and courtship at the center. Readers of regional fiction will enjoy a gentle, good-natured portrait of a New England town.
16522-the-nursery-no-106-october-1875-vo:
This October 1875 number of The Nursery, published in Boston by John L. Shorey, offers youngest readers a fresh batch of stories and verses. The Delights of the Seaside opens the contents. Mabel and her friend Carlo, Playing King, a true antelope story, The Apple Tree, a council of horses, and a visit to the lighthouse follow. Roly-Poly, Elsie's ducks, and fishing for trout follow.

The pieces are short, gentle, and made for reading aloud, at a dollar sixty a year. As with its November sister number, the issue shows Victorian nursery reading at its sweetest. Collectors and parents will enjoy its simple tales of animals, seaside days, and small adventures.
16539-hero-tales-and-legends-of-the-rhin:
Lewis Spence retells the hero tales and legends of the Rhine in this 1915 volume from Harrap. Chapters run from topography and history through the Rhine in folklore and literature to Cleves, Aix-la-Chapelle, Drachenfels, Falkenburg, Worms and the Nibelungenlied, and Heidelberg to Sackingen. The opening weighs the Rhine against Nile, Ganges, Tiber, and Jordan.

Spence writes as a folklorist with a storyteller's warmth, setting each legend by its castle and town. The book suits travelers and myth lovers alike. Readers who know the Rhine's castles will find their tales told with learning and color.
1683-honorine:
A statesman named Count Octave has not seen his wife in years. The secretary who serves him slowly learns where Honorine went and why she never came back. The count's household, his committees of state, and his quiet grief all frame a mystery that is domestic rather than criminal.

What the secretary finds is a woman who chose exile over a marriage that had become a cage, and a husband who must weigh pride against forgiveness. Balzac keeps the focus on motive and manners, and the novella's force lies in its restraint: a whole marriage examined through letters, silences, and one long-delayed meeting.
17260-tempest-and-sunshine:
Mary J. Holmes's Tempest and Sunshine, in its 1909 reprint, opens on a bright October afternoon in a small Kentucky town. The Lexington and Frankfort stage rattles up to The Eagle hotel at four o'clock, where the landlord eyes newcomers for beefsteaks, coffee, sweet potatoes, and corn cakes. Aunt Esther rules the kitchen, cuffs and all, while children scramble for hoe cake.

From that stage arrival grows a long domestic novel of the kind Holmes made famous: home, love, and trial in plain, warm prose. Fans of old sentimental fiction will enjoy a gentle, colorful tale of Kentucky life. It is a classic of its genre, best read at leisure, chapter by chapter.
17367-first-book-in-physiology-and-hygie:
J. H. Kellogg's First Book in Physiology and Hygiene, in its revised 1887 edition, teaches children the laws of healthful living. Its aims are plain: stress stimulants and narcotics as new laws demand, give simple facts of body structure and function, and use clear language a pupil can grasp with little aid. Things come before names, in natural order, with pictures including the circulation.

Kellogg, a doctor of wide society memberships, writes for school use, with lessons a teacher can follow step by step. The book suits historians of health education and readers curious about Victorian school hygiene. Its mix of anatomy, temperance, and plain counsel shows a century-old classroom at work.
1737-facino-cane:
A narrator who once lived in the Rue de Lesdiguières meets an old blind musician at a wedding party. The man tells him a story that may or may not be true. The man calls himself Père Canet, but he claims a grander past: a Venetian noble who might have been a doge, robbed of name and fortune.

Facino Cane's story unfolds as a confession, told in fragments between tunes. Balzac lets the reader judge how much of it is truth and how much is the pride of a ruined man. The tale is brief and strange, and its power lies in the gap between the shabby old man in the room and the splendid life he says he lost.
17536-the-nursery-no-169-january-1881-vo:
The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers, issued this number in Boston in January 1881, as number 169 of volume twenty-nine. The Nursery Publishing Company, of 36 Bromfield Street, Boston, charged a dollar and a half a year in advance, or fifteen cents for a single copy. The issue was entered as second-class matter at the Boston post office.

As a single monthly number, it offers short stories, verses, and pictures for very young children, in the gentle tone of its era. Two pages of the scanned copy were missing from the original booklet and are left out of the transcription. Readers get a glimpse of early children's magazines, and of what Boston editors thought suitable for little readers in 1881.
17547-the-navy-as-a-fighting-machine:
Bradley A. Fiske wrote this book on the navy as a fighting machine. He was a rear admiral in the United States Navy, former aid for operations of the fleet, and president of the United States Naval Institute. Fiske, also author of works on electricity and war, writes as a reforming officer with medals from the Naval Institute and the Franklin Institute.

Part one covers general considerations: war and the nations, naval ABC, naval power, naval preparedness, naval defence, and naval policy. Readers get an American admiral's argument for a ready, modern navy, written before the Great War tested it. The book suits readers of naval history and of American defence thought.
17745-the-courage-of-marge-o-doone:
James Oliver Curwood wrote this northern romance in 1918, first run under the title The Girl Beyond the Trail. The tale opens at midnight in a bleak spruce wood, where a train glows like a thing of fire in the deep December cold.

Marge O'Doone, slender and wild as a cameo against the snow, faces hard men, cold, and danger with a brave heart. Curwood, famed for his tales of the far north, fills the book with storm, gorge, and chase. Readers who like bold, outdoor romance will find Marge a plucky heroine and the north a grand, harsh stage.
17765-gordon-craig-soldier-of-fortune:
Randall Parrish, author of My Lady of the North and When Wilderness Was King, wrote this soldier-of-fortune novel, published by A. L. Burt Company with four colour pictures by Alonzo Kimball. A frontispiece shows the hero clasping a straying hand and drawing its owner to him. Chapters open with the first step and the case of Philip Henley, followed by accepting an offer and an escape from arrest.

Beginning acquaintance, open confidences, and the woman's story follow, with facing the problem and completing arrangements ahead. Readers get a popular adventure of love, danger, and daring, in Parrish's sturdy style. The book suits readers of early twentieth-century romance and adventure.
17881-from-the-bottom-up-the-life-story-:
Alexander Irvine told his own life story in this 1910 book, issued in New York by the house of Doubleday, Page. Born poor in Ireland, he went to sea, served with the Gordon relief force, crossed to America, and at last worked among the poor of New York's Bowery.

Chapters move from boyhood in Ireland to school, ship life, and the hard streets where he preached and fed drifters, tramps, and waifs. Irvine writes with warmth and plain speech, and he never hides the low points of his climb. The book still charms as a tale of grit, faith, and a man who rose from the bottom and then turned to lift others.
1816-tattine:
Ruth Ogden, writing as Mrs. Charles W. Ide, tells of Tattine, a small child learning the world one trouble at a time. The chapters are numbered as troubles. Whether you are four or five or six or seven, Ogden says, a great many things need to be learned, everything in fact, never more than when you are small.

Tattine's lessons come through play, with Rudolph directing her to break off a piece and put it on paper near the fire. The small disasters of a child's day are treated as seriously as they feel. The book is a gentle period piece for young readers, and its charm is its respect for a child's point of view.
1826-sarrasine:
A narrator lost in reverie at a Paris ball hears the story of Sarrasine, a sculptor whose passion for a beautiful singer ends in ruin. The singer's secret — a voice from a throat almost dry, a cry like a rattle followed by a child's cough — is the tale's famous turn.

Balzac dedicates the story to Charles Bernard du Grail, and its frame lets the horror unfold slowly, through gossip and memory. The novella is one of Balzac's most discussed, because it asks what desire sees and what it refuses to see. Because its ending reorders everything the reader thought the romance had been.
18576-the-cave-boy-of-the-age-of-stone:
Margaret A. McIntyre wrote this children's story of the Stone Age, published by D. Appleton in New York in 1907 and dedicated to her mother. The frontispiece shows the making of stone tools, and the book teaches early human life through a boy's adventures.

Chapters follow Strongarm's family, the needle, the club, and the bow, the taming of the dog, and hunts for bear and lion. Later chapters bring the coming of fire, the cave tiger, the making of stone weapons, and Thorn's meetings with the shell-mound people, closing with a feast of mammoth's meat.
18730-lore-of-proserpine:
Maurice Hewlett published this book at New York in 1913 with Scribner's, dedicating it to Despoina. Its pieces bear titles such as The Windows, A Boy in the Wood, and Harkness's Fancy. Others are The Gods in the Schoolhouse, The Soul at the Window, The Secret Commonwealth, Beckwith's Case, The Fairy Wife, and Oreads. Hewlett opens by likening the soul to a house split into three flats, with a quiet landlord, a business man, and a night-walking stranger.

Fairy lore, second sight, and the border between seen and unseen run through the set. Hewlett writes in a rich, musing style, quoting Socrates on the soul's two horses before his own figure. The book suits readers who enjoy literary fantasy with a thoughtful edge.
18752-undine:
Mary MacGregor retold Friedrich de la Motte Fouque's Undine for children in this volume of the Told to the Children series, edited by Louey Chisholm, with pictures by Katharine Cameron.
