Undine is a water maiden, lovely as dawn on the waves, yet cold, since no soul looks out from her blue eyes. She comes to earth to seek the soul that would give her love, joy, and sorrow.

Chapters follow a fisherman and a knight, Undine lost and found, a wedding, a trip to Castle Ringstetten, a broken promise, and a burial. MacGregor keeps Fouque's wonder in simple words for young readers. The book is a gentle first telling of a classic fairy tale.
18886-franklin-kane:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick, Mrs. Basil de SélinCourt, wrote this novel, published by T. Nelson and Sons in London and Edinburgh. It opens in Paris, where Miss Althea Jakes, tired after a long journey from Basle, settles into a bright hotel sitting room of old-gold brocade, mirrors, and lace curtains. The title figure, Franklin Kane, stands at the center of the social world she enters.

Sedgwick follows her characters through Parisian drawing rooms, friendships, and the quiet judgments that shape lives. Her interest lies in manners, motive, and the cost of charm. Readers get an early twentieth-century novel of society, observant and well written, from a writer known for careful studies of Americans and English people abroad.
18930-history-of-the-missions-of-the-ame:
Rufus Anderson, late foreign secretary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, wrote this history of the Board's missions to the Oriental churches. Volume one appeared in Boston in 1872, from the Congregational Publishing Society. Anderson drew on forty-nine volumes of the Missionary Herald and as many annual reports, a mass of material no single volume could compress.

The preface warns that selections had to be made to do justice to each mission, and the narrative follows stations, workers, and churches across the Near East. Readers get a detailed institutional history from inside the missionary movement, valuable for its facts about schools, printing, and congregations, and for its view of American Protestant outreach in the nineteenth century.
18981-dick-the-bank-boy-or-a-missing-for:
Frank V. Webster published this boys' book in 1911, with Cupples and Leon in New York. Its hero, Dick, works in a bank, and the title points to a missing fortune at the heart of the plot. Webster, author of many boys' series books, wrote for readers who liked work, pluck, and honest dealing rewarded. The volume is illustrated, as his books usually were.

The story follows Dick through questions, suspicions, and the search for lost money, with the bank as both workplace and puzzle. Lessons about trust, care with other people's funds, and standing firm under pressure run through the adventure. Readers get a cheerful period boys' novel, typical of its series, and a window into how work and virtue were presented to young readers.
19103-the-discovery-of-a-world-in-the-mo:
John Wilkins, in this early English work on the Moon, asks whether another world can exist there. The text, in old spelling, reviews ancient writers on the antipodes, on lands under the Earth, and on whether men could live beyond our globe. Bede, Lucretius, and later scholars all get a hearing.

Wilkins weighs scripture, reason, and the new astronomy of his day, and answers objections one by one. His aim is to show that a lunar world is not absurd, even if travel there lies beyond human reach. Readers get a landmark of early science writing, curious, learned, and bold for its time.
19435-the-mule-bone:
Langston Hughes and Zora Hurston wrote this comedy of Black town life in three acts. Jim Weston, a guitarist, and Dave Carter, a dancer, are fast friends until both fall for Daisy Taylor, a domestic servant proud of her looks and her clothes. A fight with a mule bone sends the quarrel to the town's church court.

Mayor Joe Clark, two rival ministers, and a chorus of townsfolk turn the trial into a comic contest of pride, faith, and talk. The play's music, dialect, and humor preserve a world its authors knew well, and it stands as a rare joint work by two major writers.
19703-madame-delphine:
George W. Cable wrote about Creole New Orleans with unmatched local knowledge. Madame Delphine is one of his best-known stories of that city. Its opening shows a quarter sunk into long decay. Old commercial glory has shrunk into small shops. Bright market stalls stand out like patches of mould. Cable sets mood before he sets plot in motion.

Cable's New Orleans tales deal with caste, color, and old French families. Madame Delphine stands at the center of such a tale. Her story turns on sacrifice within a rigid social order. Cable wrote the city's speech and streets from life. His work helped define Southern local-color fiction. This short novel remains a fine place to meet it.
19779-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1867 is volume 20, number 118 of the magazine. One essay here treats grief with striking practicality. Grief, it says, must be fed with thought or starve to death. The best plan is keeping the mind busy with other work. The essay calls busyness a spiritual anesthetic for sorrow. Such counsel filled postwar American magazines.

The Civil War had ended two years before this issue. Its readers knew bereavement at national scale. The Atlantic mixed essays, fiction, and reviews for educated households. A single issue preserves the era's whole mental diet. Scholars read such numbers to hear 1867 thinking aloud. This one speaks in a Boston accent, thoughtful and composed.
19939-history-of-the-missions-of-the-ame:
This history covers missions of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Its ground is the Ottoman world: Armenians, Greeks, and the Turkish empire. In March 1846, Sir Stratford Canning reported from Constantinople. Thirty-six evangelical Armenians stood persecuted by their Patriarch, he wrote. Canning added personal efforts to soften their treatment. Diplomacy and missions intertwine through the narrative.

The American Board sent its first missionaries abroad in 1812. Its Near East missions built schools, presses, and colleges. Armenian converts stood at the center of this volume's story. Persecution reports shaped American sympathy and policy. The history is both record and advocacy. Scholars of missions still work through its documents.
19941-with-our-army-in-palestine:
John Morecroft wrote With Our Army in Palestine about the British campaign there. He corrects the home public's short version of that war. Most people think the Great Crusade began with taking Jerusalem, he says. They think it ended when the Turks surrendered in autumn 1918. That view is entirely erroneous, he insists. The campaign was longer, wider, and harder than the famous dates suggest.

Palestine saw fighting from Gaza to Damascus over two years. Allenby's army mixed British, Indian, Australian, and Arab forces. Morecroft marched with them as an official observer and writer. His book restores the campaign's full length. Desert, water, and distance are its real antagonists. It is solid campaign history from a participant.
1998-thus-spake-zarathustra-a-book-for-a:
Friedrich Nietzsche speaks through Zarathustra, a prophet who leaves his mountain home to teach a new way of living. In Thomas Common's translation, the book unfolds in discourses on virtue, war, friendship, marriage, and death. Nietzsche wrote Zarathustra in bursts between 1883 and 1885, as a poetic break from his earlier prose works.

Zarathustra urges readers to move past old idols and herd morals, and to shape values of their own. The prose is poetic and dense, full of images and paradox, and it rewards slow reading rather than a search for a simple system. Common's early English version helped carry the book to readers who knew Nietzsche only by reputation.
19996-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1865 is volume 16, number 96. The Civil War had ended six months before this issue. One article attacks a fashionable claim about American health. Physical decay, it is said, threatens the American people. Unwise stimulation of the brain gets the blame. A deficiency of physical health in America is assumed as an axiom. The writer questions that assumption sharply. Postwar nerves were a national topic that autumn.

The magazine now spoke for a victorious, grieving Union. Its pages balanced reconstruction politics with science and letters. Health anxiety ran through much postwar writing. This article shows the argument in its first form. A single number captures the culture re-sorting itself. Scholars still read these volumes as America's diary.
20071-sue-a-little-heroine:
L. T. Meade wrote Sue, A Little Heroine, one of her many books for young readers. Sue is a small girl with a freckled face and red-tinged hair. Her eyes are bright blue and keen, the book notes at once. She pushes through a crowd to hear a street preacher speak.

A rough man lays a hand on her shoulder in that crowd. From such small scenes, Meade builds a tale of a brave child. Sue faces hard city life with faith and pluck. Readers get a Victorian tale of poverty, courage, and a child's good heart under strain.
20263-boswell-s-correspondence-with-the-:
James Boswell's correspondence with Andrew Erskine appears here with notes by George Birkbeck Hill. Hill praises a young Scot who dared to tour Corsica's interior. No traveler from Britain had visited that interior before him. Turkish corsairs still swarmed the Mediterranean in that risky age.

Corsica itself sat in a very unsettled state at the time. Boswell's letters show his wit, ambition, and love of great men. Erskine, a poet and soldier, proved a bright partner in letters. Readers get lively eighteenth-century correspondence, richly framed by a top editor.
20340-a-little-maid-of-old-maine:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Little Maid of Old Maine, a tale of the Revolution. Two girls carry a big basket toward the Machias River in Maine. It is a pleasant May morning in 1775, full of pine scent. Freshly cut logs have been poled downriver to the big sawmills.

War news from Lexington has just reached the Maine coast that spring. Machias would soon fight one of the first naval battles of the war. Curtis sets her little maid amid lumber, ships, and patriots. Young readers get Maine's own Revolution story, told at a child's height.
20378-christmas-sunshine:
Christmas Sunshine is a seasonal gift book of verse and readings for the Christmas season. Its pages mix classic religious poetry with pieces on winter, snow, and the birth of Christ. The selection suits family reading by the fireside.

One passage praises winter as it hides the bare earth under innocent snow. It speaks of a saintly veil of maiden white thrown over the year's shame. Such lines show the book's mix of nature writing and devotion, and the warmth its makers hoped to bring into the home at Christmas.
20496-legends-of-the-rhine:
Legends of the Rhine brings the old tales of Germany's great river to English-speaking readers. Castles, knights, water spirits, and doomed lovers crowd its pages. The book mixes travel talk with the legends themselves, in the manner of a journey up the river.

One scene has a young woman smile at a compliment to her mother. The mother, it turns out, was English by birth. The traveler remarks that Germany is the land of romance for the English, just as Italy is for the Germans. The legends that follow show why the Rhine earned that name.
20513-how-to-succeed-or-stepping-stones-:
Orison Swett Marden's How to Succeed, published in 1896, is one of the founding books of the success movement. Its full title promises stepping stones to fame and fortune. Marden told young readers that will and character, not luck, make a life.

Do not look far for the successful man, he writes. This man is you, it is I, it is each one of us. How do we constitute ourselves men? Nothing is harder if we do not know how to will it, and nothing easier if we will it. Such bracing talk made Marden's books steady sellers.
20616-the-old-front-line:
John Masefield walked the Somme battlefield soon after the fighting and wrote The Old Front Line about what he found. Masefield had served in France and wrote with a poet's eye. The book describes the trenches, villages, and graves of the 1916 battle.

He looks ahead to peace. The ground full of death will grow food again, he writes, and this frontier of trouble will be forgotten. When the trenches are filled in and the plough has gone over them, the land will not long keep the look of war. The book became a classic of battlefield writing.
21027-the-trial-of-charles-random-de-ber:
False word of peace with France, spread to lift the funds, charges the Crown in this trial. Charles de Berenger, Lord Cochrane, and others stood accused of that fraud in 1814. The Trial records a plot to make the king and public believe peace was near.

Stock Exchange fraud, a fake colonel, and a staged ride from Dover fill the case. Cochrane, a sea hero, swore his innocence to his death's door. The verdict wrecked his career, though later ages cleared his name in part. Trial reports like this preserve court drama word for word, cross-talk, proof, and all.
21119-flaming-june:
A tidy elderly spinster in a seaside town keeps a large house. It has private access to a shared garden, and her settled life is upset by a visitor. Her brother, now rich in America, sends his daughter Cornelia to England as part of her education. Cornelia arrives with plenty of pocket money and American habits.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sets the girl among polished, well-bred people who expect chaperones and strict manners. Cornelia gads about with young men as she pleases, to her aunt's dismay. The aunt proves right in the end: among all the nice people hides one bad character, revealed only near the close.
21250-sir-walter-scott-a-lecture-at-the-:
William Paton Ker delivered this lecture on Sir Walter Scott at the Sorbonne on May 22, 1919, in the Louis Liard series. He takes his text from Scott's own account of seeing Ivanhoe turned into an opera at the Odéon in Paris. Scott, who dictated much of that novel in pain at Abbotsford, marvelled that it now amused a foreign crowd.

Ker contrasts Scott's regional Scotland, its dialect barely clear outside its own ground, with the Europe-wide market that fought for his novels. The lecture first appeared in the Anglo-French Review in August 1919. It is a short, warm weighing of Scott's European fame.
21273-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-2-no-1:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1858, volume two, number fourteen, opens with an essay on the ideal tendency in art. Its writer argues that art is the largest expression, pointing toward what cannot be measured or lodged in systems. Shakespeare, Plato, Michelangelo, Beethoven, and Goethe stand as its witnesses.

The young Atlantic, founded in Boston the year before, aimed to lead American letters, art, and politics in one magazine. A single monthly number like this one mixes essays, stories, poems, and reviews by the New England circle. Kept whole, it shows the magazine in its second year, when its table of contents was itself an argument about American culture.
21288-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1866, volume seventeen, number 101, leads with passages from Hawthorne's notebooks, published two years after his death. One entry describes a July 1837 drive near Augusta, Maine, to fish for white perch through a crooked, winding brook. The pilot talks politics and the bank between hearty tugs at a whiskey bottle.

Several dozen fish, yellow perch, a great chub, and horned pouts come home in an hour or two. Ticknor and Fields published the magazine in Boston as a monthly of literature, science, art, and politics. A single issue preserves its post-Civil War table, where Hawthorne's private journals shared space with the day's essays.
21325-outlines-of-greek-and-roman-medici:
James Sands Elliott was a New Zealand doctor and editor of the New Zealand Medical Journal. He wrote these outlines after a stay in southeastern Europe stirred his interest. Published in 1914, the book traces the main stages of healing in the Greek and Roman worlds. Those are the two empires to which modern civilisation owes most. Asklepios, the Greek god of healing, fronts it.

Elliott complains that the history of medicine is much neglected, even by doctors, so that many discoveries are only rediscoveries. He keeps the book a general outline rather than a full treatise, leaning on German historians like Baas and Sprengel. It serves as a short, readable first map of ancient medicine.
21408-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The April 1866 number of the Atlantic Monthly, volume seventeen, number one hundred and two, leads with the last days of Walter Savage Landor. Landor had died at Florence in September 1864, and many readers barely knew his name. The piece asks why so bright a writer was so little read.

The Atlantic was then a leading magazine of letters, science, art, and public life. Its pages mixed essays, reviews, poems, and tales for a broad, keen readership. This number preserves a slice of that world just after the Civil War. Emerson's own account of Landor, from English Traits, is quoted and weighed.
21572-percival-keene:
Percival Keene grows up near Southampton in Captain Marryat's novel of 1842, his nineteenth book. An old mansion house, known by its name for centuries, stands a few miles from the town. Sea service, in the channel frigate world of the day, shapes the hero's path.

Channel service, Marryat jokes, meant a captain with a seat in Parliament. His frigate rarely went to sea while the House was sitting, lest his vote be missed. Against that sly background, young Keene learns the navy as it truly was. Love, patronage, and action fill a tale told with Marryat's usual pace and humour.
21642-lady-cadogan-s-illustrated-games-o:
Lady Cadogan's Illustrated Games of Solitaire, in a new revised edition of 1914, adds American games. David McKay of Philadelphia issued the book, under the motto that patience conquers. A line from Othello asks how poor are they that have not patience.

Terms come first: foundation cards, suitable cards, and marriage, meaning a card placed on its neighbour in suit. Games run from Canfield, or Klondike, to Napoleon at St Helena and the Besieged City. La Belle Lucie, the Flower Garden, and the Sultan crowd the long contents list. Players get clear rules and pictures for dozens of single-player card games.
21716-the-battery-and-the-boiler-adventu:
A baby born at sea in a howling storm grows up to work with the newest wonder of his age in this Ballantyne tale. The boy's early squalls mark him, the ship's cook jokes, as one who will make his mark somehow. He finds his chance in the laying of submarine telegraph cables, the wires that first linked lands across the oceans.

Ballantyne studied cable laying firsthand, as he did for many of his books on trades and crafts. Storms, ships, sparks, and mishaps fill the story, mixing sea adventure with early electrical work. Readers get a lively look at the crews who strung the world's first ocean telegraph lines.
2198-stories-from-the-pentamerone:
Giambattista Basile's Pentamerone, retold here in English, is a treasury of old Neapolitan fairy tales told across five days. Kings and peasants, witches and beasts, clever girls and foolish princes crowd these stories, which fed later tale collections across Europe. The plots are bold, funny, and sometimes dark, with magic that rarely comes free.

These are not polished nursery tales but earthy folk stories full of appetite, trickery, and revenge. Readers meet early forms of tales they may know in softer versions, told with a storyteller's gusto. The collection is a delight for anyone who loves the roots of the fairy tale.
22058-cornelius-o-dowd-upon-men-and-wome:
Charles Lever, the Irish novelist, created Cornelius O'Dowd as a comic mask for his magazine essays. The pieces first ran in Blackwood's Magazine and were gathered in book form in 1864. O'Dowd introduces himself as a man who waited fourteen years at levees for government favour. No viceroy ever gave him a post, which leaves him free to talk.

From Italian battlefields to Dublin drawing rooms, O'Dowd comments on everything. Garibaldi's worshippers, Solferino, Italian law, and organ grinders all come under his eye. The humour is broad, Irish, and topical. Readers in the 1860s took these papers as light relief with a sting.
22090-the-task-of-social-hygiene:
Havelock Ellis, the English writer on sex and society, set out his programme in The Task of Social Hygiene. Ellis says social hygiene grows out of the older idea of social reform, but goes deeper. Reform treated bad conditions as they arose. Hygiene, as he defines it, aims at prevention: finding the source of social ills before they take hold.

Ellis discusses the family, birth, education, and the health of the race. Some of his views carry the stamp of his age's faith in eugenics, which readers now judge harshly. Others look ahead to public health and planned welfare. The book is a clear statement of how one Edwardian thinker hoped science would remake society.
22097-byeways-in-palestine:
James Finn served as British consul in Jerusalem through the middle of the nineteenth century. His Byeways in Palestine gathers journeys off the beaten road of the Holy Land. Finn admits he carried no fine instruments, only sometimes a common thermometer. He had no time for digging or surveying; his consular work came first.

What he offers instead is close knowledge of the country and its peoples. Fellahin villages, Bedouin camps, Samaritan and Jewish communities all appear. Finn notices crops, ruins, customs, and quarrels with a resident's eye. The book is a useful record of Ottoman Palestine before tourists and archaeologists remade the picture of it.
22245-steve-and-the-steam-engine:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote Steve and the Steam Engine in 1921, a boys' novel with a railroad heart. Steve begins the book in disgrace. While his parents were in New York and the chauffeur lay in hospital, he took the family's big six-cylinder car without permission. He carried a crowd of friends to a football game at Torrington, and that, the narrator warns, was not the worst of it.

To earn back trust, Steve is sent to work where steam engines rule. Bassett's Cape Cod tales usually smell of salt water; here coal smoke takes over. The book teaches railroad practice inside a story of a boy making good. It is wholesome series fiction of the post-war years.
22317-george-bowring-a-tale-of-cader-idr:
George Bowring is R. D. Blackmore's tale of Cader Idris, drawn from Slain by the Doones. Cader Idris is the great Welsh mountain of legend. The story, though, opens with school days and a sudden parting.

Within a week, George and the narrator were forced to leave their school. They left the grand old town and the lovely Severn too. All they kept was one another. That loss hangs over the tale from its first pages. Blackmore blends boyhood friendship with Welsh mountain country. Readers get a short, fond, sorrowful story from a writer best known for the wilder Doone country nearby.
22470-the-bell-tone:
Edmund H. Leftwich wrote The Bell Tone, a science fiction story of alien signals. Its narrator studies a wave used for sending thought images. The wave measures .00176 meter, he reports with care.

Pictures may be sent with a clacking code or independently. The narrator can conceive no finer communications system than this. He resolves that he must learn their secret methods fully. That hunger to decode drives the tale's investigation of contact. Thought pictures cross space by tone in his account. Readers get an inventor's-eye tale of first contact by signal. It prizes clever decoding over battles or chases in space.
22511-rollo-on-the-rhine:
Jacob Abbott wrote Rollo on the Rhine for his famous Rollo travel series. Rollo tours Europe with his family, learning geography as he goes. This volume follows the great Rhine river country of Germany.

Abbott first explains how mountain waters find the sea. Thousands of smaller torrents unite into larger and larger streams. At length they make four mighty rivers of Europe. Streams of the southern slopes form one great river, the Po. It flows east into the Adriatic Sea, he teaches. Such lessons precede the castles and towns of the Rhine itself. Young readers learned Europe's rivers through a boy's journey. Abbott's calm, instructive voice made the series a household standard.
2269-cymbeline:
Imogen, daughter of King Cymbeline, marries the commoner Posthumus against her father's will, and a wager on her chastity sets the plot spinning. Cymbeline mixes a Roman invasion of Britain, a wicked queen and her son Cloten, lost princes raised in a cave, and a headless corpse mistaken for a husband. Shakespeare piles romance on romance until a final scene of mass revelation sorts it all.

The play's famous bedroom scene, with Iachimo stealing from a sleeping Imogen, shows Shakespeare's late style at its most lyrical. Forgiveness and reunion win out over revenge. Readers who enjoy tangled romance will find this late play rich and strange.
22833-alcyone:
Vast, empty space opens Alcyone, a long poem named for a bright star. Its opening crosses a lifeless waste where night rules alone, vast and still. Nothing lives there now. Only the crumbled remains of ancient worlds lie scattered through the silence.

From that cosmic graveyard the poem ranges over time, death, and the fate of worlds. Its manner is grand and solemn, closer to meditation than to story. Readers should expect sweeping questions rather than characters. The verse belongs to a period when astronomy fed poetry, and new knowledge of deep space stirred awe as much as fear. Alcyone preserves that awe in period dress.
23005-eli-first-published-in-the-century:
A boat needs painting in Eli, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. A boy comes down to the shore, and his father rises, surveying the green bottom of the boat. Mother sent word that dinner is ready, the father guesses. He must eat fast, he says, and finish painting the boat's far side before the tide turns.

Tide rules everything in Chaplin's fishing world, even dinner. His Eli is built from such small, true pressures, work against water, hunger against duty. The dialect stays light on the page and exact to the ear. Stories like this one made his name in the great magazines. They preserve the speech and labor of the New England shore, net by net and coat of paint by coat.
23006-five-hundred-dollars-first-publish:
Captains swap a story in Five Hundred Dollars, Heman White Chaplin's tale first published in the Century Magazine. Captain Bennett opens the yarn by recalling David Prince's whaling voyage on the Viola. Captain Philo agrees that Prince's departure, at the time, looked suspiciously hurried. With most anyone else, he'd have thought something was up.

Whaling money and a hurried departure promise the rest. Chaplin lets two old sailors unfold the tale at harbor pace, hint by hint. Five hundred dollars, the title's sum, hangs over Prince's voyage from the first exchange. The frame is half the pleasure, gnarled narrators weighing a younger man's luck. It is a yarn in the true sense, spun dockside.
23007-the-village-convict-first-publishe:
Snow crunches at the store door in The Village Convict, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. Trade's looking up, William, Captain Seth tells the storekeeper, as someone kicks snow off his boots on the doorstep. Somebody's found he's got to have a shoestring before morning, he jokes.

Inside that warm store waits the village's judgment on a man marked by prison. Chaplin's convict returns to a place where everyone knows his record and measures his worth by his work. The story asks how much mercy a small town keeps in stock. Its setting does quiet argument, neighbors talking a man's fate over in the ordinary run of trade. Chaplin handles the question without preaching.
23040-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1866 argues about reunion. One essay imagines a statesman nearly despairing of the South after four years of war. Can anything good come from that quarter, he wonders. Yet a small, bright spot now shows at the Carolina cloud's very edge.

Hope and suspicion share this number, as they shared the country. Around the political essays sit poems, fiction, and reviews from the magazine's strong bench. The Atlantic stood at the center of American letters, and a monthly number shows its range in a single binding. August 1866 catches the nation mid-argument about what the war had settled. The spider's golden and silver silk of one image becomes, hopefully, a bond of union.
23108-chester-rand-or-the-new-path-to-fo:
Silas Tripp keeps the store in Chester Rand, or The New Path to Fortune. Silas Tripp may be Wyncombe's best-known citizen, the narrator figures. He runs the store in that Pennsylvania mountain village, lodges travelers in three spare rooms, serves as town treasurer, and fills other local offices besides.

Against Tripp's settled standing, young Chester Rand must find his path. Horatio Alger wrote this tale of a boy's rise, and its machinery is his, a good lad, a rich man to impress, luck that rewards virtue exactly on schedule. Store, town office, and mountain town fill the stage. Readers get the Alger formula in working order, cheerful, moral, and sure that fortune favors the deserving.
23137-diary-in-america-series-one:
Travelers contradict each other in Diary in America, series one. Talented travelers described the same nation in wildly clashing ways, the diarist marvels. Their harvests of fact, he adds, were generally meager for all their talent. The judgments pronounced on America, and pronounced so unjust by Americans, excited his curiosity.

Captain Frederick Marryat, the naval novelist, crossed the Atlantic to see for himself in the late 1830s. His diary records steamboats, prisons, elections, and manners with a sailor's bluntness. America fascinated and exasperated him by turns. Marryat's diary stands among the sharpest of the many British travel books on the young republic. Its author sized up a whole country with a naval officer's eye.
23246-mistress-anne:
Temple Bailey's Mistress Anne is a novel that opens in the afterglow of the holidays. The second day of the New Year fell on a Saturday, stretching the festive mood across the whole weekend. Wreaths from Christmas still hung in the windows. There had been an extra day of feasting, too.

Holidays always brought people in from town, Bailey notes, and they ate with sharp appetites. That warm, well-fed household sets the stage for Anne's story. Readers get a gentle period novel of home, guests, and manners, where small social moments carry the weight of the plot.
23292-ted-and-the-telephone:
Sara Ware Bassett's Ted and the Telephone, from 1922, is set in Freeman's Falls. Ted Turner lives in that sleepy New Hampshire town, beside a small river. Cotton mills stand in the town, and without them, Bassett notes, there would probably be no town at all.

The mills were not drawn to the town; the town arose because of the mills. That plain fact shapes Ted's world of work, family, and small-town ties. Readers get a novel of mill-town life in which a telephone, still a modern device, gives the story its title and its spark.
23368-the-courting-of-lady-jane:
Josephine Daskam set this domestic comedy in a house where a sister is packing to leave and her brother, a colonel, sulks at being left alone. Mrs. Dick counts boots, towels, sweaters, and a muff as she readies trunks, while her brother pleads, jokes, and mourns his lost comforts.

Into this stir comes the courting of the title: a suitor's slow, formal pursuit of Lady Jane, watched with keen interest by kin and friends. Daskam keeps the tone light, with naval talk, talk of Nagasaki, and the small wars of family life. The tale charms through its talk and its types, showing how a household bends, grumbles, and laughs around a love affair.
23455-plain-jane:
G. M. C. Fry and G. M. George made this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty seven in the series, about Plain Jane, a model miss. She breakfasts on milk and bread, calls it wholesome, keeps her bed and chamber neat, and counts saying her tasks to her mama a treat above all.

Prim and sedate, back straight and toes turned out, Jane walks rather than romps, and neighbours cry out at what a model miss she is. Trouble brews when her uncle, bound for a fortnight in Bagdad, hopes his sad, naughty daughter may stay with Jane, and mama fears bad tricks will rub off. The verse stays arch and funny, with pictures to match, poking gentle fun at priggish virtue while liking Jane all the same.
2374-dora-thorne:
Charlotte M. Braeme's Dora Thorne is a Victorian sensation novel in which a lord's daughter marries beneath her and faces disinheritance, separation, and a long road back. The plot piles on lost children, cruel relatives, and dramatic reunions, all delivered in Braeme's earnest, emotional style. Her books sold in enormous numbers to readers hungry for romance and tears.

The novel's appeal lies in its sincerity and its swift reversals. Modern readers will find its sentiment old-fashioned but its story hard to abandon. It offers a window into the popular fiction of its age.
23859-a-venetian-june:
Anna Fuller published A Venetian June in 1896, with sixteen color illustrations by Frederick S. Coburn. Its chapters are a June in Venice, told in scenes: a Venetian thoroughfare, a pair of Pollys, a reverie, the signora, and a festa. May watches a yacht until it disappears from sight on the frontispiece.

Later chapters gather poppies, feel the pulse of the sea, wander the by-ways of Venice, and end with a benediction and a visit to Torcello. Fuller, author of A Literary Courtship and Pratt Portraits, writes Venice as a place of light, water, and quiet feeling. It is a gentle travel romance for readers who love the city.
23955-chicken-little-jane:
Lily Munsell Ritchie published Chicken Little Jane in 1920, dedicating her first book to Olive F. Y. Dart, the kind friend who first encouraged her to write. Its heroine, Jane, moves through a childhood of small adventures, told in twenty chapters with pictures of water dripping from noses and chins.

Contents run from Alice and the Siege of Acre and the millinery store to the Duck Creek treasure and the back-yard furnace. A wedding, Christmas and the day after, skating, and a birthday follow, with forbidden books, candy hearts, and May baskets. Cousin May's party, exploring children, and things that happen lead at last off to the ranch. It is a warm, episodic girls' book of an American childhood.
24126-maw-s-vacation-the-story-of-a-huma:
Emerson Hough wrote this humorous story of a farm mother, published at Saint Paul in 1921 with pictures. Maw has spent her life working from sunup to sundown, cooking, sweeping, washing, and ironing, with no movies, no travel, and Sundays lost to the Sunday dinner. She notes how times have changed, with daylight saving on the clock and new ways all around.

At last Maw gets her vacation in Yellowstone, the famous park of geysers and wild land. Hough tells it in her own plain voice, full of dry comment on modern life and old work. Readers get a warm, funny tale of an ordinary woman seeing grand country for the first time.
24192-the-first-one:
Herbert D. Kastle wrote this science fiction story for Analog in July 1961, with pictures by von Dongen. A man comes back from beyond the Great Frontier and is welcomed — yet is he a marvel or a hero? A crowd gathers at the airport, now engulfed by the growing city, and the mayor's handshake is moist and cold, his eyes remote.

The mayor had seemed far more at ease at his last great welcome, for Corporal Berringer of the spaceship Washington, which carried the first Americans to Mars. This home-comer rides in triumph up Main Street to a grandstand, seated between the mayor and a nervous homecoming queen. Readers get a sharp tale of fame, unease, and a hero's chilly return.
24244-a-girl-of-the-commune:
G. A. Henty, author of In Freedom's Cause and With Lee in Virginia, wrote this adventure novel, published by R. F. Fenno and Company in New York in 1895. It opens in the cathedral town of Abchester, where Jeremiah Brander stands among the most prominent personages, dwelling in a red brick house of old fashion near the town's heart. Henty builds his tale, as always, from history and sturdy incident.

The Commune of the title gives the story its crisis, as a girl's fortunes cross the upheaval of the Commune itself. Henty writes for young readers who like their history with adventure in it. Readers get a brisk historical novel of a girl caught in a city's upheaval.
24331-an-old-sweetheart-of-mine:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote this poem, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company in Indianapolis, with drawings by Howard Chandler Christy and decorations by Virginia Keep. It is inscribed to George C. Hitt, whose steadfast friendship began with the first publication of these verses, now expanded by the writer, honored by the publisher, and graced by the artist. The poem moves between the then of changeless sunny days and the now of shower and shine.

Pictures trace the tale: old bookshelves and prints, a smiling old sweetheart, and a truant's fancies. Children's voices and a mother singing join memory's mellow wine, childhood days and spring. A first kiss follows, an apple slipped where the teacher did not know, a photograph marked Ever Thine, and at last a door softly opened, where his wife stands. Readers get Riley's tender poem of first love grown old.
24335-margaret-tudor-a-romance-of-old-st:
Annie T. Colcock wrote this historical romance, published by Frederick A. Stokes Company in New York in 1901, with pictures by W. B. Gilbert. Its note grounds the tale in the Shaftesbury Papers: the names of John Rivers, kinsman and agent of Lord Ashley, Dr. William Scrivener, and Margaret Tudor are listed among the Carolina's passengers. A brief account tells of the capture at Santa Catalina of Rivers, Captain Baulk, seamen, a woman, and a girl.

A memorial to the Spanish ambassador touches the delivery of the prisoners, one referred to as Margaret, likely Margaret Tudor. The story opens at San Augustin on June 29, 1670, more than a month into captivity, with scant likelihood of a speedy close. Readers get a romance of old St. Augustine, built on documents of capture and prison.
24431-peggy-alone:
Mary Agnes Byrne wrote this girls' story, published in 1909 with drawings by Anna B. Craig, under the title Peggy-Alone. Peggy, left much to herself, joins a lively circle of girls and fills her days with theatricals, picnics, tissue-paper hats, taffy pulling, berry picking, and a club the girls call the Happy-Go-Luckys.

Later chapters bring a garden party, a trip to China in a glass boat, a crimson bag, and a birthday for Mrs. Kump, as Peggy learns to rub along with friends, rivals, and grown-ups. The book is gentle, cheerful, and episodic, offering young readers a warm picture of girlhood friendship and small adventures in early twentieth-century America.
24651-old-times-at-otterbourne:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this memoir of Otterbourne, published at Winchester in 1891 in a second edition. She notes that few remember the village from before trains, a new church, or cheap postage changed it, and she tries to catch recollections before those who can tell them are gone.

Yonge traces what is known or guessed of the village, from a Roman road in Otterbourne Park and a quern stone found near it, to tithe disputes and parish life. Her account is gentle, detailed, and affectionate. Readers who love English village history will enjoy this small, personal chronicle of a Hampshire parish.
24692-a-bit-of-sunshine:
Published at New York in 1879 by Dodd, Mead, this illustrated story for beginners prints its words broken into syllables, so a child learning to read can sound them out. Little Kate stands at the door after rain, lets puss in, and begs to go out and play, since the clouds are gone and the sun shines warm.

Her mamma sends her to papa, who promises a drive in half an hour. Their drive takes them to the seaside, past a fishing village, a boy in a boat named Phillis, and a girl making lace at her door. The story is short, sunny, and simple, a perfect first reader for a young child.
24771-tutors-lane:
Wilmarth Lewis published Tutors' Lane in New York in 1922 with Alfred A. Knopf. The book is hard to pin down, and Lewis admits as much in his opening syllabus. A thin love story trickles through essays, talk, and scenes of literary life, but no grand plot ever arrives. Charades, dinner talk, and bookish jokes fill the pages instead.

Readers meet Tom and his circle as they argue about plays, fail at parlor games, and court in a mild, witty way. Lewis writes with light irony about writers and their fashions of the 1920s. The book suits readers who enjoy talk and tone more than action, and who like a novel that jokes about what novels usually do.
24818-sketches-of-travel-in-normandy-and:
Edward A. Freeman published these travel sketches in London in 1897, with drawings by his own hand and a preface by W. H. Hutton. The essays first ran in the Saturday Review and the Guardian between 1861 and 1892, and they follow Freeman through Normandy and the French province of Maine.

Stops include Caen, Falaise, Bayeux, Coutances, and the old Norman battle grounds, with long walks in the footsteps of the Conqueror. Freeman writes as a historian on foot, reading churches, castles, and town walls for their past. The book suits travelers and history lovers who like their guidebooks with deep roots.
24852-the-wonders-of-the-jungle-book-one:
Prince Sarath Ghosh wrote The Wonders of the Jungle, Book One, published by D. C. Heath in 1915 as a school reader. Its chapters follow jungle beasts at the midnight pool, where elephants drink first and buffaloes stand guard in rows. The law of the jungle gives clear water to all, while wild pigs stray careless and red dogs fear nobody.

Young readers learn how an elephant child bathes, swims, swats flies, and walks under water, and how buffaloes read danger three ways while they feed. Ghosh writes in short, direct chapters that suit a classroom. The book gives children a lively first look at Indian jungle life, with the elephant as its great hero.
25357-a-hundred-fables-of-la-fontaine:
A Hundred Fables of La Fontaine, illustrated by Percy J. Billinghurst and published by John Lane, presents the French fabulist in English verse. A second edition from the Bodley Head gathers favorites from La Fontaine's classic collection.

Animals teach the morals: an ass in a lion's skin, a cat and a fox, a cock and a fox, and a council of rats. A countryman warms a frozen serpent by his fire, only to be bitten for his charity and to answer with an axe. The sun and the frogs, the dog and his master's dinner, and the acorn and the pumpkin complete a witty, humane set.
25384-ben-s-nugget-or-a-boy-s-search-for:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s Ben's Nugget, copyrighted in 1882, closes his Pacific Series and follows Ben Stanton's search for fortune on the Pacific coast. Though complete in itself, it continues characters from The Young Explorer, including Ki Sing, the faithful Chinaman.

Ben, young for a miner, seeks gold in early California, where boys his age did drift to the diggings. Chapters visit a mountain cabin, a missing Chinaman, gentlemen of the road, and Golden Gulch, where landlord Jim Brown greets Bill Mosely and Tom Hadley. Alger warns readers not to follow Ben's example too eagerly.
25420-the-early-history-of-the-airplane:
The Early History of the Airplane, by Orville and Wilbur Wright, tells how two bicycle makers learned to fly. Issued by the Dayton-Wright Airplane Company, it opens in childhood, when their father tossed a toy helicoptere into the air late in 1878.

The toy, a cork and bamboo frame with paper screws driven by rubber bands, flew across the room and lodged in memory. Larger copies flew worse, teaching the brothers that doubling size demands eight times the power. The narrative follows their trials to the Kitty Hawk camp, where December winds, a short rail, and the Kill Devil Hill lifesavers shaped the attempts.
2544-from-sand-hill-to-pine:
Bret Harte gathers California and Sierra stories in this volume, beginning with a night stagecoach ride driven by the gruff Yuba Bill through rain and mountain roads. The tales that follow visit mining camps, redwood forests, and small towns where luck, love, and old scores settle accounts.

A niece of a notorious outlaw, a hidden treasure among the redwoods, and a belle of a raw new town each get their turn. Harte writes in dialect and in crisp narration, mixing comedy with sudden feeling. The book captures the West he knew best: rough, hopeful, and always ready for one more twist of fate.
25565-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Langdon Mitchell's play The New York Idea appears here with an introductory sketch of the playwright, born in Philadelphia in 1862. Its performance at the Lyric Theatre, New York, on 19 November 1906, struck the editor as a rare, distinguished event in American theatre.

Mitchell, the sketch argues, wrote a drama comparable with the best European models, scintillating with clear, cold brilliance and carried by dialogue of exceptional literary style. Its satire of New York social life aims beyond local manners, giving the play a universal import that should keep it alive in revival.
25953-kalevala-the-land-of-the-heroes-vo:
W. F. Kirby translates the Finnish epic Kalevala, the land of the heroes, in this Everyman's Library first volume, printed by Dent in 1907. Runos, or cantos, run from the birth of Väinämöinen and his sowing. His strife with Joukahainen, the fate of Aino, his fishing, his wound, the origin of iron, and the forging of the Sampo follow. Lemminkainen's tales fill the later runos.

Väinämöinen, old and steadfast, sets out to build a boat on a cloudy headland but finds no timber. Pellervoinen, earth begotten, goes seeking an oak for the minstrel's keel. Kirby's verse keeps the epic's plain, singing tread, and Eric Ravilious decorates the edition. The volume gives English readers the first half of Finland's great song of heroes, smiths, and spells.
26033-how-i-know-god-answers-prayer-the-:
Rosalind Goforth, missionary in China since 1888, tells how she knows God answers prayer in this 1921 book from Harper. Chapters run from getting things from God and early lessons in faith. Later chapters cover go forward on your knees, deliverance from the Boxers, the story of one furlough, and a God of the impossible. Early lessons include a bird's leading, toothache taken away, funds given, and scholars granted.

Goforth writes of China without sanitation, where smallpox, diphtheria, and scarlet fever raged as chronic plagues, and where four of her children died. Taking three little ones into such danger felt like stepping over a precipice in the dark, yet she knew the language, saw appalling need, and found no other woman for the work. The book is a plain, earnest testimony of a lifetime.
26047-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-15-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume fifteen, Boston, 1865, from Ticknor and Fields, gathers literature, art, and politics for a nation at war. Its contents list a Hawthorne dolliver romance, Stowe's chimney corner papers, Holmes as battle laureate, and pieces on Andersonville, Richard Cobden, and George Cruikshank in Mexico. Fitz Hugh Ludlow, Gail Hamilton, John Burroughs, and Bayard Taylor join the roll.

One passage voices anxiety for freed people after the war, fearing revolutions may run backward and old injustice may cling too deep for hope. The writer praises freed slaves' fitness for drill and discipline, now thoroughly shown, and dreads seeing their regiment disbanded. The volume gives a full shelf of Civil War era writing in one stout magazine year.
2611-confiscation-an-outline:
William Greenwood wrote this short outline making a case for confiscation as an instrument of reform. The argument turns on city life: business crowded onto one or two principal streets, property values warped by that crowding, and human beings packed into tenements for want of room.

Greenwood suggests that spreading business across more streets would raise the value of side streets, extend city limits, and open space for habitable homes. The essay is brief and programmatic, more a sketch of an idea than a full system. It now reads as a curious relic of reformist economics, plain in style and bold in claim.
26168-the-success-machine:
Henry Slesar's science-fiction story takes aim at office machines that judge workers without tact. At General Products, the Personnelovac spits out cards rating each employee, and Colihan's card is pink. It cites falling coordination, wasted motion spent on horseracing, and hostility to superiors, and it ends with one word: fire him.

Colihan counts twenty-four pink cards in a month, out of forty, and he knows something is wrong. A department meeting brings President Moss, pep talks, and talk of an honest man hunt like Diogenes with his lantern. The story turns its satire on bosses who trust a machine's verdict over human judgment, and on workers caught in its gears.
26235-the-mistress-of-shenstone:
Florence L. Barclay's 1910 novel opens on a dank November afternoon at Shenstone, where great bare trees spread over sodden grass. Contents list a terrace scene, a forerunner, what Peter knew, safe hands, and Lady Ingleby's rest-cure. Later chapters bring the Moorhead Inn, Mrs. O'Mara's letters, Horseshoe Cove, and Jim Airth to the rescue.

Further titles promise a voyage cry of yeo ho, we go, a morning star, golden days, and a question: where is Lady Ingleby? Michael Veritas, Lord Ingleby's wife, and Mrs. Dalmain's review of the situation deepen the plot. The novel treats marriage, duty, and second chances with Barclay's earnest, romantic warmth.
26381-uncle-sam-s-boys-as-lieutenants-or:
H. Irving Hancock's 1919 boys' novel follows Hal Overton and Noll Terry, the Uncle Sam's Boys, as they receive their commissions as lieutenants. The opening chapters find them on waiting orders, uniforms ready, while a surprise awaits Mrs. Overton and neighbors watch the new officers with mixed pride and spite. A discharged worker, Bunny Hepburn, nurses a grudge and plots revenge.

Twelve men set on the two lieutenants, false charges follow, and a court of inquiry must sort perjured tales from truth. The War Department acts, the town divides, and Hal and Noll clear their names before the call to duty sends them out at night with escort wagons and platoons marching in fours. The book is one of a series tracing the pair from the ranks upward.
26532-over-the-line:
Harold M. Sherman's 1929 school and football novel follows Judd Billings, who refuses to go back to school and is called a quitter by his older brother Bob. Bob, a Bartlett College man working in a sporting goods store, counted on Judd to take his place on the Trumbull High team. Farm work has given Judd the muscles of an ox and a grip that makes fellows yell, but he does not know his own strength and fears to use it.

Chapters trace a strange contract, a kicker discovered, fighting spirit, a scrap of paper, and an attempted hold-up, through confession and promotion to the first and second halves of the big game. A teammate called Cateye, angered by Judd, is won over when Judd's humor saves the day. The novel preaches grit, loyalty, and fair play.
2661-the-story-of-a-mine:
Bret Harte dedicated this little volume to Udo Brachvogel, whose translations introduced Harte to German readers, and dated the dedication New York, December 1877. The story opens on a steep trail over the Monterey Coast Range, where Concho seeks a mine.

Who sought it, who found it, and what it cost them drive a compact tale of greed, luck, and California law. Harte writes with his usual irony about fortunes made and lost on paper claims. The book offers a short, sharp western, where a hole in the ground tests every man's character.
267-the-touchstone:
Stephen Glennard, a struggling New York writer, owns letters from a dead novelist who once loved him. Edith Wharton's Touchstone follows Glennard as he sells Margaret Aubyn's letters to pay for his marriage. Professor Joslin's newspaper appeal for Aubyn papers opens the tale.

Glennard's wife Alexa learns the source of their comfort, and his conscience sharpens. Wharton weighs love, money, and literary honor in a short, tense novel. The touchstone of the title tests character, not gold. The book shows Wharton's moral irony at full strength. Wharton's short novel pairs well with her longer studies of Old New York.
26718-health-on-the-farm-a-manual-of-rur:
H. F. Harris, secretary of the Georgia State Board of Health, published this manual with Sturgis and Walton Company at New York in 1911. It is one volume in The Young Farmer's Practical Library, edited by Ernest Ingersoll, cloth volumes illustrated at seventy-five cents net each. Sister volumes cover home water-works, animal competitors, farm management, and electricity on the farm.

Ingersoll presents the series as small, compact, authenticated books for readers far from city libraries and daily notes of progress. Its direction is humane, not commercial: easier work, securer health, and a home the whole family enjoys. Harris opens with personal care, household sanitation, and infant and child hygiene. He then turns to eating, bread, meat, milk, vegetables, fruit, pickles, and drinks. Good cooking, seven avoidable diseases, sick-room care, and accidents close the manual.
2678-poems-by-emily-dickinson-series-one:
Emily Dickinson's poems, first series, introduced the world to a poet who had written in near secrecy. The slim lyrics, in short lines and dashes, speak of death, immortality, nature, and the soul with startling directness.

This first series set the pattern for her fame: poems that seem simple, then open into depths. Readers meet the bee, the bobolink, and the grave as neighbors in one strange household. The book marks the beginning of Dickinson's public life, and it still astonishes new readers. Her fame grew slowly, but these poems fixed it.
26994-when-life-was-young-at-the-old-far:
C. A. Stephens's 1912 memoir gathers boyhood tales from the old farm in Maine, on the Pennesseewassee, written for readers of The Youth's Companion. The chapters recall a nose in common, White Sunday, sheep-washing, a first Jersey cow, and a vermifuge bottle, each told as a small country adventure.

Later chapters add bird songs, outlaw dogs, the old squire's panther story, and a heartfelt Thanksgiving. Stephens writes with fond detail and gentle humor, preserving a Maine farm childhood of chores, cousins, and long summer days before the world changed around it.
27096-the-boy-ranchers-on-roaring-river-:
Willard F. Baker's 1926 volume The Boy Ranchers on Roaring River, or Diamond X and the Chinese Smugglers, sends the Diamond X boys after a smuggling ring. The frontispiece promises a win, and the story opens among wrecked outbuildings, with a bunk house down and a roof turned clean around.

The Kid moves stock nearer the house while Dick hunts for the cook, last seen frying bacon. The boys must sort smugglers from ranch hands on a river that gives the book its name, in a brisk series tale of work, suspicion, and chase.
2719-greville-fane:
Henry James wrote this tale of a literary life, opening as the narrator comes in to dress for dinner and finds a telegram. Mrs. Stormer is dying, the paper asks, can you give us half a column for tomorrow evening, and let her off easy, but not too easy.

The narrator, late and hurried, promises what he can, and the story unrolls the career of Greville Fane, a popular novelist of the old school. James writes with irony and pity about fame, hack work, and the gap between success and art. The tale bites as a portrait of a writer's trade.
27383-master-of-none:
Neil Goble wrote this short science-fiction tale around a wry opening claim. Specialization seems so plainly useful that few can still spot a competent syncretist, a person who joins many kinds of knowledge. His hero is Freddy the Fish, found dozing on a park bench with a newspaper over his face.

A small headline wakes Freddy's interest: strange signals out of space, likely from Cygnus. Sparrows quarrel over a peanut shell, a statue gets an undignified tribute, and then an excited friend shakes Freddy awake with news of an extra edition. The story plays its space mystery against an ordinary afternoon, and against the case for the all-rounder.
27804-the-boarding-school-familiar-conve:
Published in London in 1823, The Boarding School presents familiar conversations between a governess and her pupils, written for the amusement and instruction of young ladies. Its preface argues that early impressions shape character for life.

By contrast between amiable and unamiable tempers, the author hopes to make young readers eager to imitate virtue and avoid vice. The book is a window into Regency ideas of girls' education: manners, morals, and conduct taught through dialogue rather than lecture. The preface quotes the maxim that just as the twig is bent, the tree is inclined.
28129-the-nursery-january-1877-volume-xx:
The Nursery for January 1877, volume twenty-one, number one, is a monthly magazine for youngest readers, published in Boston by John L. Shorey. Its prose opens with Work and Play, in which two boys seek snow-shovelling work on New Year's morning, and goes on to animal tales, a drawing lesson, and a letter to Minnie. Music by Linda Cantoni closes the number.

Verse pieces include Bumble-Bee, Gretchen, and a noonday lullaby, all short enough for small children to learn. Pictures and large, clear type suit early readers. The issue shows Victorian children's publishing at its most gentle: kind conduct, useful work, and quiet fun.
28137-the-nursery-september-1877-vol-xxi:
The Nursery for September 1877, volume twenty-two, number three, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers from John L. Shorey. Its prose opens as three cousins from Kentucky meet the Atlantic Ocean at Brant Rock Beach. It goes on to roses and insects, a true partridge story, a letter from Minnesota, and a lazy shepherd. Astronomy and drawing lessons continue the teaching.

Verse includes Top-Knot, a brook crossing, a pig-drawing rhyme, and The Pedlar, set to music. The mix of seaside fun, farm tales, and simple lessons fits children learning to read. The issue shows how the magazine taught nature, manners, and geography through stories.
28141-the-nursery-february-1878-vol-xxii:
The Nursery for February 1878, volume twenty-three, number two, continues the Boston monthly for youngest readers. Its lead tale, Ebony and Lucy, has Lucy skate across a pond pulled by her black dog Ebony, tied by scarves into a harness. Other prose covers Daisy, a first fishing trip, a new way to catch mice, and Jamie Canfield's sand heap.

Verse includes a terrible trio, a shy pansy, a song for baby, and three little chicks, closing with Blow, Blow, East Wind set to music. Drawing lessons and short animal tales fill the rest. The issue is a good sample of the magazine's winter stories for small children.
28184-the-rubaiyat-of-omar-cayenne:
Gelett Burgess wrote The Rubaiyat of Omar Cayenne in 1904 as a parody of Fitzgerald's Rubaiyat, aimed at the literary trade of his day. Burgess, in quatrains that mimic Omar Khayyam, mocks hack writers, publishers, and critics who boom new books sky-high. The penny-a-liner is abroad, he warns, striking modern letters with blight.

Verses name Dumas, Scott, Aldrich, and the great houses: Century, Doubleday, Macmillan, and Harper. The joke is fond, not bitter, and the verse keeps Fitzgerald's music. Readers who know the original Rubaiyat will enjoy Burgess's sharp, funny take on publishing.
2825-undine:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué wrote Undine as a German Romantic tale about a water spirit who takes the shape of a young woman. A knight seeking shelter in a fisherman's remote cottage meets the foundling girl Undine, whose laughter and sudden moods hide her true nature. She marries the knight Huldbrand in the hope that human love will grant her a soul.

The marriage is tested when Huldbrand's old love returns and when the laws of the water folk press on the household. Undine stays loyal while the knight wavers, and the ending turns on what a soulless being gains and loses by loving a mortal. Readers still return to it for its clear fairy-tale plot and its sad view of promises kept too late.
28356-the-ranch-at-the-wolverine:
B. M. Bower's 1914 western novel The Ranch at the Wolverine begins with pioneers Marthy and Jase crossing rough prairie with four oxen toward the Wolverine stream. Marthy, hard-voiced and stubborn, finds a hidden grassy cove where the oxen stray, and claims it as the family's home.

Years of hard work tame the cove into a ranch, and later chapters follow ranch hands, wolf hunts, corrals, and the troubles and jokes of frontier neighbours. Bower writes in the plain, humorous style that made her westerns popular, giving readers a lively picture of ranch life in the early American West.
28383-the-love-story-of-abner-stone:
Edwin Carlile Litsey's The Love Story of Abner Stone, published in 1902, is told by an old man looking back over the long path from middle age toward seventy. He writes on a grey autumn afternoon, listening to birds outside his window, and lets his mind travel back more than twenty years.

What returns most clearly is a love: a sweet voice he still hears, a face he still sees, and a hand he imagines in his own. Litsey frames the romance with quiet reflection on mercy, nature, and a life nearly spent. The result is a gentle, backward-looking love story rather than a tale of action.
28589-frances-kane-s-fortune:
L. T. Meade's Frances Kane's Fortune, published by M. A. Donohue and Company of Chicago, opens on a sunny June day in an old-fashioned garden. Frances paces a sheltered path past a ribbon border and laden peach and pear trees, planning to sell most of the fruit. She grudges gardener Watkins his geraniums and calceolarias, which cost too much and pay nothing.

A midday letter from the carrier breaks her rounds of cabbages and early peas, and her father summons her indoors. Two more tales complete the volume: Monsieur the Viscount's Friend and The Yew-Lane Ghosts. Readers get a sensible heroine, a thrifty household, and a fortune that turns on a letter.
28706-oklahoma-sunshine:
Freeman E. Miller wrote this 1905 book of verses and short prose from Oklahoma Territory, gathered from a newspaper column. Beginning in June 1904, Miller published a column called Oklahoma Sunshine in the Stillwater Advance, writing in the moments of a busy life. Readers liked the pieces so well that he collected a full year of them, from June 1904 to June 1905, into this volume.

The contents mix cheerful poems with homely prose: a contented farmer, a date with joy, a song of green valleys, a prayer, and an April 22 poem marking the land run anniversary. Miller's gospel of sunshine preaches love and happiness as a creed. The book captures the booster spirit of a territory about to become a state, in verse meant to be read aloud and shared.
29041-the-education-of-eric-lane:
Stephen McKenna wrote this 1921 novel, The Education of Eric Lane, part two of his Sensationalists series, published by George H. Doran in New York. The chapters run from an experiment in emotion and Lady Barbara Neave through Lashmar Mill-house, an intermezzo, and mortmain, to a dame's school education and education for those of riper years. The book closes with the strongest thing of all and the education of Barbara Neave.

McKenna opens with a quotation from Shane Leslie on romance, and a hero who peers over a bath's steam at a traveling clock. The novel follows fashionable London life and its emotional lessons, in the style of the author's Lady Lilith and Sonia Married. Readers get a witty period novel of manners, love, and self-knowledge between the wars.
29555-rural-hygiene:
Henry N. Ogden, professor of sanitary engineering at Cornell and special assistant engineer to the New York State Department of Health, wrote Rural Hygiene in 1911 for Macmillan's Rural Science Series, edited by L. H. Bailey. Its chapters open with vital statistics of rural life: death rates, ideal rates, and rates in New York State. Later sections treat soil air, drains, damp cellar walls, tar and asphalt, and dry masonry.

Ogden writes for farmers, teachers, and health officers who must make country homes safe without city sewers. The book is practical, plain, and full of detail. Readers of public health history will find a clear record of how rural sanitation was taught in the age before modern plumbing reached the farm.
29626-our-young-folks-vol-1-no-1-an-illu:
Volume one, number one of Our Young Folks, an illustrated magazine for boys and girls, dated January 1865, opens with Hum, the Son of Buz, at Rye Beach. During summer vacation, cold, chilly, rainy days come to seaside visitors, when skies long dry pour water by pailfuls, wind whistles, and bushes bend beneath the flood. A friendly hand takes in a small creature, which gives a faint, watery squeak.

The magazine promises stories, pictures, and instruction for young readers, in the earnest, kindly voice of its age. Later numbers would carry work by beloved authors for children. Readers of children's magazine history will find a charming first number from the Civil War's final winter.
29690-hampstead-and-marylebone:
G. E. Mitton wrote Hampstead and Marylebone in the Fascination of London series, edited by Sir Walter Besant. The series, priced at one shilling and sixpence in cloth, covered the Strand, Westminster, Chelsea, Kensington, Holborn, and Bloomsbury beside these two districts. Its pages run from a prefatory note through Hampstead, Marylebone, and an index, with maps of Hampstead facing page one and Marylebone facing page 104.

A picture of Church Row, Hampstead, fronts a book that records a great city in a form its editors called practically unique. Mitton writes as guide and antiquary, noting streets, houses, and history. Readers of London topography will find a charming, compact guide to two beloved districts.
30004-a-bottle-of-old-wine:
Richard O. Lewis wrote A Bottle of Old Wine, with pictures by Kelly Freas. Its headnote calls it a grim tale of a future in which everyone is desperate to escape reality, and a hero who wants to have his wine and drink it too. Herbert Hyrel settles in his easy chair by the fireplace and watches his wife from the corner of his eye. She sits curled in her chair, the upper half of her face hidden in a personalized, three-dimensional telovis.

For three hours she will give no sound, movement, or sign of life, since breaking the thread of her show would ruin its emotional build-up. Hyrel once hated those long, silent evenings when he was ignored. Now they give him time for an escape of his own, at the flick of a small switch beneath his trouser leg.
30179-the-note-book-of-an-attache-seven-:
Eric Fisher Wood records seven months in the war zone as an attaché, with pictures from photographs, in a Century volume published in June 1915. He presents himself at the American Embassy in Paris on Tuesday, August 4, offers his services to Mr. Herrick, and finds them promptly accepted. With no time to settle his official status, he cannot say whether he is a doorman or an attaché, since the duties of the two seem identical.

Chapters follow the Germans nearing Paris, the British army on the night before the Marne, the battle and its analysis, and the battle of the Aisne. The American Ambulance, Germany and Berlin, dispatches carried from Berlin to London, Vienna, Hungary, and a German prison camp complete the tour. Wood writes as an eyewitness in the first months of war, close to embassies, armies, and camps.
30270-that-mother-in-law-of-mine:
That Mother-in-Law of Mine, published in Philadelphia by the Keystone Publishing Company in 1889, under an 1879 copyright by John E. Potter and Company, is a comic domestic novel dedicated to all those having mothers-in-law or expecting to have one. Its epigraph advises being kind to her virtues and a little blind to her faults. Bessie and her husband, a month married and on honeymoon at a summer resort, open the story in argument.

Charlie exasperates his wife by demanding that her mother give up objections and show deference to her son-in-law, while Bessie begs him to conciliate her for her sake. Chapters follow their marriage, mountains and more mother-in-law, the rise and fall, and Miss Van's party and another unpleasantness. Another Charlie in the field, a shadow on their life, and, at last, a mother-in-law subdued and a happy prospect follow.
3029-real-soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis wrote Real Soldiers of Fortune as profiles of adventurers who sold their swords around the world. The first subject, Major-General Henry Ronald Douglas MacIver, appears on Fifth Avenue or in University Place restaurants. He stands stiffly erect, gray-haired, with a Louis Napoleon imperial, fierce blue eyes, and a sabre cut across his forehead. His career ran from ensign in the Sepoy Mutiny to lieutenant under Garibaldi, captain under Don Carlos, and major in the Confederate army.

Davis lets MacIver speak for himself, asking a London crowd where the Englishman always finds welcome on returning battle-scarred and travel-worn. The answer, the ladies of the Empire Promenade, draws laughter and cheers. The book mixes biography with adventure, and it remains a lively gallery of nineteenth-century mercenaries.
30501-collected-poems-volume-one:
Alfred Noyes gathers his early verse in Collected Poems, volume one, published in New York in October 1913 by Frederick A. Stokes. Copyrights run from 1906 to 1913, with earlier pieces from Macmillan, and the volume reserves dramatic and acting rights.

Contents open with The Loom of Years and In the Heart of the Woods, then move through Art, triolets, ballads of old Japan, and poems on the mystic and the symbolist. Later pieces include Apes and Ivory, A Song of Sherwood, The World's May-Queen, Pirates, and A Song of England. Noyes blends romance, legend, and music into a rich early collection.
30558-claim-number-one:
George W. Ogden writes Claim Number One, copyrighted in 1922 by A. C. McClurg and published in May of that year by Grosset and Dunlap, with a frontispiece by J. Allen St. John. Ogden, author of The Duke of Chimney Butte and Trails End, opens with Comanche, guests for the Metropole, and unconventional behavior.

Later chapters add the flat-game man, skulkers, the drawing, a midnight extra, and the governor's son. Double crookedness, Hun Shanklin's coat, number one, and the other man follow. Ogden builds a western tale of claims, gambling, and frontier justice, with a hero navigating crooked deals and rough towns toward a fair outcome.
30796-the-dueling-machine:
Ben Bova and Myron R. Lewis wrote this science fiction tale, printed in Analog in May 1963, about a duel fought inside a machine-made dream. Dulaq rides up to a busy city level, full of crowds, perfumed trees, and a reddish sun. He knows the whole scene is an illusion built by a machine from his own mind. Somewhere in that city waits Odal, the man he must kill, and who may kill him.

The terms are stark: find Odal before sunset, on foot, with a small weapon of Dulaq's own making. Odal is a fair, cold professional, expert with all weapons, yet Dulaq hopes the city of his own choice will trip his foe. The story turns a formal duel into a test of nerve, place, and mind, and it asks whether a fight can be fair when the ground itself is one man's dream.
309-rhymes-of-a-rolling-stone:
Robert W. Service, the rolling stone himself, spatters seas of ink and asks the gods' pardon. Rhymes of a Rolling Stone, in the 1912 edition printed in 1917, opens with a prelude on literary sins. The contents run from A Rolling Stone to The Wanderlust.

Poems cover soldiers of fortune, gramophones at Fond-du-Lac, Athabaska Dick, and a trapper's Christmas Eve. The Lunger, the Quitter, and the Cow-Juice Cure mix comedy with frontier hardship. Service's rolling verse carries readers from Yukon to prairie. The book shows his range beyond gold-rush fame.
3105-that-fortune:
Warner opens this novel with a twelve-year-old boy in a tall hickory. The tree stands at the edge of a mountain forest, above rocky pasture and cornfields. Maples line an amber river below, and its murmur reaches the boy like a voice of nature he cannot yet grasp. He climbs to take the full swing of the tree in its sport with the western wind.

That high perch sets the book's mood: youth, air, and a landscape felt before it is understood. The story grows from this boy's world, where urging forces meet resisting ones. Home, valley, and river pull at a young life learning its own weight.
31140-young-auctioneers-or-the-polishing:
Edward Stratemeyer's 1897 boys' book, published by W. L. Allison in New York, follows Matt, a boy who attends a sale, argues, looks back on his past, and is discharged before striking a business partnership. Thirty chapters carry him onto the road at last, through harsh treatment, a fire, a corn-salve doctor, a confidence man, a storm, and a hold-up.

Later adventures bring an accusation of stealing, a tell-tale cap, a shanty in the woods, something missing along the river, and a dash from danger before a return to the village. In Stratemeyer's working-upward manner, the story polishes its rolling stone through honest work, pluck, and timely help.
31245-acadian-reminiscences-the-true-sto:
Judge Felix Voorhies's 1907 book, published by E. P. Rivas in New Orleans, presents itself as the true story of Evangeline, drawn from Acadian reminiscence. Voorhies, twelve years old when his memories begin some sixty years before, pictures his father's house in the Teche country, its rows of china trees and towering oaks. He also pictures the generous hospitality of the Acadian settlers.

Nine chapters follow Acadian manners and customs, rumors of war, threatening clouds, exiles, a night of terror, generous friends, Evangeline herself, and Louisiana, with illustrations including the Evangeline Oak. Whether history or legend, the book preserves a Louisiana judge's loving memory of a people Longfellow made famous.
31290-right-on-the-scaffold-or-the-marty:
Archibald H. Grimké's 1901 paper, number seven in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, tells the story of Denmark Vesey, hanged at Charleston, South Carolina, on July 2, 1822. Grimké paints him as a man of royal body, great strength, uncommon intelligence, force of will, and a lion's heart. He was no old man at his death though his hair was white, being not more than fifty-six.

Vesey's early name is lost; Denmark corrupts Telemaque, the name given him at fourteen by a new master, a captain in the African slave trade whose surname he bore. Calling Vesey a man without a past, Grimké honors him as a martyr of 1822, whose planned rising and gallows death became a landmark of Black resistance.
31306-bride-of-the-dark-one:
Florence Verbell Brown's story, printed in Planet Stories in July 1952, opens in Mytor's Cafe on Yaroto. There, the last light in the galaxy is a torch burning over a gallery of the damned. Outcasts and hunted men from brighter worlds crowd the tables while an Earth-girl dances in torchlight, and fat Mytor watches each face, judging mind, senses, and wallet at a glance.

The magazine's blurb frames the tale around Ransome, a jinx-scarred acolyte seeking salvation on a night of expiation, Bani-tai, among the photo-memoried priests of dark Darion. Lurid, atmospheric, and pulp-swift, the story turns a frontier dive into a stage for guilt, desire, and ritual.
31314-the-trumpeter-of-sa-kkingen-a-song:
Joseph Victor von Scheffel's Trumpeter of Säkkingen, translated by Mrs. Francis Brünnow and published in London and New York in 1877 with the poet's authorization, is a song from the Upper Rhine in eleven parts and more. Young Werner rides into the Schwarzwald, stays with its pastor, keeps St. Fridolin's day, adventures on the Rhine, meets a baron and his daughter, and becomes the baron's trumpeter.

Later parts follow an excursion to a mountain lake, a concert in a garden pavilion, teaching and learning, and Werner in a gnome's cave, among other episodes. Romantic, musical, and rooted in Black Forest legend, the poem made Scheffel's name a household word in Germany.
3137-the-rise-of-roscoe-paine:
Joseph C Lincoln sets this Cape Cod novel in a village where everyone knows everyone else's business. The narrator tells Dorinda he is going up to the village just for the walk, and her skeptical Um-hm answers him at once. That exchange fixes the book's tone: dry, neighborly, and alert to the gap between what people say and what they mean.

Roscoe Paine's rise gives the story its arc, from village obscurity toward a wider standing. Lincoln, a master of Cape Cod types, fills the background with fishermen, shopkeepers, and summer folk. Small dealings prove character here, and a village's opinion weighs more than any great event.
31492-rossmoyne:
Rossmoyne, by the author of Phyllis, Molly Bawn, and Portia, is a novel of an Irish country house, published by Butler Brothers in New York and Chicago. Its epigraph, quoted from Romeo and Juliet, asks who set an ancient quarrel new abroach and answers that there is much to do with hate, but more with love. The first chapter, "How a Dove-cot was fluttered in Rossmoyne," opens in a breakfast room where roses knock against the panes and pigeons demand their daily crumbs, while no one heeds them.

The novel that follows is a romance of family quarrels, affection, and reconciliation in a comfortable, old-fashioned household. Its pleasures are domestic: conversation, courtship, and the small disturbances that unsettle a settled house. Readers of Victorian Irish romance will find a warm, readable story, where love, as the epigraph promises, outweighs hate.
31590-scouting-with-daniel-boone:
Everett T. Tomlinson's boys' adventure opens in September 1773, when two pioneer boys halt at the snap of a branch in the forest. Under Daniel Boone's leadership, five families besides his own are making their way through unbroken wilderness from the Yadkin settlement in North Carolina. At Powell's Valley, forty men have joined the little company.

An advance guard of five opens the way, while rear guards stand at intervals against surprise by hostile Indians or by prowling beasts of prey. Tomlinson's novel follows the young scouts of Boone's party through the dangers of the trail, where caution and woodcraft decide whether a family reaches new ground.
3166-doctor-thorne:
Anthony Trollope published Doctor Thorne in 1858. The Greshams of Greshamsbury open the story, with Frank Gresham's early loves and matrimonial prospects close behind. Doctor Thorne himself, the country physician, keeps the family's secrets and his own counsel. Sir Roger Scatcherd and his will, Courcy Castle, and Miss Dunstable, the heiress, drive the plot's turns.

Money and marriage govern Barsetshire here, as love tests birth and fortune. Frank must choose between a match that saves the estate and one that follows his heart.
