Trollope tells it with his usual ease: long scenes, plain motives, and a moral sense that favors honesty over rank. The novel remains a fine entry to the Barsetshire world.
31726-poems-and-ballads-of-heinrich-hein:
Emma Lazarus translated Heine's Poems and Ballads, with a biographical sketch of Heine prefixed, and R. Worthington published them at New York in 1881, with copyright the same year. The volume opens with the sketch, then early poems, and sonnets to Heine's mother, B. Heine, née von Geldern. It gives English readers Heine's lyric voice in a translator's careful English.

Lazarus, herself a poet, renders Heine's songs, ballads, and sonnets with attention to their music and feeling. The book serves both as an introduction to Heine and as a collection to read for pleasure, from early work to the mature poems.
31936-the-cathedrals-and-churches-of-the:
Francis Miltoun's Cathedrals and Churches of the Rhine, published at Boston in 1905 by L. C. Page and Company with ninety illustrations, plans, and diagrams from Blanche McManus, follows the Rhine valley's great churches. Miltoun, author of books on the cathedrals of northern and southern France and on Dickens's London, writes for travelers who love church-building.

It starts by claiming medieval folk had grown fond of church-building, delighting that even their seals and shoe patterns took the shape of tiny buildings and tiny tabernacles. Readers get an architectural guide to Cologne and the Rhine churches, tracing Gothic from its introduction into Germany to its full-blown fourteenth-century form.
32049-the-lay-of-havelok-the-dane:
The Lay of Havelok the Dane is a medieval English romance, presented here in its original Middle English verse. This version follows the Early English Text Society edition of 1868, edited by Skeat, in a plain-text form for readers whose devices cannot show the full Unicode text. Letters that could not be shown in full are unpacked in brackets, and the old letter thorn is kept unchanged. Footnotes are grouped at the ends of text sections.

The romance opens with a direct address to its audience: hearken to me, good men, wives, maidens, and all men. From that minstrel opening, it tells the tale of Havelok, the Danish hero of the title, in the language of medieval England. Readers get a foundational work of English romance literature, with the editor's notes and errata kept alongside the verse, for study or for reading aloud in its original tongue.
32051-on-the-right-of-the-british-line:
Captain Gilbert Nobbs, late of the London Rifle Brigade, published this First World War memoir with Charles Scribner's Sons in September 1917. He dedicated it to the woman who waits, in humble tribute to her silent heroism, noting that beside the man who fights there stands the woman at home. The memoir opens at Fovant orderly room, where Nobbs learns he has forty-eight hours' notice to report at Southampton for reinforcements to France.

Later chapters follow him through fighting, wounding, and capture: a basin of soup at a hospital in St. Quentin, blindness, and ward life in a reserve lazarette at Hanover. Prison camp chapters cover Osnabruck, rations, parcels, and news, with comedy and drama among prisoners. A final chapter, called Free, tells how he bluffed a German sergeant, reached Aachen, and crossed the frontier. Readers get a soldier's account of battle, prison, and escape.
32068-world-of-the-drone:
Robert Abernathy's story, printed in Imagination in January 1955, is set in a world where men fight each other in machines, with no bond of brotherhood between them. Its hero is Dworn, twenty-one in flesh, whose steel-armoured shell, wheels, engine, and electric senses feel as much a part of him as his own skin. Each night he wakes at sunset in a desert, checks his instruments, and scans the dunes for prowling machines of prey.

Dworn knows that if his machine fails him in battle, he will die. His fuel gauge already stands near empty as he sets out to reach his people. The story follows his night journey and his foraging for fuel, building tension from simple needs: water, food running low, and a machine that must keep running. It is a compact portrait of war reduced to lone survival inside armour.
32108-the-ego-machine:
Henry Kuttner's short story, printed in Space Science Fiction in May 1952, opens with a film man facing a robot across a desk. Nicholas Martin tells the robot he will not ask what it wants, since he already knows: it should go away and tell St. Cyr that he approves. A small Christmas play set among Florida fishermen needs a robot, Martin argues, and why not six robots, or a baker's dozen.

The robot answers with an odd question: was Martin's mother's name Helena Glinska? Martin says it was not, and the robot murmurs that she must then have been the Great Hairy One. The story's sidenote theme warns against joining a slightly mad robot's experiment in optimum ecology, drunk on alternating current. Readers get a witty Kuttner comedy about art, machines, and a robot with opinions.
32199-a-house-party-don-gesualdo-and-a-r:
Ouida's A House-Party, Don Gesualdo, and A Rainy June, published in Philadelphia by J. B. Lippincott Company in 1902, gathers three tales by the author of Othmar, Princess Napraxine, Under Two Flags, and Wanda. The title tale opens on an August morning in an old English manor-house, in a breakfast-room hung with old gilded Stuart-era leather, with oak furniture of the same period.

Leaded lattices with stained glass fill some frames, and the house motto in old French, J'ay bon vouloir, is emblazoned there with a crest of a heron resting in a crown. Windows open onto a green, quaint, lovely garden, laid out by Monsieur Beaumont, the garden's planner. Readers get Ouida's late short fiction, where manor-house atmosphere, French mottoes, and old gardens set the stage for Don Gesualdo and a rainy June.
32232-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1865, volume sixteen, number ninety-four, is a magazine of literature, art, and politics, entered by Ticknor and Fields of Boston. It opens with Among the Honey-Makers, an essay on summer's sweet sensation. It pictures lying at length in warm, fragrant grass, soaked with sunshine, aware of blossoming clover and a high heaven full of innumerous bees' hum.

That happy hum, the essayist writes, seems to the closed eyes as if silent sunbeams had found a voice. They brim the bending blue with music while pursuing their busy chemistry. It tunes the mind to its own key: the murmuring voice of all pleasant things, a chord of sunshine, scent, and flowers. Readers get a Civil War-era literary monthly at its most lyrical, opening on bees, clover, and the chemistry of summer.
32253-the-frontier-boys-in-the-sierras-o:
Captain Wyn Roosevelt's The Frontier Boys in the Sierras, or The Lost Mine, illustrated by S. Schneider and published in New York by A. L. Chatterton Company, continues the Frontier Boys series. Its companions include Frontier Boys on the Overland Trail, in Colorado, in the Rockies, in the Grand Canyon, in Mexico, on the Coast, and in Hawaii. The boys' adventures move on, and this volume promises the Sierras and a lost mine.

Its first chapter, In the Channel, opens aboard ship, where Jo Darlington exclaims at a fierce sea and longs to clear the Hawaiian channels for open water. Jim, his brother, stands with him on the bridge of the Sea Eagle. Shouting above the wind, he says the ship will weather it if they meet no other vessel in the dark. Readers get a boys' adventure of sea, mountains, and a mine, told in brisk dialogue.
32409-seeds-of-pine:
Janey Canuck's travel book, copyrighted in Canada in 1922, follows a westward trip on the Grand Trunk Pacific to a frontier post and beyond the end of steel. Chapters move through bitter waters, motoring to Athabasca Landing, travel on the Athabasca River and the Lesser Slave River, and a portage between waters. The writer meets northern pioneers, Ruthenian settlers, and hero priests of the north, and visits the Bishop of the Arctic.

Later chapters cover coal mining in Alberta, northern gardens, a country woman at the city races, and the overland trail of 1898. Canuck writes with warmth about a wide, new country and the people building homes in it. The book offers a lively, first-hand picture of western Canada in the railway and pioneer years.
32425-maurice-tiernay-soldier-of-fortune:
Charles James Lever's novel follows Maurice Tiernay, a soldier of fortune. His strange incidents and rapid reversals first appeared as a serial in the Dublin University Magazine from April 1850 to December 1851. The book edition, edited by Lever's daughter with illustrations by A. D. M'Cormick, was published in London in 1898. Lever notes that the strangeness of the tale almost kept him from print until friends urged him on.

Tiernay's career carries readers through war, travel, and shifting loyalties in an age of armies and empires. The hero's luck turns fast, and each new post brings fresh danger, new allies, and hard choices. Lever writes with pace and colour, making the novel a strong example of nineteenth-century adventure fiction about a man living by his sword.
32677-the-invention-of-the-sewing-machin:
Grace Rogers Cooper, curator of textiles at the Smithsonian, traces the sewing machine in Bulletin 254, published in 1968. Four chapters move from early efforts to the elements of a successful machine, then to the Sewing-Machine Combination and to cheaper machines for the home.

Appendixes list notes on growth and trade, American companies of the nineteenth century, patent models in the Smithsonian, leaflets, cotton thread, and short lives of makers. Cooper shows how models, drawings, and patents together prove who made what, and how a workshop idea became a household tool.
327-the-princess-aline:
Princess Aline of Hohenwald enters Morton Carlton's life exactly when his heart and time stand free. Richard Harding Davis's Princess Aline follows Morney Carlton, a rich young New Yorker, through wise and foolish deeds for love. Had she come sooner or later, she might have passed unnoticed.

Carlton can look back with modest satisfaction and forward with pleasure, yet Aline unsettles both. Davis mixes European courts, American wealth, and romantic comedy. The novella's charm lies in timing: love arrives at the one open moment. It remains a light Davis favorite.
32731-sube-cane:
Edward Bellamy Partridge tells of Sube Cane, a twelve-year-old in knickerbockers with big dreams. Perched on his father's stable roof, Sube fancies himself a range rider beside a dark-haired maiden, and he rubs his upper lip in hopes of a mustache.

His chance comes when a doctor praises a hair restorer, a Boon for Baldness, said to sprout hair on house walls. Sube steals the bottle for science, and thirty chapters of pranks follow: cats, shows, barnstormers, movies, an auction, and a trial. The book is a warm, comic portrait of boyhood mischief.
32902-villa-eden-the-country-house-on-th:
Berthold Auerbach's romance of a country house on the Rhine, translated by Charles C. Shackford, appeared in Boston from Roberts Brothers in 1871. Its copyright entry is dated 1868. The novel opens on a boat, where a gray-haired man in a new summer suit boards with a beaded wallet at his belt.

Opposite him sits a tall, stately woman in pale-yellow silk, vexed at delay, with a fair maiden in blue beside her. The household that gathers around Villa Eden includes Eric, the soldier-scholar, and Clodwig and Bella, who grow close to him. Sonnenkamp and his family, the young Manna, and a prince move through assemblies and woodland walks. Eric wonders whether men might go somewhere each year for the cure of their souls, as they already go for the cure of their bodies.
32929-thereby-hangs-a-tale-volume-one:
The first volume of this tale opens at Tolcarne with a comic household scene: a mistress calling for Edward, a stiff, high-shouldered footman. The first volume questioning him about Sir Hampton, hot water, and young ladies gone walking on a damp morning without waterproofs or goloshes. Edward, wise in his generation, answers with care, and his mistress corrects his grammar as firmly as his errands. The domestic comedy sets a household where servants and masters watch each other closely.

From that breakfast-room start the novel widens into a story of family, fortune, and reputation, with Sir Hampton's money, made by tea, hanging over its characters. The tale moves between drawing room and countryside, letting small social blunders carry larger consequences. It is a Victorian novel of manners with a light touch, fond of its household and sharp about the rules that govern it.
33023-an-address-delivered-before-the-wa:
Henry R. Schoolcraft's address opens with a claim about American letters. It was delivered before the Was-ah Ho-de-no-son-ne, or New Confederacy of the Iroquois, at its third annual council on August 14, 1845, and printed at Rochester in 1846. In a country whose institutions rest on the popular will, social and literary honors must come from personal exertion springing from society itself. Schoolcraft argues they must not come from kings, patronage, or ministerial power.

The volume pairs the address with Genundewah, a poem by W. H. C. Hosmer, pronounced on the same occasion and published by the confederacy. Together they show a mid-nineteenth-century attempt to honor Native history and literature through a new society's councils. For students of Iroquois history and of early American literary societies, the pamphlet preserves a formal moment of that effort, with its ideals stated in full.
3304-the-machine:
Upton Sinclair names this play for the political machine it exposes. Julia Patterson, a magazine writer, opens the cast, with Jack Bullen, a parlor Socialist, and Laura Hegan, daughter of the traction king. Allan Montague, a lawyer, and Jim Hegan himself follow, with Annie Roberts, a girl of the slums, and Robert Grimes, the boss. Andrews and Parker, secretary and clerk, complete the order.

Act one sits in Julia's rooms in a model tenement on the lower East Side. Reform, business, and poverty meet there, and the machine grinds between them. Sinclair writes the city as a system, where traction franchises and tenement votes trade hands. Traction franchises and tenement votes trade hands while reformers argue: the machine's real plot.
3322-east-lynne:
Mrs Henry Wood's sensation novel East Lynne remains her most famous book. This text follows the 1883 New York edition from John B Alden. Lady Isabel Vane, wife of the upright Archibald Carlyle, leaves home for the villain Francis Levison and pays for the choice with everything. Ruined and repentant, she returns in disguise as the governess Madame Vine to watch her own children.

The novel made Victorian readers weep and moralize in equal measure. Wood mixes domestic melodrama with a stern lesson on marriage, sin, and forgiveness. Its stage versions ran for decades. Readers today get the original sensation pattern intact: a fallen woman, a patient husband, and a deathbed reckoning that forgives without forgetting.
33226-no-moss-or-the-career-of-a-rolling:
Harry Castlemon, pen name of Charles A. Fosdick, wrote No Moss, or The Career of a Rolling Stone, in the Go-Ahead Series, entered in 1868 and copyrighted in 1896. Its chapters run from fire quarters and Sam Barton's harboring place, through a new plan, Tom in trouble, and Atkins refusing duty, to the governor's strategy. The governor storms the rebels, crossing the shoals, and Johnny Harding's visitors. Later chapters bring a strange encounter and a phantom schooner.

The tale follows a rolling stone of a boy through river, army, navy, and robbers punished, with a battle at the bridge and a chapter of incidents before its conclusion. Castlemon, author of the Gun-Boat and Rocky Mountain series, writes boys' adventure . The novel remains a example of the genre, where a restless hero learns, through scrapes and service, that a rolling stone gathers no moss but may gather character.
3324-a-rebellious-heroine:
John Kendrick Bangs, author of A House-Boat on the Styx, turns author against heroine in this 1896 Harper story. W T Smedley supplied the illustrations, and one picture notes the scene laid at Lakewood. Bangs built his career on comic fantasy, and here the fantasy turns literary: a heroine who refuses to play the part her story assigns her.

The comedy grows from that rebellion. Plot, author, and character argue over who controls the tale, and the heroine keeps slipping her author's leash. Metafiction before the name existed: a heroine who talks back to her own story. It is light, clever, and fond of its own machinery, with a heroine bent on writing herself a better fate.
33262-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for January 1866, volume seventeen, gathers literature, science, art, and politics in one thick number. Its contents range from Bayard Taylor's Beauty and the Beast and Mrs. Agassiz's Amazonian picnic to Mrs. Stowe's Chimney-Corner papers and a study of the actor Edwin Booth. The issue thus spans travel, tale, essay, and stage, all in the magazine's serious, wide-ranging voice.

Published in Boston by Ticknor and Fields, the number captures American letters just after the Civil War, when writers weighed both the nation's wounds and its hopes. For modern readers, it is a rich miscellany: short fiction beside criticism, science beside politics. It rewards dipping in, piece by piece, as readers of 1866 would have done.
33333-the-statute-of-anne:
The Statute of Anne, presented here in both a modern formatted version and a transcription from the original, is the landmark 1710 act that founded modern copyright. Its preparer's notes explain that Latin introductions and endings were translated into English, line-end breaks removed for searching, and small typos corrected. The word penny was restored, and reasonable was set in place of seasonable.

The volume serves readers who want the act itself, not just talk about it: the text that gave authors a fixed term of protection and set the pattern for later law. For students of copyright, publishing, and literary history, it is a short but essential source, showing in plain legal prose how the age of authors' rights began.
33427-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers entries from Chariot to Chatelaine, in alphabetical order. Its articles span history, warfare, places, and arts, each set out in the dense, exact style of the great reference work. Readers will find long treatments of major topics beside short entries on smaller terms, all arranged for quick lookup.

As a slice of the famous eleventh edition, the volume shows how knowledge was summed up before the First World War: thorough, confident, and rich in detail. It serves best as a work to dip into, whether for a vehicle, a town, or a term in history. Scholars still prize this edition, and this volume gives a full taste of its scope.
33559-at-the-fall-of-port-arthur-or-a-yo:
Edward Stratemeyer sends young American Larry into the Russo-Japanese War in this volume of his Soldiers of Fortune series, copyrighted in 1905. Larry and his friends face a storm on the Pacific, a Russian sailor's plot, and signs of mutiny. They also face a fight for their ship, before the mutineers take possession and the tables are turned. A waterspout, an order to lay to, and capture as a prize of war carry the boys deeper into the conflict.

Later chapters follow the progress of the war, a sharp naval battle, and service aboard a Japanese warship toward the fall of Port Arthur itself. Stratemeyer writes brisk boys' adventure with attention to ships, guns, and naval routine. The book suits young readers interested in sea stories and in how Americans of the period imagined Japan's rising naval power.
33657-cinderella-jane:
Marjorie Benton Cooke writes a society comedy in this 1917 novel, published by arrangement with Doubleday, Page. The story opens with the Pageant of the Prophets, which gives handsome Jerry Paxton his first chance, and follows a primrose chain of fortune. These include Mrs. Abercrombie Brendon, who opens her house for a portrait exhibition and annexes Jerry for his looks as well as his art. They also include Jerry's sense of dramatic values in playing up to his elderly siren and the gods who smile on him.

Cooke, author of Bambi and The Girl Who Lived in the Woods, moves her hero through clubs, leagues, and drawing rooms where charm and timing matter as much as talent. Cinderella Jane herself enters that world of patronage and performance. Readers who enjoy light, witty novels of American society life will find the book bright, theatrical, and good-humored.
33680-highway-pirates-or-the-secret-plac:
Harold Avery writes a boys' adventure of hiding places, ghosts, and smugglers in this 1920 book. The narrator and his chosen friend Miles Coverthorne flee through underwood in May, stung by hazel switches and tripping in tufts of grass, crying that they have been seen. Their pursuers are not keepers but Eagles, a word that quickens their pace as if their lives were at stake. Nineteen chapters follow from a day of trouble and a knocking on the wall.

Men in hiding, a singing ghost, Nicholas Coverthorne showing his hand, a mad prank, trial and sentence, a journey, and a rising build the mystery. So do highway pirates, the last of the True Blue, a cavern, brandy kegs, abandonment, desperate straits, a subterranean tunnel, and daylight at last. Avery mixes schoolboy friendship with secret-passage suspense, and young readers will enjoy its pace and its hidden world.
33977-miss-million-s-maid-a-romance-of-l:
Berta Ruck wrote this romance of love and fortune, published in New York in 1915 by arrangement with Dodd, Mead. A young woman next door becomes maid to Miss Million, a rich employer, and moves into new quarters with her. Shopping, parties, afternoons out, proposals, and a word of warning fill the chapters.

Ruck, author of His Official Fiancee and The Girls at His Billet, writes briskly for readers who enjoy society romance. The heroine watches wealth from the servant's side of the door. The novel offers a bright, gossipy tale of money, manners, and marriage.
34037-under-the-southern-cross-or-travel:
Maturin M. Ballou wrote this travel book on the South Pacific, published in Boston in 1888 by Ticknor and Company, with copyright in 1887. Under the Southern Cross, or Travels in Australia, Tasmania, New Zealand, Samoa, and other Pacific islands, follows Ballou's earlier Due West, Due North, and Due South. An epigraph from Shakespeare on rough quarries and hills touching heaven opens the volume.

Ballou writes as a cheerful, wide-ranging traveler, keen to make foreign places feel at home to American readers. The book mixes description, story, and notes on peoples and places. It remains a lively nineteenth-century guide to the Pacific world.
3416-william-ewart-gladstone:
James Bryce studies William Ewart Gladstone as both a man and a statesman in this short biography, first copyrighted in 1898 and issued in book form in 1919. Bryce opens with a puzzle: Gladstone seems a bundle of opposite qualities, called with equal truth a conservative and a revolutionary. The chapters then follow his early influences, his long parliamentary career, and his character in office.

Bryce knew Gladstone's world from inside British politics, and he weighs oratory, conscience, and stubbornness rather than retelling every debate. The book suits readers who want a compact portrait of the Victorian prime minister, explaining why admirers and critics could both claim him and why he dominated his age.
3605-on-the-firing-line:
Anna Chapin Ray and Hamilton Brock Fuller write a novel whose hero, Harvard Weldon, stands six feet one in his stockings, broad shouldered and without an ounce of extra flesh. He halts before a line of deck chairs and tells a young woman, Miss Dent, that he usually gets what he wants. Her dry answer, that he is more fortunate than most people, sets the tone for their sparring.

The title points to war and to the front line of action, where Weldon's confidence will meet real danger and real feeling. Ray and Fuller mix romance with adventure, following a strong, self assured hero who must learn limits. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth century tales of brave young men and sharp tongued heroines.
3691-little-wars-a-game-for-boys-from-tw:
Herbert George Wells writes rules for a war game played with toy soldiers on a floor, in this book for boys from twelve to adult age, with an appendix on Kriegspiel. Wells notes that Laurence Sterne had already observed Uncle Toby and Corporal Trim playing Little Wars on a scale exceeding even his own richness. His chapters cover the legendary past, the beginnings of modern little warfare, and the rules themselves.

The rules treat the country, the move, the mobility of arms, hand to hand fighting, capturing, the composition of forces, and the size of soldiers. A sample battle, the Battle of Hook's Farm, shows the game in play. The book suits readers interested in war gaming history and in Wells as a playful inventor of indoor battles.
3717-the-parson-s-daughter-of-oxney-coln:
Anthony Trollope sets this tale among the lanes and moors of Devon, on the skirts of Dartmoor, where the rivers Dart, Avon, and Teign wind through half wild country. The parson's daughter keeps house for her father at Oxney Colne, and her quiet round of kitchen, maids, and parish calls hides a restless heart. A walk to a lone farmhouse on the moor edge becomes the pivot of her story, as duty and desire pull in opposite ways.

Trollope opens with a proud claim for Devon as the prettiest scenery in England, then earns it with lanes, tors, and moor light. The tale moves slowly and tenderly, and its interest lies in a good girl's choice rather than in grand events. Readers who like village life drawn with care will find a small story with a firm moral center.
3723-a-ride-across-palestine:
Anthony Trollope recounts a lone horseback ride through the Holy Land in this travel tale. Left without a companion, he plans a loop from Jerusalem to Bethany, the Mount of Olives, the Dead Sea, the Jordan, and Jericho, then back for a steamer at Jaffa. He dislikes solitary travel and says so plainly, which gives the narrative its charm, since the reader shares both his nerves and his wonder.

Arab escorts, a dragoman named Joseph, and wrangles over tariffs slow the party, while the glitter of the Dead Sea at sunset rewards the dust. The tale is short and brisk, with biblical sites seen through a plain English eye. Readers who like Victorian travel writing will enjoy a ride that mixes devotion, comedy, and the small frictions of the road.
403-soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis sets this romance in New York drawing rooms and a South American revolt. Alice Langham meets a rough westerner at a dinner party, then finds him again as a soldier of fortune abroad. Reginald King, a polished rival, offers wealth and ease, while the westerner offers danger and a cause.

Davis writes bright society scenes, then shifts to jungle camps, plots, and a fight for a small republic. Love and loyalty test Alice at each turn. The novel charms as a dashing tale of its age, where a woman must choose between safe comfort and a man who lives by risk.
4052-address-to-the-inhabitants-of-the-c:
A missionary address to settlers in the colonies, including Norfolk Island, presses the gospel of Christ on its hearers in plain terms. The second part recalls the views laid out in the first, and urges an experimental, lived knowledge of faith over mere hearing.

The speaker asks whether his hearers have paid the subject the attention it deserves, and stresses its great weight for conscience and life. The address belongs to the age of missions and penal settlements, when preaching reached far-flung outposts. Readers interested in colonial religion will find a direct, earnest document of its time.
4279-winter-sunshine:
John Burroughs, the American naturalist, made this the second volume of his collected writings. The book joins winter essays from his home country with foreign sketches from his travels. In his short preface he notes, with a story about the writer De Lolme, how a brief visit tempts a man to write a book, while long residence makes him more cautious.

Burroughs writes about snow, birds, and the quiet of the winter woods in his plain, observant style. The foreign sketches add a traveler's notes on new scenes. Together they give a calm, seasonal book, meant for readers who enjoy nature writing at a walking pace.
4288-the-rich-mrs-burgoyne:
Kathleen Norris wrote this novel about wealth and its costs, opening with a dedication to her namesake Kathleen Mary Thompson. A sonnet prefixed to the book complains that modern life is dressed only for show. It praises plain living and high thinking, and mourns a homely beauty now lost to rapine, avarice, and expense.

Mrs. Burgoyne herself is rich, and the story examines what riches do to a household, its servants, and its guests. Norris, a popular novelist of domestic life, keeps the focus on manners and morals. The book asks whether money buys comfort or merely a glittering surface, and what is lost when show replaces substance.
4321-margot-asquith-an-autobiography-two:
Margot Asquith, wife of Prime Minister Herbert Henry Asquith, wrote this autobiography in two volumes, here joined in one. She recalls her Scottish youth, her marriage into politics, and her life at the center of Edwardian society and government. The chapters run through friendships, quarrels, and the great houses of the age.

Asquith writes with wit and candor, naming names and settling scores in a style that made the book famous and controversial. Readers get an insider's view of the years before the First World War, from a woman who knew its leaders well. The autobiography remains a lively, partisan memoir of a political age.
4388-the-jesuit-missions-a-chronicle-of-:
Thomas Guthrie Marquis wrote this volume in the Chronicles of Canada series on the Jesuit missions in New France. It follows the missionaries who carried the cross into the wilderness, among Huron, Iroquois, and other peoples of the Great Lakes and the Saint Lawrence. Their letters and relations supply the narrative's detail.

Marquis tells of long canoe journeys, winter missions, martyrdoms, and the founding of stations that became towns. The chronicle balances admiration for courage with the facts of disease, war, and cultural clash. It gives a compact history of a mission that shaped early Canada, in the series' plain, readable style.
4571-master-sunshine:
Mrs. C. F. Fraser wrote Master Sunshine for children, about a boy whose real name was not Master Sunshine at all. His mother said he chose the name himself, long before he could speak. Even as a baby he was full of cheery good humour, sparkling in winning smiles and a rippling laugh. His golden curls seemed to catch the glory of the morning sun, and no better name could be found for the merry, helpful little fellow.

Chapters follow who he was, the wanderer and his wife, a rainy day, a Sunday with father, being a hero, kind deeds, and a happy ending. The tales praise small services, good temper, and thought for others, in simple language for young readers. Parents and children get a gentle Victorian storybook, easy to read aloud, about how a sunny temper can brighten a whole household.
4626-married-life-its-shadows-and-sunshi:
T. S. Arthur published Married Life, Its Shadows and Sunshine, at Philadelphia in 1852. For him, marriage stands as life's most exalted, pure, and sacred bond, not a bargain struck for worldly gain. He presents it as a joining of two minds, each gaining fresh strength and wider power to enjoy life and do good.

Much has been said about equality of the sexes and rights of woman, Arthur notes, but little rests on a discriminating sense of difference between man and woman. The Creator, he argues, made them for each other, stamping each spirit with a tendency toward conjunction. Evils in marriage, he claims, come less from failing to recognise equality than from hasty, ill-judged, discordant alliances made from external motives. Readers get a Victorian marriage essay, earnest and old-fashioned.
490-life-and-adventures-of-calamity-jane:
Martha Cannary, known as Calamity Jane, tells her own life in this brief memoir, written in her own rough voice. Born in Princeton, Missouri, in 1852, she rode horses young, crossed to Montana by wagon in 1865, and won fame as a shot and fearless rider. Scouts, camps, and frontier towns fill her pages.

Jane writes plainly of hunts, river crossings, and hard trails, with little polish and much pluck. Scholars debate how much is tall tale, but the voice rings true to her legend. The memoir endures as a frontier self-portrait, brisk, boastful, and full of dust, danger, and pride.
4927-legends-of-charlemagne:
Thomas Bulfinch's Legends of Charlemagne retells the medieval romances of the Frankish emperor and his paladins for general readers. The stories follow Charlemagne's court and his wars against the Saracens. They celebrate knights whose names became bywords for loyalty, daring, and tragic pride.

This etext holds only the Charlemagne legends from Bulfinch's complete Mythology. Its preface ranks The Age of Fable beside Pilgrim's Progress, Gulliver's Travels, the Arabian Nights, and Robinson Crusoe. All are works every educated reader should know. Readers get the Charlemagne cycle as lively tale rather than scholarly edition, a doorway into medieval romance.
497-tracks-of-a-rolling-stone:
Henry Coke recalls a wandering life in this memoir, written in five months without diary or notes. Coke, a younger son with little fortune, roams schools, clubs, and continents, telling tales of friends, duels, and scrapes. A second edition adds fresh stories after readers welcomed the first.

Coke writes with easy, anecdotal charm, opening on how little we recall our own childhood. His tracks cross Victorian high life and low adventure alike. The memoir charms as a gentleman's ramble through a vanished age, where a rolling stone gathers more tales than moss.
4986-the-four-epochs-of-woman-s-life-a-s:
This study in hygiene follows a woman's life through four epochs, beginning with sexual development and puberty: physical changes, first menstruation, and psychic changes at that age. Later sections take up home life, corsets, shoes, underwear, nutrition, diet, water, constipation, school life, spinal curvature, and exercise.

Anatomy of the female generative organs follows in plain, clinical terms, including the vulva, hymen, bladder, vagina, uterus, and fallopian tubes. The catalog record gives no author name. Readers get a period health manual, frank for its time, valuable now as much for what it reveals about early twentieth-century ideas of women's health as for its advice.
5094-the-romance-of-elaine-sequel-to-exp:
Arthur B. Reeve's detective novel continues the adventures of Elaine, heroine of the earlier Exploits, with Professor Craig Kennedy again at her side. A criminal conspiracy pursues her through chapters named for its traps and devices: a serpent sign, a cryptic ring, a watching eye, a lost torpedo, and a submarine harbour.

Kennedy's scientific methods meet serial-style thrills here, as wireless detection, searchlights, and secret weapons enter the chase. The book reads as a fast pulp sequel, built for readers who want cliffhangers, villains, and inventions in every chapter, and it ends with Elaine's triumph over her enemies.
5122-the-trail-of-the-lonesome-pine:
John Fox Jr.'s novel is set in the mountains of eastern Kentucky, where a girl growing up among feuding mountain families meets the outside world. The opening finds her watching smoke rise from the valley below, a sign of the mining and timber men whose arrival will change her home, her schooling, and her loyalties.

Fox builds the story around mountain custom, family feuds, and a young woman's wish for learning, set against the hills themselves. The novel became one of the best known portraits of Appalachia of its time, and it still offers readers a vivid, if romantic, picture of a region on the edge of change.
5148-rodney-stone:
Arthur Conan Doyle's historical novel looks back at England at the start of the nineteenth century, when prizefighting was a national pastime. Its young narrator, Rodney Stone, grows up among the men of the ring, travels the Brighton Road, meets Lord Nelson. He watches great fights at Crawley Downs, while a mystery around Lord Avon shadows the sporting world.

Doyle drew on boxing histories and memoirs to recreate Regency sporting life, from coach journeys to ringside crowds. The book blends adventure, history, and detection, and it gives readers a colourful doorway into a vanished England of gentlemen, gamblers, and bare-knuckle champions.
5151-the-exploits-of-elaine:
Arthur B. Reeve's serial novel introduces Elaine, a young woman pursued by a master criminal known as the Clutching Hand. Chapters follow vanishing jewels, a frozen safe, a poisoned room, a vampire, a double trap, a hidden voice. A death ray appears, as Professor Craig Kennedy and his friend Jameson try to unmask the villain.

The book was written as a series of linked episodes, each ending in fresh danger. It shows Reeve's gift for invention-driven mystery. Readers get a fast, cliffhanging detective adventure from the silent-film era, in which science, disguise. Daring carries Elaine from one peril to the next.
5156-beechcroft-at-rockstone:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Beechcroft at Rockstone opens with a telegram that scatters a family: an accident to Jasper sends the Mohun sisters hurrying to Rockstone. Chapters follow the household's dispersal and regrouping, with marbles, a queen of the white ants, Christmas letter bags, St Valentine's Day, and the rocks of Rockstone itself marking the year.

Yonge traces cousins, pupils, and neighbours through courtship, duty, and small crises, in the domestic moral style she made her own. Readers of Victorian family fiction will find a leisurely, character-driven novel, where the real drama lies in how a scattered family learns to hold together again.
5157-how-i-found-livingstone:
Henry Morton Stanley's abridged narrative tells how he found David Livingstone in Central Africa. Sent by the New York Herald, Stanley organised an expedition at Zanzibar in 1871, marched inland through Bagamoyo and Ugogo, and reached Unyanyembe. After months of hardship he reached Ujiji, where he met the missing explorer and spent four months with him.

Stanley writes of caravan life, disease, desertion, and diplomacy with African rulers, in a plain, day-by-day style. The book made him famous and gave Victorian readers a first-hand account of exploration. It remains a vivid, if one-sided, record of a journey that changed how Europe saw the African interior.
5306-down-the-ravine:
Charles Egbert Craddock's Down the Ravine opens under a new moon like a gleaming scimitar over a rugged Cumberland Mountains spur. A fox barking in the laurel reminds a young mountaineer of Tennessee's premium for the scalp and ears of the red fox. The animal speeds along a cliff ledge, unaware of the legislation of extermination.

Craddock, the pen name of Mary Noailles Murfree, wrote of Tennessee mountain life with close attention to dialect and landscape. The novel follows mountain people through hardship and humour, and it offers readers a vivid early portrait of Appalachia, told from inside its ravines and laurel thickets.
5623-the-young-explorer-or-claiming-his-:
Horatio Alger wrote The Young Explorer, or Claiming His Fortune, about Ben, a young man seeking his inheritance and his chance. Contents run from Ben's Inheritance and Deacon Pitkin's Offer through Sam Sturgis's New Idea, a brilliant chance, and a search for a place, to Mr. Fitch the senior partner, a dinner guest, a strange acquaintance, and the Astor House.

Ben's story carries him to San Francisco, the Canon Hotel, and a polite hostess. A tight place, a midnight excursion, and a thief's disappointment follow, before savings and the arrival at Murphy's among the Sierras. Readers get a gold-rush adventure of pluck and honesty, in Alger's familiar hopeful style.
5747-do-and-dare-a-brave-boy-s-fight-for:
Horatio Alger follows Herbert Carr, a brave boy fighting for fortune, from the post office at Wayneboro onward. Herbert tells his mother that if they could only keep the post office, they should be all right, but she fears there will be little chance of it. Chapters follow Herbert's chance, a prodigal son, losing his place, Eben's scheme, good luck, envy, a solitary farmhouse, and a trial for theft.

The book introduces a classic Alger hero tested by rivals, false charges, and sudden turns of luck. Herbert's pluck, honesty, and willingness to work carry him through schemes meant to ruin him. The novel suits young readers who enjoy stories where steady character wins, and it offers a clear example of Alger's hopeful view of American boyhood.
5757-the-maid-of-maiden-lane:
The Maid of Maiden Lane opens in New York in the bright spring of 1791. The city, proud and opulent, had put British rule behind it. Its homes and sacred places stood restored. Its heroine, Cornelia Moran, lingers in a garden and discovers love almost without knowing it, as a handsome youth named Hyde stirs a shy, trembling happiness she has never felt. The chapter called This Is the Way of Love names her awakening.

Here is a post-Revolutionary romance of manners, where a young woman's heart must navigate family, society, and a new republic's hopes. The novel favors feeling and period detail over grand action, with gardens, visits, and formal meetings carrying the plot. It suits readers who enjoy early American historical romance told with warmth and old-fashioned charm.
5764-doctor-therne:
Rider Haggard's Doctor Therne follows a doctor through diligence rides, a hacienda, a trial, and a gate of darkness. Chapters name Sir John Bell, Stephen Strong going bail, crossing the Rubicon, fortune, Jane meeting a doctor named Merchison, a red-headed man, the shadow of pestilence, and harvest. Medicine, law, and personal ambition tangle as Therne's career turns.

The volume offers a Victorian adventure with a medical hero, where plague, courts, and colonial enterprise test character. Haggard writes briskly, mixing romance with moral pressure, and the doctor's choices carry real cost. Fans of Haggard beyond his African romances will find a darker, more modern tale here, concerned with science, conscience, and the price of success.
5875-the-rover-boys-on-the-ocean-or-a-ch:
Winfield sends the Rover Boys to sea in The Rover Boys on the Ocean, subtitled A Chase for a Fortune. The story opens aboard the Spray on the Hudson, where Dick warns Sam to luff up a little or the boat will run on the rocks. Sam admits he has not got sailing down as fine as Dick yet. Dick reckons they are eight or nine miles from Albany. They should make that city by six if the wind holds.

This gives a boys' sailing adventure, where seamanship, brotherhood, and a fortune chase drive the plot. The Hudson setting gives the tale fresh water, wind, and river towns as its stage. Young readers who enjoy vintage adventure will find brisk chapters and earnest heroes, with the Rover brothers' teamwork carrying them from river sailing to ocean danger.
6010-what-s-bred-in-the-bone:
Grant Allen, in a thousand-pound prize novel, opens with Elma, hot-faced from a wild rush for her ticket, grasping uncounted change in a gloved hand and thrust into a crowd. Chapters follow Elma's stranger, two's company, a brother, a tunnel, and two strange meetings, with Kelmscott of Tilgate at the center.

Later pages bring a family jar, business first, music's power, the path of duty, struggle and victory, and visions of wealth. A colonel repents, a colonel is punished, and mistaken identity, fresh discoveries, and golden joys complicate the plot. Allen tests whether blood or upbringing shapes a life.
6065-the-perils-of-pauline:
Charles Goddard opens in a stately mansion on the lower Hudson. There old Stanford Marvin, president of the Marvin Motors Company, dozes over papers while his secretary Owen eyes him across a mahogany desk. A soft purring floats through the window from one of Marvin's own cars, six cylinders chanting power to the modern god of gasoline.

Marvin has lived with motors since the industry started, wrestling with them at meals and carrying them into dreams. Now their rhythm sounds in his brain just before fainting spells that come frequently of late. Owen, who never lies when truth will do, watches with care. Peril gathers around the old manufacturer.
6071-the-rover-boys-out-west-or-the-sear:
Arthur M. Winfield, in his introduction to boys, calls this the fourth Rover Boys volume, complete in itself. Dick, Tom, and Sam first appeared at Putnam Hall, a military academy in New York State, then survived a daring ocean rescue and a jungle adventure showing true American courage.

Now the boys return to Putnam Hall and head for the mining district of Colorado, where all trace of a valuable mine has been lost. They hunt the property, little dreaming of the perils awaiting them, and overcome one obstacle after another, getting the best of their enemies. The tale praises pluck, loyalty, and fair play.
6158-the-true-citizen-how-to-become-one:
W. F. Markwick and W. A. Smith wrote The True Citizen as a supplementary reader for seventh and eighth grade pupils, meeting a real need of the times. Many textbooks treat citizenship politically, they argue, while its higher moral and ethical aspects have been seriously overlooked.

The authors searched in vain for aid to joint development of natural faculties and moral instincts, aiming at well-rounded manhood on which a higher citizenship might be built. Character development matters more, they insist, than mere political instruction for public duties. Only loftier ethical standards can raise citizenship's grade.
6163-the-romance-and-tragedy-of-a-widely:
William Ingraham Russell tells, by himself, the romance and tragedy of a widely known New York business man. He dedicates the book to his wife, still his sweetheart after more than forty years of married life. He gives a true story unfinished, since the romance of youth has lingered through later years.

Tears fell on some manuscript pages, smiles on others, and still others were scorched with indignation. Russell writes to honor a noble woman's love, set straight matters misunderstood, and show friendship that comes in prosperity and vanishes in adversity. He hopes, too, that an appreciative public will buy the book.
6339-the-boy-scouts-on-a-submarine:
Captain John Blaine opens on a sleepy summer afternoon broken by joyous barking, as Elinor Pomeroy lays down her knitting and walks round the house. A young man races up the drive with three big dogs leaping about him, crying three cheers, for he has won out and his invention is a success. Elinor leads her excited brother to a hammock and orders him to begin at the beginning, and he tells of a meeting with the bureau of management that very morning.

The Boy Scouts of the title soon take to a submarine. Porky sits tied in a knot all night, Beany and the Sergeant race to cut him free, and a sergeant's knife ends the jest. Blaine writes a boys' book of invention, teamwork, and underwater adventure, where a brother's success becomes a patrol's mission. The tone is cheerful and brisk, with dogs and machinery sharing the stage.
6401-harlequin-and-columbine:
Booth Tarkington opens in a November week when horse show, football climax, and opera season crowd New York, and girls thank that conjunction for a glimpse of the great Talbot Potter. Potter, hearing multitudes, walks to rehearsal by Fifth Avenue, turning from Forty-fourth Street into a people sea whose northward eyes beat on his face like surf. His Fifth Avenue knows its Talbot Potter, and strangers who think the avenue notices nothing are wrong.

Neighbours later tease Canby, who took charge of a rehearsal for Potter's company. They ask how it felt to sit like a king making everyone step to suit him, whether pretty girls filled the company, and when he will hire a valet chauffeur. Tarkington writes theatre folk with comic affection, as Harlequin and Columbine play their old parts in modern dress, and a rehearsal room becomes a small kingdom.
6405-john-keble-s-parishes-a-history-of-:
Charlotte M. Yonge, an old inhabitant, writes the history of Hursley and Otterbourne, parishes of John Keble. Her source is a history compiled in 1808 by Reverend John Marsh, curate of Hursley, well and carefully done. The South Downs descend eight miles from the sea into clay, gravel, sand, and peaty bog, brought down by rivers Itchen and Test. West of the Itchen, where chalk gives way to other deposits, lies the uneven ground of this memoir, gravelly hills above clay valleys, both favourable to woods.

Fossils lie in the chalk, echini are picked up as Shepherds' Crowns, and great boulders puzzle observers. Great changes begin at the Restoration, when Robert Maunder becomes vicar in 1660 and parish registers turn to Latin, while Cranbury and Brambridge pass through Youngs and Wyndhams. Yonge writes parish history as geology, genealogy, and faith in one place.
6483-the-life-of-john-milton-volume-3-16:
David Masson's Life of John Milton, volume three, covers 1643 to 1649, narrated in connexion with the political, ecclesiastical, and literary history of his time. Book one runs July 1643 to March 1644. It pairs history of the Westminster Assembly's first eight months, civil war, and the Long Parliament with biography. Biography covers Milton still in Aldersgate Street, his marriage misfortune, and his first divorce treatise. The Assembly met first on Saturday, July 1, 1643, in Henry the Seventh's Chapel, after Dr. Twisse preached on John fourteen, eighteen.

About sixty nine members attended, Episcopal members conspicuous in canonical dress among plain Puritan suits. A mid passage turns to a poor inventive spirit, alchemist and husbandry writer, who dropped dead in London streets for want of food. He hung on Hartlib with a schedule of new inventions, including a process for making pure gold, though not with profit. Masson writes Milton inside his age.
6502-the-acadian-exiles-a-chronicle-of-t:
Arthur G. Doughty traces Acadia from its first French founders to the great sorrow that made its name known in song. He weighs where the name came from, whether from a Native word for a camp or a place of plenty, or from the old Greek Arcadia. Early maps, French writers, and the St. Lawrence valley all help fix the land on the page.

The chronicle then moves toward the Acadian people, their homes by the sea, and the expulsion that scattered them far from home. Doughty writes as a historian, careful with names and dates, yet alive to the human cost of the tale. Readers meet a small French world on the edge of a new continent, caught between empires.
6690-the-revolution-in-tanner-s-lane:
Mark Rutherford sets his novel in a dissenting chapel world, where the world outside, Pike Street, the theatre, and a friend of the people widen a young man's horizon. Chapters on tea à la mode, Jephthah, unconventional justice, and a strain on the cable lead to disintegration by degrees, politics and Pauline, and one body and one spirit.

The revolution here is inward as much as outward, a slow break with old faith and old ways. Rutherford writes with quiet, moral force, in plain, thoughtful prose. The Revolution in Tanner's Lane is a searching, humane novel of faith, doubt, and change in Victorian England.
6735-over-the-border-acadia-the-home-of-:
Eliza Chase travels over the border to Acadia, home of Evangeline, with chapters on the Bay of Fundy, the Basin of Minas, Port Royal, Annapolis, Digby, Halifax, Grand Pré, and Clare. A chronology opens in 1604, with De Monts' first landing, his arrival at Port Royal, and the colony's early hopes and losses. Jesuit priests, Argall's raid, and a Scotch colony follow.

Chase writes as a traveler with a poet's eye, quoting Julius Caesar on the day breaking in the east. Her Acadia is both a real shore and Longfellow's dream land. Over the Border is a charming, historic travel book for readers who love Evangeline's country.
69-the-32nd-mersenne-prime-predicted-by-:
Prime numbers of the form two to a power minus one have lured hunters for centuries. This file records the 32nd Mersenne prime, found by David Slowinski and published in honor of Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. The note dates the find to February 1993.

Computing the giant number took about 26.56 minutes on a four-processor Cray-2 running Maple. The bulk of the file is the prime itself, printed in long digit blocks. Readers can check its size and form against the Mersenne list. The file stands as a raw artifact of early supercomputer number hunting.
6926-memories-of-hawthorne:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop presents memories of Hawthorne that are, as she plainly says, really written by Sophia Hawthorne. The volume draws on Sophia's letters from earliest girlhood in 1820 to her last year in 1871, weeded only where a page could give no pleasure to a descendant. Lathrop found scarcely one such page, and she marvels at their thought and loveliness.

The book returns, in company with friends of her father and mother, to an old garden, familiar talk, and a circle of life full of beauty. Early chapters set the Hawthornes beside the Peabodys, with Sophia's mother and grandmother and General Palmer of the Revolution. It is a daughter's gift of a mother's voice, kept for family and for readers alike.
694-stories-from-everybody-s-magazine:
This volume gathers stories from the 1910 issues of Everybody's Magazine, a popular American monthly of the Progressive Era. The magazine mixed fiction with reform journalism, and its stories reflect that busy, hopeful age. Everybody's Magazine, a muckraking monthly, mixed fiction with exposes of trusts and fraud.

Readers meet a cross-section of 1910 taste, from adventure and romance to tales of city life and social change. The collection works as a time capsule, showing what a mass magazine offered its readers before the First World War. The 1910 stories show a magazine at its peak, before war and radio changed reading habits.
7170-the-life-and-genius-of-nathaniel-ha:
Frank Preston Stearns builds his life of Nathaniel Hawthorne from the writer's own words first: the passages Hawthorne addressed to readers, and the notebooks never meant for print. He then draws on the family books, Julian Hawthorne's life of his father, Rose Hawthorne Lathrop's memories, and George Parsons Lathrop's study, with reminiscences from friends filling out the rest.

Stearns pairs the life with a reading of the genius behind it, tracing how a shy, inward man made tales of guilt, pride, and grace. The portrait of Hawthorne that opens the book sets a grave, thoughtful tone, and the text moves between fact and judgment with ease. Readers get both the man and the mind that shaped his fiction.
7301-nathaniel-hawthorne:
George E. Woodberry's Nathaniel Hawthorne builds the life partly from Hawthorne's own autobiographical passages and the notebooks never meant for print. The rest comes chiefly from Julian Hawthorne's family biography of his father and mother, Rose Hawthorne Lathrop's memories, and George Parsons Lathrop's study, with books of reminiscences by contemporaries adding collateral matter.

Woodberry sifts these printed sources with a biographer's care, letting Hawthorne's inward life emerge from his own pages first. The result is a life that respects its subject's reserve while tracing how Salem, family, and conscience shaped the tales. Readers get a scholarly portrait, grounded in documents rather than gossip.
7380-alone:
Norman Douglas sets this novel in wartime London, where a narrator adrift in the city tries to find useful work. He calls at an Emergency Bureau, a hastily improvised shelter for privileged young men, and meets a pink-faced official in tortoise-shell goggles who fills in forms with cheerful optimism. Nothing is doing just then, but the narrator is told to call again.

From that small scene the book grows into a portrait of a man alone among institutions, officials, and polite evasions. Douglas writes with dry, amused detachment, letting the gap between grand wartime talk and small bureaucratic reality do the satirizing. The novel suits readers who like social comedy with a sting: a solitary figure navigating a city that promises much and delivers forms.
747-anomalies-and-curiosities-of-medicin:
George M. Gould and Walter L. Pyle compiled this vast medical reference on the strange and rare in human bodies and disease. Drawn from journals and case reports, it gathers accounts of giants and dwarfs, extra limbs, long life, strange births, and freaks of nature, each with its source noted. The scale is huge, running to thousands of cases.

The doctors present each case in sober, clinical prose, sorting wonders from frauds where they can. The book was meant for physicians, yet it fascinates lay readers too. It stands as a monument of Victorian medical curiosity, and as a record of what doctors saw, believed, and tried to explain before modern genetics.
748-the-brother-of-daphne:
Dornford Yates wrote this light comedy about Daphne and her brother, told with wit and a keen eye for manners. Chapters with titles such as Punch and Judy, Clothes and the Man, and The Judgement of Paris set the tone: social games, love scenes, and points of honour played for laughs. Daphne, at ease in her long chair, spars with the narrator from the first page.

Yates moves his people through parties, pictures, and country houses, where pride comes before a fall and love scenes turn on a word. The humour is urbane and a touch mischievous, never cruel. The book charms readers who enjoy a well-bred farce, where charm and cheek carry the day and all is found out in the end.
7551-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
Michel de Montaigne's Essays founded the personal essay, and this companion volume gathers short passages from them alongside pictures. It draws on the Essays in five volumes, which carry five etchings. Montaigne made his own mind, habits, and judgments his main subject. The passages are set out for browsing, so a reader can dip in anywhere and follow one thought at a time.

Read together, the passages sketch a thinker who trusted close self-study more than grand systems. Custom, schooling, honor, and the limits of knowledge recur across them, as does his habit of testing old sayings against his own conduct. The pictures give the browsing reader a face and a setting for the voice. It works best as a slow companion: a few pages at a time, then time to weigh what they suggest.
788-the-red-one:
Jack London gathered four tales in this 1919 volume, headed by the title story of Bassett, a sick man in the Solomon Islands. Bassett hears a vast, unearthly sound rolling from a mountain gorge, a peal he likens to an archangel's trump, and he strives to trace it to its source. The other tales follow in the same Pacific world.

The Hussy, Like Argus of the Ancient Times, and The Princess turn on love, fate, and the clash of white men and island peoples. London writes with his usual force, though the title tale leans toward mystery and awe. The book shows his late work at its most strange and haunting, far from the Yukon of his fame.
7923-american-historical-and-literary-cu: The series-one index volume of American Historical and Literary Curiosities by John Jay Smith and John F. Watson, closing the first run at part twenty-three, holds in text only the editor's note and title page. Like its companions, it is an illustration work whose plates live in the HTML edition, linked from the note.
819-the-history-of-the-telephone:
Herbert N. Casson wrote this history of the telephone just thirty-five years after its birth, when the art was already full grown. Three million telephones stood abroad, he notes, and seven million in America, the land of its birth. The book tells how ridicule gave way to wonder, and how the phone remade business and home.

Casson follows Bell and his rivals, the growth of exchanges, and the spread of wires across cities and farms. His prose is brisk and popular, full of anecdotes of first calls and early mishaps. The book is a vivid snapshot of a new technology in its first triumph, written while the wonder was still fresh.
8206-the-pilgrims-of-the-rhine:
Edward Bulwer Lytton, Lord Lytton, wrote The Pilgrims of the Rhine, prefixing The Ideal World, and dedicated the work to his brother Henry Lytton Bulwer. Much of the book, namely the tales that vary and relieve the voyages of Gertrude and Trevylyan, was written during a pleasant excursion the brothers made together some years before. Lytton recalls that their friendship, unlike that of near relations in general, grew stronger as their footsteps receded from the fields where they played as children.

The narrative follows the pilgrims down the Rhine, pausing for stories, legends, and reflections on love and art. Lytton's romantic prose suits the river's castles and vineyards. For readers of early Victorian romance, the book offers a leisurely, picturesque journey, and a window onto how the Rhine became a landscape of the imagination.
8412-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-v:
Francis W. Halsey selected and edited this third volume of Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, covering France and the Netherlands. In ten illustrated volumes, the series lets famous writers show Europe to readers at home. This volume gathers their accounts of Paris, the Seine and its bridges, and the Low Countries, with Halsey's introductions tying the selections together.

The idea is travel by anthology: instead of one guidebook voice, readers get many authors, each writing at their best about places they knew. For armchair travelers, the volume offers France and the Netherlands through literary eyes. It also preserves how earlier generations imagined Europe, before cheap travel made such books common.
8426-poems-of-paul-verlaine:
Gertrude Hall translated these poems of Paul Verlaine, the French symbolist, with pictures by Henry McCarter. Contents draw on Fêtes Galantes, with Clair de Lune and Mandoline, and La Bonne Chanson, love songs written in Verlaine's musical, melancholy voice. Hall's translations aim to carry Verlaine's music into English, a hard task with a poet who prized sound above statement.

Verlaine, whose life mixed brilliance and disorder, wrote poems that later poets took as models of suggestion over declaration. Readers new to French symbolism get a classic introduction, in translations made when Verlaine's fame was still fresh. The book suits reading aloud, where the music Hall sought can be heard.
8530-a-study-of-hawthorne:
George Parsons Lathrop wrote A Study of Hawthorne. Its contents trace the novelist's life and work: Point of View, Salem, Boyhood, College Days, and Fanshawe. Twilight of the Twice-Told Tales, Boston and Brook Farm, The Old Manse, and The Scarlet Letter follow, with Lenox and Concord, England and Italy, The Last Romance, and Personality.

Lathrop, himself a writer and editor, knew Hawthorne's circle, and his study mixes biography with criticism. Readers follow Hawthorne from Salem boyhood to the productive years that gave The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables, and on to the unfinished last romances. The book remains a readable, early critical life, from a near-contemporary.
8596-the-wheel-o-fortune:
Louis Tracy wrote this adventure novel about fortune turning fast, with pictures by James Montgomery Flagg. Chapter titles map the plot: a compact struck, a change of sky but not of habit, a woman seeking an ally, a shock for Mrs Haxton, and Massowah asserting itself. Desert chapters follow, with a Bisharin camel, a gallop in the dark, a flight and a fight, and three travellers whose road keeps twisting.

Tracy, known for The Wings of the Morning and The Pillar of Light, builds his story on sudden reversals of wealth and standing. Alliances form and break, and the wheel of the title lifts one character while dropping another. Readers who enjoy brisk Edwardian adventure, with colonial ports, desert travel, and romantic intrigue, will find a well-paced yarn that never lingers long on any single scene.
860-baby-mine:
Margaret Mayo wrote this domestic comedy about Alfred Hardy, a young man of fixed ideas and high ideals, proud of both. His college friend Jimmy Jinks, who has few ideas and no ideals, is glad of it, and the contrast between the two men drives the fun. Marriage, pride, and a baby soon test Alfred's fine theories.

Mayo writes with warmth and pace, turning a household tangle into farce without losing sympathy for her people. The comedy made her name on stage and in print, and its situations still ring true. The book suits readers who enjoy a light, well-made comedy about love, pride, and the gap between ideals and life.
8945-the-life-of-cicero-volume-one:
Anthony Trollope, the English novelist, wrote this life of Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman, published in New York in 1881. This first of two volumes follows Cicero from his youth and schooling through his early court cases, his rise as quaestor, aedile, and praetor, and his year as consul. Trollope admits at once his boldness in adding one more life.

Chapters deal with the Rome of Cicero's day, the trial of Verres, the plot of Catiline, and the shift of power toward the triumvirs, ending with exile. Trollope judges Cicero with warmth and candor, as a man of words in a violent age. Readers get a clear, humane life of a figure who shaped Latin prose.
8947-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-0:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume one, number three, January 1858, opens with Notes on Domestic Architecture. Arguing that if building many houses taught us to build well, Americans ought to excel, since never was there such a house-building people. Elsewhere, the writer notes, laws, customs, traditions, capital, land, or existing houses limit building. Houses are built wholesale by capitalists, with only a small minority building for themselves. The Atlantic, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, was only months old.

The issue's mix of essays, stories, and poems set the pattern for America's leading literary magazine, with contributors who would define the era. Readers get a first-year Atlantic in full: serious, curious, and confident that American letters deserved a magazine of their own. Historians of publishing and general readers alike will enjoy seeing a great magazine find its voice, starting with the very houses its readers lived in.
9051-sanine:
Mikhail Artsibashev, here spelled Artzibashef, wrote this Russian novel in the years after the failed 1905 revolt, and Percy Pinkerton turned it into English. Its hero, Vladimir Sanine, comes home to a small town and lives by his own code, scorning church rules, old morals, and the gloom of those around him. He urges friends to seek joy and truth in life itself.

Critics of the day praised the book's frank talk of sex and its vivid picture of Russian life, while others were shocked by its attack on common morals. Sanine remains a key novel of a despairing age, and a bold test of how far a hero can push freedom before it turns to harm.
9173-youth-its-education-regimen-and-hyg:
G. Stanley Hall, president of Clark University and professor of psychology, wrote this study of youth, its schooling, body, and health. The book opens with pre-adolescence, ages eight to twelve, close to nature and fit for drill, memory work, and habit. Later chapters treat muscles as organs of will and character.

Hall argues that schools stress small muscles and fine work too much, and neglect the body's larger powers. He surveys chorea, play, and spontaneous movement in children. The work remains a landmark of early child psychology, bold, wide, and of its age.
9265-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-2:
This August 1859 issue of The Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, opens with The Dramatic Element in the Bible. The essay stresses dramatic element in the Bible, not of it, since drama is an aspect of form, not of inspiration. It claims the painter's license, not the stage's tricks, in treating sacred themes.

Other pieces in the number, typical of the young magazine, join letters to public affairs. The Atlantic, founded just two years before, already shaped American thought. The issue is a fine sample of mid-century American letters at their most serious.
9312-from-whose-bourne:
Robert Barr, as Luke Sharp, wrote this mystery novel in 1893, with forty-seven illustrations. Its pictures trace a Venetian café, a murder, a broken toy, and a woman in the prisoner's dock crying, Guilty of what? William Brenton, Jane Morton, and a detective move through Venice and London as the plot tightens.

The title, from Hamlet's bourne of death, hints at the undiscovered country beyond life. Barr keeps the mystery taut and the scenes vivid. The novel is a fine sample of the Victorian detective tale, before Sherlock Holmes set the mold.
9381-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-2:
This October 1859 issue of The Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, opens with Daily Beauty. Toward four in the afternoon, Stanford Grey and his guest Daniel Tomes pause in an earnest argument of half an hour. What they debated matters not, the essay says; we take them leaning back, each convinced of his own case and his foe's rectitude.

The friendly strife subsides like boxers resting between rounds, in the essay's cheerful image. Other pieces join it in the young magazine's fourth volume. The issue is a fine sample of the Atlantic's early blend of letters and public thought.
9831-the-court-of-the-empress-josephine:
Imbert de Saint-Amand's history, translated by Thomas Sergeant Perry and published in 1900, follows Josephine at the height of Napoleon's empire. It opens with the empire's beginning and the journey to the Rhine, then moves to the Pope's arrival at Fontainebleau.

Chapters describe the coronation, the palace etiquette, the empress's household, the court festivities, and the journey to Milan for a second crowning. Napoleon himself appears often, charming and restless. Readers get court life in detail: ceremony, dress, gossip, and the strain behind the glitter of empire, from Paris to Italy.
9876-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-5:
This August 1862 number of the Atlantic Monthly, a magazine of literature, art, and politics, leads with an article on the new gymnastics. Its writer notes that physical culture is widely praised but little practiced, and that parents worry over children's decaying teeth, bent forms, and pallid faces.

The article then teaches dumb-bell exercises, ring and wand drills, and rules for wearing weights on the head, with a gymnastic crown. Other pieces in the number carry the magazine's usual mix of essays and stories. It is a window on Civil War America discovering exercise, health, and the gymnasium.
a-catechism-of-the-steam-engine: John Bourne explains the steam engine in question and answer form for every class of reader. The revised edition treats the power and performance of engines and boilers, the indicator, gauges, and the dynamometer. Further chapters give the proportions of boilers, heating surface, and the working of marine and locomotive engines. Bourne makes a complex machine plain through short questions answered in order.
a-florentine-tragedy-la-sainte-courtisan:
Oscar Wilde left both of these verse plays unfinished, and they appear here in a 1917 Methuen volume of his miscellaneous works, with a preface explaining their history. A Florentine Tragedy is set in Renaissance Florence, where a merchant comes home to find his wife with a young noble. La Sainte Courtisane turns to the Egyptian desert, a holy hermit, and a beautiful courtesan.

In Florence, talk of cloth and money turns to swords before the night ends. In the desert piece, the hermit and the courtesan trade faith and desire in rich, strange speeches. Both fragments show Wilde reaching beyond drawing-room comedy toward dark, poetic drama, and both break off before completion.
a-rebellious-heroine:
John Kendrick Bangs plays a literary game in this tale from the 1896 Harper and Brothers edition, illustrated by W. T. Smedley. A novelist finds that the heroine he invented will not stay inside the story he planned for her. She has opinions about her own plot, her hero, and her author, and she acts on them.

The comedy runs on the collision between the author's intentions and his character's free will, a joke Bangs handles with the light touch of his House-Boat on the Styx. Chapters move between the writing desk and the world of the book. The piece is an early, cheerful example of fiction laughing at its own machinery.
a-ride-across-palestine:
Anthony Trollope tells how circumstances took him to the Holy Land without a companion, in this tale from the 1864 Tales of All Countries. He calls himself a gregarious animal, meant to go in pairs, and owns he was sad at heart in his Jerusalem hotel. Next morning he starts on horseback for the Dead Sea, Jordan, and Jericho.

Alone among strangers, he falls in with a fellow traveler whose company changes the ride, and the tale turns from sightseeing to character. Church of the Sepulchre, Mount of Olives, and Bethany pass by, but Trollope's interest is the living people on the road. The piece is travel writing worn as fiction, in his easy, confiding voice.
a-study-of-hawthorne: George Parsons Lathrop offers a portrait of Hawthorne in this study, expressly not designed as a biography. Assisted by sympathy with his subject rather than personal acquaintance, he follows Salem, boyhood and college days, and Fanshawe. The twilight of the Twice-Told Tales, Boston and Brook Farm, and the Old Manse follow. The Scarlet Letter, Lenox and Concord, England and Italy, the last romance, and a closing comparison with Poe and Irving complete the portrait.
address-to-the-inhabitants-of-the-coloni: Richard Johnson, chaplain to the New South Wales settlements and Norfolk Island, addresses settlers, prisoners and convicts at Port Jackson in a pastoral letter written in 1792. He writes as a friend and preacher who once spoke to a small settlement face to face, now grown and scattered. The address urges its readers toward faith, good conduct and mutual care in a distant colony.
alone:
Norman Douglas wrote Alone as a book of travel sketches, most of them Italian, and dedicated it to his friend Edward Hutton. The contents run from Mentone and Levanto to Siena, Pisa, Viareggio, Rome, Olevano. Sorrento, with an introduction that looks back at the Great War and his comic failure to find patriotic employment in London offices.

Each place gets a loose essay of walks, inns, food, talk, and people met by the way, written in Douglas's dry, amused voice. Nothing is systematic: a town is a starting point for memory, argument, and appetite. Readers who know South Wind, named on his title page, will recognize the manner — a cultivated idler thinking aloud in Mediterranean sun.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith's first series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities presents the opening sequence of the plate collection in full. The work reproduces historic documents and literary relics as images, so the text file holds only what scanning could capture, with the editor pointing to the HTML edition. Series one sets the pattern the later series follows.
anomalies-and-curiosities-of-medicine:
George M. Gould and Walter L. Pyle compiled this encyclopedic collection of medical anomalies. Its title page announces the scope: rare and extraordinary cases, and the most striking instances of abnormality in all branches of medicine and surgery. The material is drawn from medical literature from its origin to the present day, then abstracted, classified, annotated, and indexed.

The introductory essay argues that the anomalous has always driven science: monsters and strange growths show nature's workshop with its guard down. The body of the book then catalogs case after case from journals and older authors — unusual births, giant and dwarf growth, strange injuries survived, foreign bodies, and odd diseases. It became a standard sourcebook for physicians and, later, for writers of medical curiosities, valued for its citations as much as its wonders.
baby-mine:
Margaret Mayo built her farce Baby Mine around Alfred Hardy, a young husband of fixed ideas who wants children. His college friend Jimmy Jinks happily lets Alfred make up his mind for him. Alfred's wife Zoie has other plans, and deception begins. The novel follows the hit stage play Mayo also wrote.

Zoie and her friend Aggie borrow babies to sustain a lie. The borrowed infants multiply until husbands find themselves holding three youngsters at once. Smashed glass, whispered warnings, and doors closed softly mark the escalating panic. Mayo keeps the machinery brisk and the dialogue rapid. The comedy was a Broadway success, and its situation, a wife's fib meeting a husband's obsession, still plays cleanly.
beechcroft-at-rockstone:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Beechcroft at Rockstone opens with a telegram in the Mohun sisters' parlour. Jane Mohun reads it: Lily, Jasper, accident, come. Her delicate sister Adeline stipulates conditions from her chair. Jane packs her ever-ready bag and catches the 11.20 train.

Sir Jasper's accident disperses his children among relations, and Beechcroft takes its share of the household. Gillian's help, the Halfpenny mother, and little Primrose arrive in Jane's planning. Rockstone is the family's seaside place, where invalids and schoolgirls must be fitted into a small house. Yonge's dispersion becomes an education: duty distributed among the willing and the reluctant. The novel belongs to her Mohun family chronicle. Its pleasures are small, exact, and moral, the management of a household standing in for the government of a soul.
betty-zane:
Zane Grey's first novel, Betty Zane, honors his own ancestor, Elizabeth Zane. Her heroism came at the siege of Fort Henry in 1782. His author's note calls that fight the last battle of the American Revolution. Grey dedicates the book to the Betty Zane chapter of the Daughters of the Revolution and doubts the magazine versions he had read. Colonel Ebenezer Zane's frontier settlement at Wheeling anchors the story.

Betty runs powder through enemy fire to save the fort. The hunter Lewis Wetzel moves through the woods chapters like a force of nature. Betty herself must hold his knife arm when he rises against an enemy. Grey built a career on this mixture of family legend, frontier history, and romance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dunf: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dunfermline describes a Scottish abbey founded about 1070 by King Malcolm Canmore and Queen Margaret. David the First remodelled it as a Benedictine house with an abbot and twelve monks from Canterbury. Its buildings were so vast that three sovereigns with their retinues might lodge there together, though Edward the First burned them in 1304.
