Dunfermline took Iona's place as Scotland's royal burial ground, the Westminster Abbey of Scotland, holding Malcolm, Margaret, David the First and Robert Bruce. Its tombs survive within the ruined Lady chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Augustine's describes a Benedictine monastery at Canterbury, founded in 605 on the site of St. Pancras' church. King Ethelbert had given that church to St. Augustine in 597. Named for Sts. Peter and Paul, it was enlarged and renamed in 978 by St. Dunstan for Peter, Paul and Augustine, whose body lay in the crypt. At the dissolution in 1538 the abbot and thirty monks gave it up for pensions. Henry the Eighth took it as a palace, and in 1844 its remains were sold for a college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-bisho:
Acacius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, was disciple and biographer of Eusebius the historian, succeeding him in the see in 340. Nothing is known of his birth date or country, though he was probably a Syrian. His nickname, monophthalmos, one-eyed, likely came from a personal defect, though possibly also as a sly comment on his shiftiness and his rare gift for ambiguous statement.

He was a deeply learned prelate and a patron of studies, author of a treatise on Ecclesiastes and of six books of miscellanies surviving only in fragments. He is chiefly remembered for opposing St. Cyril of Jerusalem bitterly and for his shifting part in the Arian controversy. He professed the Nicaean formularies under Jovian in 363, swung back under Valens in 364, was condemned at Lampsacus, and, Baronius says, died in 366.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-perse:
Adam of Perseigne was a French Cistercian, Abbot of Perseigne in the diocese of Mans, born about the middle of the twelfth century. Thought first a canon regular, later a Marmoutier Benedictine, then a Cistercian. About 1180 he became Abbot of Perseigne, where his holy, wise reputation drew leading figures of his time for counsel.

At Rome he conferred with Calabria's celebrated mystic Joachim, Abbot of Flora, on the latter's revelations, and he helped Foulques de Neuilly preach the Fourth Crusade. Rome published his letters and sermons in 1662 under the title Adami Abbatis Perseniae Ordinis Cisterciensis Mariale. The entry cites Mignon in the dictionary of Catholic theology for this brief monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonse-de-l:
Alphonse de Lamartine, French poet, was born at Mâcon in 1790, died at Paris in 1869. Born of a noble Christian family, he read the Bible. Later he read Fénelon, Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, Chateaubriand, Mme de Staël, Racine, Voltaire, Parny, Tasso, Dante, Petrarch, Shakespeare, Ossian, especially the last. About twenty, he met Graziella, a cigarette girl, at a relative's house in Naples.

Hitherto an imitator, henceforth his guide was his own inspiration. Madame Charles is his Raphael's Julie and his poems' Elvire. He entered poetry with Les Méditations Poétiques of 1820, awaking famous. Other works: Les Secondes Méditations (1823), Harmonies Poétiques et Religieuses (1830), Jocelyn (1836), La Chute d'un Ange (1838). Two epic fragments dreamed for humanity and Recueillements Poétiques (1839) returned to lyricism, below his early works. In 1835 he published Voyage en Orient, a brilliant account of his Orient journey, losing his daughter. Thenceforth he wrote prose only.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alsace-lorrai:
Alsace-Lorraine is the German Imperial Territory so known, divided for state purposes into three civil districts. Lower and Upper Alsace and Lorraine include the bishoprics of Strasbourg and Metz, immediately subject to the Holy See. The census of 1 December 1900 distributes the population as follows. Strasbourg diocese: 821,612 Catholics, 304,204 Protestants, 3,192 Dissidents, 25,414 Jews, 319 of unknown religion, 1,154,741 total. Metz diocese: 488,838 Catholics, 67,874 Protestants, 1,224 Dissidents, 6,850 Jews, 43 of unknown religion, 564,829 total.

These figures exclude 34,367 Strasbourg soldiers and 44,491 Metz soldiers, under the Army Bishop in Berlin's jurisdiction. The entry treats cathedral chapters, diocesan administration, parishes, stipends, church taxes, and religious houses. It also covers clerical seminaries, episcopal gymnasia, collections among the faithful, elementary education, art monuments, and institutions of charity. The Bishop of Strasbourg has made six church collections obligatory. They fall on the Sunday after Epiphany for the African missions, on Good Friday for the Christians of the East, and at Easter and Pentecost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-stone:
The altar stone is one solid piece of natural stone, blessed by a bishop, big enough for Sacred Host and chalice. The stone must be natural and solid, not some other material at all. It is set into or placed on a structure serving as an altar where the whole altar is unconsecrated. Sometimes the whole table, or mensa, replaces the smaller stone.

Called a portable altar, it lets Mass be said where no consecrated altar stands. Its consecration by a bishop gives even a makeshift altar its sacred character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-wine:
Altar wine is one of the two elements required for the Eucharist, pure grape juice naturally and properly fermented, called vinum de vite. Raisin wine may serve if colour and taste judge it pure, and it comes sweet or dry, weak or strong, white or red. Since only genuine wine makes the sacrifice valid and licit, the celebrant must procure pure wines. Safest is buying directly from a conscientious manufacturer rather than second hand.

Vinegar, putrid or corrupted wine, unripe-grape pressings, and wine so watered it can hardly be called wine are forbidden. Wine turning to vinegar or putrid, and unfermented juice, are grievous matter to use yet still valid. Weak wines may be conserved with a little grape brandy or alcohol against souring in transport, under stated conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-borg:
Ambrogio Borgognone, real name Ambrogio Stefani da Fossano, was a distinguished Italian painter and architect, born at Milan about 1455 and dead there in 1523. His name's origin is variously explained. He painted in tempera, in oil in tempera's style, and in fresco; early work lacked freedom, but Leonardo da Vinci's beneficent influence later shaped him.

The Certosa near Pavia's façade is credited to him, its choir stalls and woodwork carved from his designs, with his Crucifixion altarpiece painted there. Great refinement and deep religious feeling shape his work, with beautiful celestial and mundane types. Public galleries hold his Marriage of St. Catherine at London's National Gallery and Madonna pictures at Berlin, Munich, and Dresden. Milan's Brera holds the Assumption, and Pavia Academy holds Christ Bearing His Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Lindisfarne, now called Holy Island, lies about two miles off the Northumberland coast, south-east of Berwick. About three miles long and one and a half wide, it joins the mainland at low water. A three-mile track from Beal crosses the sands, marked by wooden posts. Saint Aidan, a Columban monk-bishop from Iona, founded his see here in 635 at King Oswald's request.

The island became the mother church of Northumbria, seat of sixteen bishops and a centre of missionary work. It earned the name Iona of England. Bishop Carileph gave Lindisfarne to the Benedictines of Durham in 1082. Its Norman church rose under them, and the priory lived until 1536. The site passed to the Dean and Chapter of Durham, then to the crown in 1613. Its famous gospel codex, lost for a century, reached the British Museum by way of Sir Robert Cotton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-ciccio:
Doubt surrounds Andrea Ciccione, a sculptor and architect born at Naples in the early fifteenth century. Writers of note omit him entirely, while others, found reliable, record him. A pupil of Masuccio the younger, he is said to have built San Severino's cloister, the church and monastery of Monte Oliveto, and several palaces.

He carved the monument of Giosue Caracciolo. Queen Joanna II picked him to make the tomb of her brother King Ladislaus in San Giovanni a Carbonara. It towers three stories, flanked by allegorical figures, with Ladislaus on his war horse at the top. Joanna hired him again after her lover Gian Caracciolo was murdered. Above that tomb stands a sarcophagus carried by three armed knights for Justice, Strength, and Prudence. Caracciolo stands above, coloured as if alive. The tombs draw notice for colour work and virtues dressed as soldiers. No dates survive for Ciccione.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-byrne:
Andrew Byrne, Bishop of Little Rock, was born at Navan in Ireland in 1802 and died at Helena, Arkansas, in 1862. A student when Bishop England sought volunteers in 1820 for the new Diocese of Charleston, he accompanied the bishop to the United States. Ordained at Charleston in 1827, he did missionary work in the Carolinas and served years as vicar-general.

In 1836 he moved to New York, serving at Saint Patrick's, Saint James's, and the Nativity. In 1843 he turned Carroll Hall, cradle of New York's school system, into Saint Andrew's church. While pastor in 1844, the Diocese of Little Rock was created, and Byrne was named its bishop. Arkansas then held only about 700 Catholics with one priest and two churches. Before his death he claimed nine priests, eleven churches, thirty stations, and twelve schools. He visited Ireland for workers, introduced the Sisters of Mercy from Dublin, and nearly arranged a Fort Smith college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiochus-of-:
Antiochus of Palestine, seventh-century monk born near Ancyra, lived first solitary, then became Abbot of St. Saba's laura near Jerusalem. He witnessed the 614 Persian invasion and Bedouin massacre of forty-four companions. After Chosroes conquered the Holy Land, Ancyra fell in 619, forcing Attaline's monks to wander homeless. Unable to carry many books, they had Eustathius ask Antiochus for a Scripture abridgment and martyrdom account.

In compliance he wrote the Pandects of Holy Scripture, 130 chapters of moral sentences drawn from Scripture and early ecclesiastical writers. He also wrote an Exomologesis prayer relating Jerusalem's miseries since the Persian invasion and begging divine mercy for the Holy City. The Pandects' first chapter tells the martyrdom; its last lists heretics from Simon Magus to Severus of Antioch's Monophysite followers. The book is specially valuable for extracts of lost works, showing an then-uncommon interest in early Christian literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-elisa:
Antoine-Elisabeth Dareste de la Chavanne, a French historian born in Paris in 1820, taught history for decades at Lyons. After study at the Ecole Normale, he took a doctorate in letters. He held chairs at Grenoble and then at Lyons, where he served twenty years and became dean of letters in 1865. Several of his books won prizes from the French Academy.

His works ranged from a study of French administration since Philip Augustus to a history of farming classes. His largest work was an eight-volume history of France. Written clearly and fully, they treated the Roman Church fairly despite his Gallican leanings, a French view that stressed local church rights. Late in life he helped found the Catholic University of Lyons and served as rector of its academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assistant-at-:
Assistants at the Pontifical Throne, in Latin assistens throno pontificio, are bishops belonging to the Papal Chapel who stand toward the pope much as cathedral canons stand toward their bishop. At solemn functions these assistants, wearing cope and mitre, surround the pope's throne, while other bishops lack privilege to stand in his immediate vicinity.

To this college belong ex officio certain archbishops and bishops, plus those to whom the pope has given the privilege by brief, or short papal letter. Throne assistants rank immediately after cardinals, may celebrate Mass in private oratories, and may dispose of a set sum from their episcopal benefices for clerics or relations. They may also set it aside for their own obsequies. They are always made counts of the Apostolic Palace and belong to the Pontifical Family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asylums-and-c:
Asylums and Care for the Insane argues against a common reproach. That reproach says proper care for the insane and fitting institutions arose only in recent generations, and that the church, so active in humanitarian work, failed here. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries hospital treatment and nursing fell to their lowest ebb in history, and care for the insane shared that decay and was its worst feature.

As a matter of fact, the article argues, the church from earliest times arranged care for the insane, and some arrangements anticipated important modern advances. It was following the religious revolt in Germany, felt in other countries, that church charitable institutions suffered and hospitals and asylums of all kinds declined. Insanity has been known as long as recorded history runs, and the entry follows care from early church provision through Pinel and modern reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augusta-theod:
Augusta Theodosia Drane, known in religion as Mother Francis Raphael, was an English Dominican writer born near London in 1823 who died at Stone in 1894. Her parents were Protestants, and her father managed an East India trading house. Wide reading in youth fed her gifts, and Burnet's History of the Reformation, she said, first caused her conversion. She consulted Keble and Pusey without satisfaction, but a local vicar's talk of the Third Order of St Dominic moved her deeply.

She was received into the Church at Tiverton in 1850 and entered the Dominican Third Order at Clifton in 1852. At Stone she taught, wrote, and rose through office: mistress of novices, mistress of studies, prioress, and finally provincial in 1881. Her books ranged from lives of St Dominic and St Catherine of Siena to histories of England, tales, and school texts. She also translated Lacordaire's Inner Life and edited the papers of Archbishop Ullathorne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldassare-ca:
Baldassare Castiglione was an Italian prose writer born near Mantua in 1478, who died at Toledo in 1529. After classical schooling at Milan, he served Ludovico il Moro, then Francesco Gonzaga of Mantua. In 1504 Urbino became his home, in service to Duke Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, where he spent his best years. That court's splendor drew the age's finest writers and artists.

In 1513 Guidobaldo's heir made him a count and later ambassador to the Holy See. Pope Clement VII sent him as envoy to Charles V in 1524, but Rome was sacked in 1527 and Clement captured. The disaster broke Castiglione in health and spirits and hastened his death. His fame rests on the Cortegiano, in four books, picturing the ideal courtier's accomplishments and character. Begun in 1514 and finished four years later, it waited until 1528 for print and reached a dozen languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bayonne:
Bayonne, ancient Lapurdum, is a diocese covering the Basses-Pyrénées, reorganized in 1802 to absorb Oloron, Lescar, and parishes of Dax and Tarbes. Suffragan to Toulouse until 1822, it then passed to Auch. Tradition names the martyr St Leo, of the miraculous fountain, its first bishop, but no bishop is historically known before the sixth century. Until 1655 it held Spanish lands, four archpresbyteries left from Charlemagne's conquests beyond the Pyrenees.

Lescar's legend claims St Julian as first bishop, but history names Galactorius of Lescar and Gratus of Oloron, both at Agde in 506. Christopher de Beaumont, later Archbishop of Paris, held Bayonne from 1741 to 1745, and Astros from 1820 to 1830. Betharram's Auxiliary Priests of the Sacred Heart, founded in 1841, teach and mission from Bethlehem to Buenos Aires and Montevideo. The Bernardines of Anglet, founded in 1846, keep perpetual silence between prayer and needlework.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-bo:
Bernard of Botone, generally called Parmensis after Parma, his birthplace, was a noted thirteenth-century canonist, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. His birth date is unknown, and he died in 1263, or by another account in 1266. Under Tancred he studied canon law at Bologna, where he later held the chair and taught Durantis.

A canonry at Bologna cathedral and chaplaincies to Popes Innocent IV and Alexander IV placed him at the centre of church law. His glosses, or line-by-line notes, on the Decretals became a standard teaching text. His tomb inscription calls him chancellor of the University of Bologna, a fitting honour for a master of the schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berne:
Berne, the Swiss federal capital since 1848, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Fourth city of Switzerland in population and capital of its canton, it stands nearly 1,800 feet above sea level on a peninsula thrust into the River Aar. Its people grew from about 5,000 in the Middle Ages to 64,064 in 1900, mostly German-speaking Protestants.

Bridges, churches, and civic buildings fill the middle of the piece, from the iron Kirchenfeld bridge to the Holy Trinity church and the parliament buildings of 1895 to 1902. Catholic life, a minority of about 6,278 souls, gets its own count of parishes and schools. The entry joins topography, history, and church statistics in one civic portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-payne:
Blessed John Payne, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in the Diocese of Peterborough, he died at Chelmsford on 2 April 1582. He reached Douai in 1574 and took orders at Cambrai two years later, and sailed for England with Blessed Cuthbert Mayne, living mostly with Anne Petre at Ingatestone in Essex.

Early in July 1581 he and George Godsalve were arrested in Warwickshire through the spy Eliot, examined by Walsingham, and sent to the Tower, where Payne was racked twice. Eliot charged him with a plot against the queen's life, and though no proof backed the tale, a Chelmsford jury gave the expected verdict. At his execution the crowd stopped the final barbarities until he was dead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-stone: Blessed John Stone, an English martyr, was executed at the Dane-John in Canterbury, likely in December 1539, for rejecting the king's supremacy. An Austin friar of Canterbury and doctor of divinity, he was the friar of whom Bishop Ingworth complained in December 1538. Ingworth said Stone held at all times that the king may not head the Church of England. In prison, after three days of fasting, he heard a voice urging courage for the truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-delph: Blessed Delphine, a member of the Franciscan Third Order, was born in Provence in 1284 and died on 26 November 1358. Orphaned in infancy, she was raised under her uncles' guardianship and her aunt, Abbess of St. Catherine of Sorbo. She took a vow of virginity and kept it faithfully. Married at twenty to Elzéar, Count of Sarban, the couple took the Third Order habit and lived in prayer, penance, and charity until his death in 1323.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret of Lorraine, Duchess of Alencon, turned from court life to found a Poor Clare monastery at Argentan. Born at Vaudemont in 1463 and orphaned young, she was raised by her grandfather Rene of Anjou. She married the Duke of Alencon in 1488 and was widowed in 1492.

After ruling her duchy and raising her children, she retired to Mortagne with sisters following the rule of Saint Elizabeth. She then brought nuns to Argentan and placed the new house under Saint Clare's rule. She took the habit there and made vows in October 1520. She died a year later at sixty-two. Efforts to gain Roman recognition of her cult were still under way when the entry was written.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bodone:
Bodone, a titular see of Albania, stands on the site of ancient Dodona in Epirus, below Mount Tomaros near Janina. A Christian church rose there on the temple of Zeus. Bishops of Dodona appear at Ephesus in 431, Chalcedon in 451, and in letters to Emperor Leo in 458 and Pope Hormisdas in 516.

When Naupactus replaced Nicopolis late in the tenth century, Dodona became its first suffragan see. Later lists call it Bounditza or Bonditza, and John of Bonditza signed a synodal act in 1229. The Greek residential bishopric vanished at an unknown date. Rome long used the forms Bodona and Bodonensis, and an 1894 decree ordered the see suppressed at its titular's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brisbane:
Brisbane, the Queensland diocese south of the 24th parallel, covers some 200,000 square miles with its cathedral city as state capital. Settled as a convict station in 1825 and opened to free settlers in 1842, the Moreton Bay District held only 2,257 white souls in 1843, with one shanty church and no school. Passionists tried an aboriginal mission on Stradbroke Island in 1843 and left by 1846.

Fathers McGinnety and Hanly arrived in December 1843 as the first stationed priests, and the diocese rose in 1859 with James O'Quinn as first bishop. He found two priests, two churches, two schools, and 7,676 Catholics in a vast see. Arriving with five priests and six sisters in 1861, he organized immigration, endured bare-earth beds and damper fare on visitations, and built the church across Queensland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caltagirone:
Caltagirone is a Sicilian city in the province of Catania, built on two heights about 2,000 feet above the sea and joined by a bridge. Some take it for ancient Hybla Minor, others for ancient Gela. In the Middle Ages Saracens made it a stronghold, and its name's first syllables come from the Arabic kalaat, castle. Genoese failed to drive the Arabs out, but the Normans later took it with the rest of Sicily.

It once belonged to Syracuse, and when Syracuse became a metropolis, Caltagirone rose as its suffragan, its first bishop being Gaetano Maria Trigona, later moved to Palermo. The diocese counts 115,500 people, with 25 parishes, 112 churches and chapels, and 199 secular and 48 regular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carcassonne:
Carcassonne is a French diocese covering the whole department of Aude as suffragan to Toulouse. The Concordat of 1802 joined several older sees into one. The old diocese of Carcassonne, nearly all of Narbonne, most of Saint-Papoul, parts of Alet and Mirepoix, plus the old Perpignan diocese formed the new see. Perpignan was restored as its own diocese in 1822.

The diocese itself dates from after 533, when Visigoths sought a bishopric to offset losing Lodève and Uzès, with Sergius in 589 as its first known bishop. The entry also traces Narbonne, whose first bishop Paulus is linked by local tradition to Sergius Paulus of the Acts. Later holders include Guy Goulques, who became Pope Clement IV, and Bishop de la Bouillerie, a mystical writer, at Carcassonne from 1855 to 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-vercell:
Carlo Vercellone was a Barnabite biblical scholar born at Biella who died at Rome in January 1869. He joined the order at Genoa in 1829. He read philosophy in Turin and theology in Rome under Aloysius Ungarelli, and taught sacred subjects in Alessandria, Turin, Perugia, and Parma. In 1847 he became president of the Barnabite college at Rome, later adding the offices of procurator and then general of his order.

His first publication, in 1857, was a five-volume edition of the Vatican manuscript of Scripture prepared by Cardinal Mai. Its preface letter admitted its flaws. He at once set out to correct it from Mai's notes, producing a new octavo New Testament at Rome in 1859. Later work defended the authenticity of the adulteress passage in John's Gospel. He edited nine Gerdil pamphlets on church hierarchy and answered Renan on Semitic languages in 1869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cavaliere-par:
Paris Bordone was an eminent painter of the Venetian school, born at Treviso in 1500 and dying at Venice in 1570. Of noble family, he entered Titian's school and studied there for several years. Afterwards he learned from Giorgione. Feeling the influence of both, he settled into Titian's manner so well that his paintings are at times taken for Titian's own.

In portraiture he yielded to none but Titian. Early work took him to Venice, Vicenza, and Treviso. At Treviso his dome paintings at San Vicenzo showed the Annunciation, Nativity, Adoration of the Shepherds, Crucifixion, Ascension, and Assumption. Invited to France, where he was knighted, he painted the royal family and court figures before returning to Italy, leaving works in Venice, Rome, Padua, and Genoa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesar-guillau:
César Guillaume La Luzerne was a French cardinal born at Paris in 1738 and dying there in 1821. Educated at the Collège de Navarre, he rose through his kinsmen the Lamoignons to the See of Langres in 1770, which made him duke and peer of the realm. He then sat in the Assembly of Notables in 1788 and the Estates-General in 1789.

His efforts to hold the Constituent Assembly to moderation failed, and he withdrew from it. In 1791 he refused the constitutional oath and left for Constance and Venice, where he housed French exiles generously and wrote at length. After the Restoration he returned, became cardinal and state minister in 1817, and regained Langres. An able apologist, he stood for an old Gallicanism whose revival failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chalons-sur-m:
Châlons-sur-Marne is a diocese comprising the department of Marne, except for the arrondissement of Reims. Joined to Meaux in 1802 and to Reims in 1821, it was re-established in 1822 as suffragan to Reims. Local legends credit St. Memmius, sent by St. Peter with his sister Poma and Sts. Donatian and Domitian, with evangelizing Châlons in the first century, but the revised Breviary list of diocesan saints suppresses these legends.

Abbé Duchesne dates the see's founding to the fourth century. Amandinus, its ninth bishop, attended the Council of Tours in 461. St. Lumier, bishop about 580, was famed for miraculous power over animals. At Capetian coronations the Châlons bishop invariably bore the royal ring. Eugene III consecrated the cathedral in 1147, assisted by St. Bernard and eighteen cardinals. At the close of 1905 the diocese counted 231,411 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charlemagne:
Charlemagne, Charles the Great, was king of the Franks and the West's first Christian emperor. He was born in 742 and died at Aachen in 814. His birthplace, Aachen or Liège, was never settled. Son of Pepin the Short, he won Rome's acknowledgment as its chief protector. Of fifty-three campaigns, only a dozen or so were not fought for the Church. Eighteen campaigns against the Saxons sought to extinguish their pagan worship.

In his later years his sons led expeditions such as Louis's capture of Barcelona. He worked to conciliate jealous Constantinople, which treated the Roman crowning as schism. He stayed healthy until his sixty-eighth year, when fevers struck and left him limping. He acted as his own physician, resisting doctors who urged boiled meat over roast. No portrait from his lifetime survives, though a very ancient statuette stands in the Musée Carnavalet at Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-erski:
Charles Erskine was a cardinal born at Rome in 1739 and dead at Paris in 1811. Son of Colin Erskine and Agatha Gigli of Anagni, he was educated by Cardinal Henry, Duke of York, at the Scots College in Rome. In 1782 Pius VI gave him the pro-auditorship and the Promoter of the Faith office, then domestic prelacy, a St. Peter's canonry, and the deanship of the consistorial advocates.

Sent as papal envoy to England in October 1793, Erskine built excellent relations with court and ministry. He left in 1801, returned to Rome, and was created cardinal in January 1803. After the French invasion of 1808 he shared the pope's confinement in the Quirinal. Napoleon ordered him to Paris in 1809, and ill health forced the journey in January 1810; he declined gradually and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-farra:
Charles Farrar Browne, known as Artemus Ward, was a humorist born at Waterford, Maine, in 1834 and dead at Southampton, England, in 1867. Schooled in his native town, he entered the Skowhegan Clarion printing office as an apprentice at fourteen. A year later he worked in Boston on the Carpet-Bag.

In 1858, at twenty-four, his national reputation began as a reporter for the Cleveland Plaindealer under the name Artemus Ward. He later edited a paper in the manner of London's Punch, succeeding Charles G. Leland. Yet it was as a lecturer that he won fame and fortune, from Babes in the Woods in New York to Sixty Minutes in Africa in Philadelphia. In 1866 he sailed for England, where London hailed him and his Punch letters recalled Yellowplush, before sickness cut his brilliant career short.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-marie:
An entry on Charles Marie de La Condamine, the French explorer and physicist who measured the shape of the earth in South America. Born in Paris in 1701, he served briefly as a soldier, then explored African and Asia Minor coasts before being chosen in 1735 to lead an expedition to the equator. Its task was to measure a meridian, a north-south arc, and so settle whether the globe flattens toward the poles.

With companions Bouguer and Godin, and Spanish officers Juan and Ulloa, La Condamine worked eight years in Ecuador, triangulating mountain country and noting that tall peaks deflect a pendulum by their pull. The expedition opened tropical America to wider science, though its instruments were crude by later standards. He is also credited with bringing rubber, called caoutchouc, into Europe and with trying to introduce smallpox inoculation in France. He died in Paris in 1774.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cheyenne:
Wyoming, an area of 97,575 square miles, forms the Diocese of Cheyenne. Founded on 9 August 1887, it had been part of the Diocese of Omaha and before that of the Vicariate of Nebraska. Its first bishop, Maurice Burke, was consecrated in October 1887. The first recorded Mass in Wyoming was said by the Jesuit Father De Smet on Green River's open prairie on 4 July 1840.

De Smet passed through Wyoming many times as missionary and army chaplain, and Canadian priests ministered at Fort Laramie. Settlement was slow on the arid soil, railroads came late, and many Catholics lived thirty years without Mass or priest. By the census of 1907 the diocese counted about 10,000 Catholics in a population of 100,000, with twenty-two churches, seventeen priests, twenty missions without churches, and St. Stephen's Mission Indian school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-doc:
A vast entry on Christian doctrine, taken first as the act of teaching and the knowledge taught, the same as catechesis and catechism. Didaskalia and didache in the New Testament, doctrina in the Vulgate, mark teaching as a bishop's chief duty in the Pastoral Epistles. Katechesis means instruction by word of mouth, above all by question and answer, for those preparing to enter Christianity.

The entry treats its subject under three heads: history of catechetics, practical catechetics, and modern catechisms. Oral question-and-answer teaching held a leading place in the moral and religious schools of the Church. The word catechism once meant the act of teaching itself, as Shakespeare uses it, and only later settled on the printed question-and-answer book. Its history runs from apostolic instruction through medieval and modern schools to the catechisms of the present day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cloyne:
Cloyne, from Gaelic Cluain-uania, Cave-meadow, covers the northern half of County Cork. It counts 140 priests, 47 parishes, 16 convents, 8 Brothers' schools, 235 primary schools, Saint Colman's College, and Loreto Convent at Fermoy, besides high schools at Queenstown, now Cobh, and elsewhere. Saint Colman's Cathedral at Queenstown, begun in 1869 under Bishop Keane and continued under Bishop McCarthy, stood near completion in 1908. The medieval cathedral still stands at Cloyne, used by Protestants since the sixteenth century.

Saint Colman MacLenin, from 560 to 601, turned from poet-historian to become first Bishop of Cloyne in 560, receiving a royal land grant. Religious poems are attributed to him, including a life of Saint Senan. Fergal, Abbot-Bishop of Cloyne, was massacred by Danes in 888, and Cloyne suffered seven devastations from 822 to 1137. Church records were destroyed, so few prelates before 1137 are known. In 1152 the Synod of Kells made Cloyne one of Cashel's twelve suffragan sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cologne:
Joseph Lins's entry covers Cologne as both a German city and an archbishopric. The city, third in Prussia, lies on both banks of the lower Rhine. It covered 45 square miles. On 1 December 1905 it held 428,722 people, of whom 339,790 were Catholics. Its history runs back before Christ. After Agrippa moved the Ubii across the Rhine in 38 B.C., their center stood on the site. In A.D. 50 Agrippina founded the colony of veterans called Colonia Agrippina.

Cologne grew rich in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In the sixteenth-century religious upheavals it stayed Catholic, thanks largely to its university. Its cathedral stands as the greatest Gothic monument in Germany. The archbishopric, first surely held by Saint Maternus in 314, later made its holders princes of the Empire. Five Wittelsbach electors ruled it to 1761, and in 1750 it counted 860 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compline:
Fernand Cabrol's entry explains Compline, from the Latin completorium, a complement. It closes the day's Hours, completing them all. Saint Benedict first used the word in this sense near the start of the sixth century, in chapters of his Rule. He even used the verb complere for the Hour itself. In the Roman Breviary, Compline falls into parts: introduction, psalmody with anthems, hymn, capitulum, response, evangelical canticle, prayer, and benediction. The shape is spare, fit for night's edge.

Its origin has lately stirred much debate among liturgists. General opinion, Cabrol notes, traces the Hour through early monastic practice, with Eastern monks before Chalcedon as witnesses. Sources run from Pargoire and Besse to Bishop's study of a seventh-century service book and Cabrol's own book on ancient prayer. The entry thus gives a short Hour a long pedigree, from Benedict's Rule to modern discussion of its roots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraternity:
Michael Glancey's entry follows the Confraternity of Christian Doctrine, founded at Rome in 1562 to give religious instruction. To about the thirteenth century, Creed and Paternoster formed instruction's base, learned by heart and explained by parish priests on Sundays and feasts. Then Commandments, sacraments, virtues, and vices widened the range. Lambeth's synod of 1281, under Archbishop Peckham, asked priests to explain faith's truths four times yearly. Lavaur's provincial council of 1368 ordered teaching every Sunday and feast day, publishing a catechism for Languedoc and Gascony clergy.

Organized instruction had already begun before 1562. Westminster's First Provincial Council urged the confraternity's members for Sunday and day schools, though Sunday schools abound while the confraternity lags. Kindred bodies include Brussels' Pieuses Unions of 1851 and the Paris Voluntary Catechists, aiding priests with laicized primary schools. Leo XIII raised that work to archconfraternity rank in 1893, with power to affiliate French sisters. Indulgences for these groups run very numerous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corner-stone:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats the corner stone, or foundation stone. The Roman Pontifical provides a rite, De benedictione et impositione Primarii Lapidis, for blessing and laying a church's foundation stone. Appearing in the same form in the Giunta Pontificale of 1520, the rite probably dates at least from Patricius Piccolomini's fifteenth century. It may in substance reach two centuries further back, to Durandus of Mende.

Before building begins, the rubric directs provision for the church's maintenance, foundations marked out with the bishop's or his delegate's approval, and a wooden cross where the altar will stand. In the ensuing function the bishop first blesses the stone. Medieval practice knew this or some analogous rite, though few Pontificals contain anything of the sort. Assigning a date to the blessing practice's beginning proves difficult. Questions arise over laying money on the stone for the fabric, and enclosing coins within or beneath it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cotrone:
Cotrone, a suffragan diocese of Reggio on Calabria's Ionian coast, stands on ancient Croton, an Achaean colony founded about 707 BC. Croton flourished in Magna Graecia, famed for strong, sober citizens, for Milo the athlete, and for Pythagoras, who founded his school there. Conquerors from Dionysius to Hannibal seized it in turn.

Local legend credits St Dionysius the Areopagite with preaching the Gospel there, and Flavianus stands as its first known bishop. Later bishops include Minturno the polished writer, the Dominican Juan Lopez, and Niceforo Melisseno Commeno, who served the Holy See abroad. The diocese counts 14,000 souls, ten parishes, and twenty-nine churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-carlo-o:
A biographical entry introduces Count Carlo Ottavio Castiglione, a Milanese philologist and numismatist, meaning a scholar of languages and of coins, born in 1784 and dead in 1849. Descended from Baldassare Castiglione, author of The Courtier, he mastered almost all the Indo-Germanic and Semitic languages while still young.

His published work ranged from a description of Cufic, or early Arabic-script, coins in Milan's Brera collection to a geographical and numismatic memoir on eastern Barbary and the Atlantic Berbers. Outside Italy he is best known for editing fragments of the Gothic Bible translation by Ulfilas, found among palimpsests, reused manuscripts, in the Ambrosian Library. He also left many unpublished writings on language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-mayn:
A biographical entry tells of Cuthbert Mayne, martyr, baptized near Barnstaple in March 1544 and executed at Launceston on 29 November 1577. Son of William Mayne, he was schooled by a schismatical uncle, ordained a Protestant minister near eighteen, and took his MA at Oxford in 1570, where Catholic leaven still worked strongly.

Warned of arrest after the Bishop of London seized a letter of his, he fled through Cornwall to Douai in 1573. After reconciling with the Church, he was ordained in 1575 and returned to the English mission in 1576, lodging with Francis Tregian in Cornwall. Arrested at Tregian's house in June 1577, he was tried that September and put to death for his priesthood, one of the early martyrs of Elizabeth's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyrene:
A historical entry describes Cyrene, a titular see of northern Africa founded early in the seventh century BC by Dorian colonists from Thera. Named for the spring Kyre, sacred to Apollo, it stood ten miles from its port Apollonia. It lay on the edge of the Green Mountains, and became chief town of Cyrenaica between Egypt and Carthage.

Prosperous under its own kings during the fifth century BC, it became a republic after 460. It then passed to the Ptolemies, and was bequeathed to Rome, becoming a colony in 74 BC. Many Jews lived there, and Cyrene gave the world Aristippus, Callimachus, Carneades, Eratosthenes, and Synesius. Six bishops are named by Lequien, and the Latin titular see was suppressed in 1894.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-digne:
Digne is a diocese in France covering the whole department of the Basses Alpes. It answers to the Archbishopric of Aix. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains how the Concordat of 1801 joined to it the old sees of Embrun, Gap, Sisteron, and Senez. Gap regained its own bishop in 1822, leaving Digne with the lands of Digne, Senez, Glandevres, Riez, and Sisteron.

Saints Domninus and Vincentius, who arrived from Africa late in the second century, first preached the faith in the old diocese. By 1905 the see counted more than one hundred thousand souls, thirty-five pastorates, and hundreds of mission churches. Hospitals, schools, and houses of religious complete a portrait of a mountain diocese at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donation-of-c:
The Donation of Constantine is a forged document by which the emperor was made to grant vast privileges and lands to the pope and the Roman Church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that the oldest known copy, from the ninth century, bears the title Constitutum of the Lord Constantine the Emperor. It is addressed to Pope Sylvester the First, who ruled from 314 to 335.

In its first part, the Confession, Constantine tells how Sylvester taught him the faith, baptized him at Rome, and thereby cured his leprosy. In the second part, the Donation itself, he bestows his gifts on the Roman Church. The entry traces how scholars unmasked the forgery and why it mattered for the Roman question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duvergier-de-:
Duvergier de Hauranne, also called Saint-Cyran from an abbey he held, was one of the authors of Jansenism. Born at Bayonne in 1581, he died at Paris in 1643. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him from humanities at home and philosophy at the Sorbonne to the Jesuit college at Louvain. There he graduated in 1604 with a thesis praised by Justus Lipsius. There he likely met Cornelius Jansen, the future theologian of the sect.

In 1605 the pair studied at Paris under the Gallican Edmond Richer, digging into Christian antiquity to restore it to honor, as they claimed, against scholasticism. Their patristic studies bore the Jansenist movement, and the entry traces Saint-Cyran's part with a long bibliography. It closes with Maynard, Faillon, and Brunetiere among his biographers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-easterwine:
Easterwine, also called Eosterwini, was abbot of Wearmouth and nephew of Saint Benedict Biscop. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives his birth in 650 and his death on 7 March 686. Of the noblest Northumbrian stock, he first served as a soldier under King Egfrid, son of Oswy. At twenty-four he gave up arms to become a monk at Wearmouth, then ruled by his uncle.

He was a noble youth, famed for humility, bodily vigor, and infinite gentleness, exact in rule and glad to do the lowliest work. Ordained priest in 679, he became abbot as his uncle's coadjutor in 682. When he had to reprove a fault, his tender sadness left the culprit unable to repeat it. On the day before his death, aged just thirty-six, he said farewell to all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Discipline, by its roots, means the shaping of one who sits at school under a master. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that all Christians are disciples of Christ, seeking to form themselves in his school and by his precepts. He called himself our master, and so do we. That is evangelical discipline, but church speech has given the word other senses, which the entry lists and defines.

Discipline may be viewed in its author, its subject, and itself. In its author it is the method of framing precepts to fit the end sought, the perfect conduct of subjects, and in that sense it is called severe or mild. The entry cites Cavagnis, Hurter, and Wilmers on public church law and the treatise on the Church, guiding readers through a word of many shades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-marten:
Edmond Martene was a Benedictine scholar of history and worship, born near Dijon in 1654 and dead at Saint-Germain-des-Pres in 1739. He entered the abbey of Saint-Remy at Reims in 1672 and was sent to train under Mabillon and d'Achery at Paris. From then on he gave his life to old books, rites, and records of monastic life.

His commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict came out in 1690, followed by large works on ancient rites of the Church and on old monastic customs. He also gathered a vast collection of old writings on church, monastic, and civic affairs, carrying on the work of his teacher. The entry is a good guide to a monk whose patient digging shaped how later scholars read medieval worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-antoi:
Etienne-Antoine Boulogne, a French bishop, was born at Avignon on 26 December 1747 and died at Troyes on 13 March 1825. Poor parents raised him, and the Christian Brothers of his native city gave him his education. Talent and industry marked him, and he was ordained in 1771. His gifts as a speaker soon ranked him among Paris's most admired preachers.

Paris's archbishop barred him from preaching for a time, then withdrew the ban after Boulogne's eulogy on the late Dauphin, father of Louis XVI, won a prize. His standing as a preacher grew steadily from there. In 1786 he preached the Lenten sermons aux Quinze-Vingts, and in 1787 at the court of Versailles. One court sermon warned of the fearful storm threatening society, caused by false philosophy and irreligion. That storm broke over France sooner and more violently than foreseen, except by the keenest observers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-charl:
Etienne-Charles de Lomenie de Brienne was a French cardinal and statesman, born at Paris in 1727 and dead at Sens in 1794. He was of noble lineage, studied at the Collège d'Harcourt and then at the Sorbonne, where, despite suggestions of unorthodoxy, he received the doctorate of theology. Ordained priest in 1752, he became Vicar-General of Rouen in 1752, Bishop of Condom in 1760, and Archbishop of Toulouse in 1762.

In 1788, forced by the philosophers upon Louis XVI, he became ministre principal and Archbishop of Sens, France's second richest see. As minister he was popular with the Assembly of the Notables. But he failed to win the Parlement to his financial schemes, and fell after announcing the convocation of the States General for 1 May 1789. To offset his fall, he intrigued his way to the cardinal's hat and had his nephew Martial de Loménie made coadjutor of Sens.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-facundus-of-h:
Facundus was a sixth-century bishop of Hermiane in North Africa. He defended the Three Chapters, writings by three theologians condemned in the East. When Emperor Justinian pressed for their condemnation, Facundus refused to comply. He wrote Pro Defensione Trium Capitulorum, a twelve-book defence of the chapters.

His stand cost him exile from his see for several years. Later works attacked the emperor's later teaching on Christ's nature. He also wrote against a bishop who had yielded to imperial pressure. Facundus stands as a firm voice for conscience against state power in church affairs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fort-wayne:
Fort Wayne is a diocese in northern Indiana, carved out of the Diocese of Vincennes by the Holy See on 22 September 1857. It began with 20,000 Catholics, 14 priests, and 20 churches across 17,431 square miles. John Henry Luers, a German immigrant ordained at Cincinnati in 1846, became its first bishop in 1858, founded parishes and missions, built a cathedral. He provided a home for orphans before dying suddenly in 1871.

His successors kept building: Joseph Dwenger, consecrated in 1872, led the first American pilgrimage to Rome and promoted parish schools, while Joseph Rademacher remodelled the cathedral in 1896. Herman Alerding took over in 1900. The entry closes with the religious orders at work in the diocese, from the Holy Cross fathers at Notre Dame to several communities of sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-mari:
Francois-Marie-Benjamin Richard de la Vergne, born at Nantes on 1 March 1819 and dead at Paris on 28 January 1908. He was Archbishop of Paris through the bitter church-state struggles of the Third Republic. Educated at Saint-Sulpice, he became secretary to Bishop Jacquemet at Nantes in 1849 and vicar-general from 1850 to 1869. He became Bishop of Belley in 1871, where he began the beatification cause of the Cure d'Ars, coadjutor to Cardinal Guibert of Paris in 1875. He succeeded Guibert on 8 July 1886 and was made cardinal in 1889.

 Politically attached by esteem to monarchist Catholics, he obeyed Leo XIII's 1892 call to rally Catholics to the Republic by founding the Union of Christian France. It was to unite Catholics solely in defence of religion, a union monarchists opposed and the pope finally dissolved. He defended religious congregations against the coming Law of Associations, and Leo XIII wrote to him on their behalf in December 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-mone:
Franz Mone, born at Mingolsheim near Bruchsal in Baden on 12 May 1796 and died at Karlsruhe on 12 March 1871, was a German historian and archaeologist of tireless energy. Schooled at Bruchsal, he entered Heidelberg in 1814 and became tutor in history in 1817. He was secretary of the university library in 1818, extraordinary professor in 1819, ordinary professor in 1822, and head of the library in 1825. From 1827 to 1831 he taught at Louvain, then edited the Karlsruhe Gazette, and in 1835 became archivist and director of Baden's General National Archives, retiring in 1868.

His early history works suffer from a tendency to trace all things possible to a Celtic origin. But his literary histories matter more: an introduction to the Nibelungenlied, a history of heathendom in northern Europe, editions of Otnit. Sources and researches on German literature and language, studies of the heroic legend, and a survey of older Dutch popular literature complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gesellenverei:
Gesellenvereine, German Catholic societies for young men's religious, moral, and professional growth, owe their shape to Adolph Kolping, the Journeymen's Father. Born poor on December 8, 1813, Kolping learned shoemaking and knew workmen's hardships on journeys, in factories, and in city lodgings. Drawn to priesthood at twenty-three, he reached ordination only in 1845 after years of study amid trouble, privation, and sickness.

As Elberfeld chaplain he found journeymen carpenters' choral society growing into a Young Workmen's Society, and as president in 1847 he gave it the Gesellenverein's marks: religious union plus mechanical skill. At Cologne from 1849 he founded a society with free instruction and a hospice for traveling journeymen, then preached the model through Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and Hungary. At his death in December 1865 some 400 branch unions stood; by 1901 they numbered 1,086, with 80,000 journeymen and 120,000 masters, and now over 1,170 unions gather under Cologne's central union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-bourn:
Gilbert Bourne was the last Catholic Bishop of Bath and Wells, who died at Silverton in Devonshire in 1569. An Oxford man and fellow of All Souls, he held preferments under Henry VIII and Edward VI while staying Catholic at heart. Under Mary he received absolution from Cardinal Pole in 1554 and was consecrated bishop that April. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his firm stand under Elizabeth.

As bishop he worked for the Catholic restoration, yet treated heretics with kindness, and none seem to have been executed in his diocese. Mary named him Lord President of the Council of Wales, but Elizabeth soon removed him from posts of trust. He refused to consecrate Parker and rejected the Supremacy Oath, and deprivation followed. In June 1560 he entered the Tower as a close prisoner, where he spent three years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giorgione:
Giorgione, born Giorgio Barbarelli at Castelfranco in or before 1477, died at Venice in the autumn of 1510. Little is known of his life, and even his birth has been disputed. In Venice he studied under Giovanni Bellini beside Titian, soon outstripped his master, and broke with the timid traditional style of the day. A Catholic Encyclopedia article hails him as the joyous herald of the Renaissance.

He painted portraits in a new modern manner, full of dignity and silvery color, and he pioneered landscapes with figures and small genre pictures made for their own sake. His glowing, melting color, broad handling, and decorative aim soon marked the whole Venetian school. He worked in tempera glazed with oil, giving his pictures brilliance and permanence, and he set the fashion for frescoed house fronts in Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giotto-di-bon:
Giotto di Bondone was a Florentine painter and founder of the Italian school of painting, born most probably in 1266 at Vespignano near Florence, who died at Milan in 1337. Nothing is known of him until he was thirty, and Vasari's tale of Cimabue finding him as a shepherd boy drawing sheep is, the article says, a pretty fancy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article refuses him a miraculous birth for Italian art.

The thirteenth century already teemed with renewal, from the Cosmati marble workers to the mosaic men of the Florence Baptistery. Giotto did not create that renewal, but it reached its highest expression in him, first found at Assisi in 1294 in the train of Cimabue. A friend of Dante and Petrarch, he painted Dante's portrait often. He loved life, and left a satire on holy poverty. He married and had eight children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antonio Pordenone, often called Licinio or Regillo, was an Italian painter born at Pordenone in 1483, who died at Ferrara in January 1539. Most of what is known of him comes from Carlo Ridolfi, including the tale of a grocer's commission painted between the start and end of one High Mass. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a fresco painter in demand across the north.

His early frescoes fill churches around Pordenone, and later work took him to Mantua, Cremona, Treviso, and Venice. In 1536 he decorated three halls for the Council of Ten, though those Venetian works have perished. He knew perspective better than most contemporaries, drew well, and threw himself into church decoration with strong religious conviction. He died at Ferrara while working for Duke Ercole II, possibly poisoned, possibly of a chill or epidemic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-bene:
Giovanni Benedetto Castiglione was a painter and etcher born at Genoa in 1616, who died at Mantua in 1670. In Italy he was called Il Grechetto for his beautiful coloring, and in France Il Benedetto. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents an artist who probably never met Van Dyck, but studied his works and Rubens's at Genoa.

He traveled through Italy, painting in nearly every large city, and in 1654 the Duke of Mantua gave him rooms in his palace and a pension. His specialty was animal painting, though he also won praise for landscape, history, and portraits. His rank rests above all on etching. More than seventy free, spirited plates, in pure line like Rembrandt's, use light and shade that often mimic aquatint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-da-p:
Giovanni da Piano Carpine was a Franciscan born at Pian di Carpine near Perugia in 1182, who probably died in 1252. A companion of Caesar of Spires on the second Franciscan mission to Germany in 1221, he helped found houses of the order and served as provincial in Saxony and Spain. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his embassy to the Mongols, the first of its kind.

In 1245 Innocent IV sent him to the princes and people of Mongolia to check their invasions and seek their conversion. Setting out early in 1246 with interpreters, he crossed Russia and the Tatar frontier to Karakorum, reaching it in mid-July. The new Khan Kuyuk answered the pope with proud independence, demanding submission instead. Carpine brought home priceless knowledge of the Far East and a remarkably accurate written account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-fran:
Giovanni Francesco Commendone was a cardinal and papal nuncio born at Venice in 1523, who died at Padua in 1584. After studies in humanities and law at Padua, he came to Rome in 1550, where Julius III made the learned young scholar one of his secretaries. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diplomat trusted with England, Germany, and the Netherlands.

In 1553 Julius sent him to Queen Mary Tudor to treat for the restoration of Catholicism in England. By chance he found an old acquaintance at court and won a secret interview. He carried Mary's letter and her wish to restore the faith back to Rome. In 1560 Pius IV sent him to Germany to invite Catholic and Protestant estates to the reopened Council of Trent, beginning at Vienna in January 1561.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-moro:
Giovanni Morone was a cardinal and Bishop of Modena, born at Milan in 1509, who died at Rome in 1580. His father was chancellor of Milan, and Clement VII named the twenty-year-old Giovanni to Modena in 1529. A rival claimant seized the see, and the dispute lasted until 1532, when Morone bought him off with a yearly pension. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a negotiator of the front rank.

Under Paul III he served as envoy to Milan in 1535 and as nuncio to Ferdinand, King of the Romans, pressing for a council in Germany. He attended the diets of Hagenau, Ratisbon, and Spires. He stood among moderates who saw faults on both sides of the Lutheran struggle. When Sadoleto was denounced for a courteous appeal to Melanchthon, Morone wrote him in sympathy, against those who made religion out of hatred of Lutherans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-perr:
Giovanni Perrone was a Jesuit theologian born at Chieri in Italy in 1794, who died at Rome in 1876. After a doctorate at Turin he entered the Society of Jesus in 1815, a year after its restoration by Pius VII. He soon taught theology at Orvieto, then dogmatic theology at the Roman College. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a teacher whose lectures ran to dozens of editions.

Driven to England by the Roman Republic of 1848, he returned after three years of exile to his Roman chair, teaching until old age stopped him. He advised congregations, opposed the errors of Hermes, and took part in the discussions that led to the definition of the Immaculate Conception. His Praelectiones Theologicae reached a thirty-fourth edition in nine volumes, and its compendium reached forty-seven editions in two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gunther-of-co:
Cologne's Archbishop Günther, consecrated in April 850, won an unhappy fame as the churchman who bent canon law to King Lothair II's divorce. A Frankish noble praised for ability, he first resisted giving his suffragan Bremen to St. Ansgar of Hamburg, yielding only when Nicholas I settled the matter about 860, and he served Lothair as arch-chaplain.

At Aachen synods in 860 and 862 Günther forced Queen Thietberga's confession and then let Lothair marry his concubine Waldrada. He carried the Metz synod's approval to Rome in 863. Nicholas rejected it, excommunicated and deposed him, and though Günther later regained Cologne and then lost it again, he died in 873 after a public retraction admitted him only to lay communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermits-of-st:
The Hermits of St. Augustine, generally called Augustinians, are a religious order formed in the thirteenth century by joining several monastic groups under one name and the Rule of St. Augustine. They must not be confused with the Augustinian Canons. From small Italian brotherhoods they grew into a worldwide order that preached, taught, and carried missions across Europe and beyond.

Their story runs from the union of the hermit groups, through schools and preaching in the later Middle Ages, to the shock of the Reformation. Luther and other Saxon Augustinians left then, and many houses emptied. The order then turned firmly to parish work and missions, sending members to the Americas, Asia, and Australia. Readers get a full sweep of foundations, reforms, branches, and mission fields.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-me:
This sweeping article tells the history of medical science as part of the general history of civilization, starting from its Greek foundation. Modern medicine rests on Greek work, the entry argues, even though the Greeks learned much from Egypt and India and absorbed it so fully that its origins rarely show. Greek medicine began with a purely religious character, with Apollo as founder and his son Aesculapius as healing god.

From temple healing at Epidaurus and Cos, the story runs through Hippocratic medicine, Alexandrian anatomy, and Roman writers. It continues through Arab transmitters and medieval schools to Renaissance anatomists and Harvey's account of the circulation of the blood. Later chapters follow microscopists such as Leeuwenhoek, the discovery of small blood vessels and blood corpuscles, and the anatomists and physiologists who built modern medicine on experiment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-digne:
Hugh of Digne was a Franciscan friar and ascetical writer, born at Digne in south-east France at an uncertain date and dead at Marseilles about 1285. His close friend Salimbene, to whom most knowledge of his life is owed, calls him one of the most renowned clerics of the world. He was a great preacher favoured by clergy and people alike, fluent of speech and trumpet-voiced.

Salimbene says hearing Hugh preach felt like hearing another Paul or Elias. Joinville records Hugh's visit to King Louis IX. The king was so moved by his preaching that he tried to keep him at court, but the friar refused and resumed his preaching tours. On one such journey he wrote to John of Parma at Greccio, prophesying the deaths of pope and Bonaventure and the extinction of the Templars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-brida:
Jacques Bridaine, a preacher, was born at Chusclan in France on 21 March 1701 and died at Roquemaure on 22 December 1767. After study at Avignon's Jesuit college, he went into St Charles of the Cross's Seminary of the Royal Missions. His gift for speaking showed itself before ordination, and even the catechetical lessons he gave stirred listeners to interest and emotion.

While he was still in minor orders, he preached Lent at the church in Aigues-Mortes, where he first tried his odd methods. His great youth brought mockery, and on Ash Wednesday the church sat empty. Unshaken, he put on his surplice and rang a bell along the main streets, calling people to come and hear him. Curiosity drew a huge crowd, and his preaching kept hold of them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-paul-:
Priest and publisher Jacques Paul Migne was born at Saint-Flour on 25 October 1800. He died at Paris on 24 October 1875. After college courses he studied theology at Orléans. While a student there he briefly taught a fourth class at Châteaudun college. He was ordained priest in 1824. The next year he became pastor of Puiseaux in the Orléans diocese. A pamphlet, De la liberté, clashed with his bishop, Brunault de Beauregard.

Migne resigned his parish and went to Paris. There in the same year he founded L'Univers Religieux, later L'Univers. He meant it as a journal free of political tendency, concerned with Catholic interests alone. He edited it until 1836 and wrote very many articles for it. Meanwhile he conceived a plan to publish the Church Fathers in vast, affordable series. That plan became the Patrologia, his life's monument. The entry follows a parish priest turned publishing giant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-la-fo:
Jean de La Fontaine, a French poet born at Château-Thierry in 1621 and dead in Paris in 1695, is best loved for his Fables. Eldest son of a deputy-ranger, he tried the Oratory for eighteen months, left religious life, studied law, and married in 1647 to a union that soon broke apart.

La Fontaine first published an imitation of Terence in 1654, then won a pension from Fouquet, sending a short poem each month as receipt. At the Luxembourg from 1664 he knew Molière, Racine, and Boileau, and issued his Tales, the first six books of Fables, and the novel Psyché. His animal tales still teach morals with wit and ease.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-lejeune:
Jean Lejeune, a French Oratorian preacher born at Poligny in 1592 and died at Limoges in 1672, was famed for holiness and for preaching. His energy in mission work earned him the name Missionary of the Oratory, and blindness from age thirty-five added the name Blind Father.

Son of a Dole lawyer, Lejeune was raised by his widowed mother, studied at Dole, and joined Bérulle's Oratory in 1614. After directing the Langres seminary he gave himself wholly to missions among the poor. Blindness struck while preaching Lent at Rouen in 1627, yet never stopped him. Bishops sought him for Lent and Advent, and the crown used him to win back Protestants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-racine:
Jean Racine, a French dramatist born at La Ferté-Milon in 1639 and dead in Paris in 1699. He lost his parents young and was raised through Beauvais college and Port-Royal, where by sixteen he read Greek at sight and wrote odes in Latin and French.

Racine's first plays, Thébaïde in 1664 and Alexandre, mattered little. Andromaque in 1667 made him famous, followed by his sole comedy Les Plaideurs and the tragedies Britannicus, Bérénice, Bajazet, Mithridate, and Iphigénie. After Phèdre failed in 1677 he quit the stage for twelve years, returning only for Esther in 1689 and Athalie in 1691 at Madame de Maintenon's request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeanne-fontbo:
Jeanne Fontbonne, in religion Mother Saint John, second foundress of the Sisters of Saint Joseph of Lyons, was born in 1759 at Bassens and died at Lyons in 1843. She entered a new Joseph house at Monistrol in 1778, took the habit next year, and showed rare skill in schools.

Elected superior six years later, Mother Saint John aided the founder, helped open a hospital, and worked among Monistrol's girls. Refusing the Civil Constitution oath with her bishop, she held her post until a mob seized the convent, then endured prison at Saint-Didier. She was saved from the guillotine only by Robespierre's fall the day before her set execution. She rebuilt the congregation after the storm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-besoig:
Jérôme Besoigne, a French Jansenist writer born in Paris in 1686 and dead in 1763, was ordained in 1715 and took a Sorbonne doctorate three years later. He served as assistant head of Plessis College until defending Jansenism and opposing the bull Unigenitus forced him to resign.

In 1729 the Sorbonne struck Besoigne from its doctors, and Paris exiled him in 1731, though he returned the next year. His books include a six-volume History of Port-Royal Abbey and lives of four bishops in its case. Two Scripture works harmonise Wisdom books and the apostles' letters, and the latter was reprinted in Migne's complete course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-rathbo:
Joseph Rathborne was an English priest and controversialist at Cowes on the Isle of Wight. Born at Lincoln in 1807, he studied at Ushaw and St. Edmund's, Old Hall, and was ordained in 1830. That November, Bishop Bramston sent him to Cowes, where he spent the rest of his short life. He died there in 1842.

Writing as Alethphilos, Rathborne published letters on prayers for the dead, on Good Friday and Easter, and addressed to Isle of Wight Protestants. He also wrote replies to critics and to Gladstone on Church and State. Under his own name he issued The Clergy of the French Revolution. The entry notes his name is sometimes wrongly given as Rathbone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-schwan:
Joseph Schwane was a German theologian who wrote the first Catholic history of dogma. Born at Dorsten in 1824, he studied at Münster, was ordained in 1847, and continued at Bonn and Tübingen. He taught church history and moral theology at Münster and succeeded Berlage in Münster's dogmatic theology chair in 1881; Leo XIII made him a domestic prelate in 1890.

Schwane's chief work, Dogmengeschichte, covered the whole history of Christian doctrine in four volumes from 1862 to 1890. He also wrote on contracts under civil law, on justice and social duties, and on special moral theology. Smaller studies treat divine foreknowledge, heretical baptism, and the Eucharistic sacrifice. He died at Münster in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jules-verne:
Jules Verne was the French novelist who brought science into adventure fiction. Born at Nantes in 1828, he began with a little play and Poe-like novelettes in the Musée des Familles. A Drama in the Air, about a madman loose in a balloon, drew notice, and his publisher Hetzel urged him to stick to the new kind of novel he had found.

Verne's tales, from Around the World in Eighty Days to Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea and Journey to the Centre of the Earth, charmed readers in every language. France, tired of pale Dumas copies, welcomed his fresh adventures. He lived and died a Catholic, and none of his books, the entry notes, offends good taste or morals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-le-moyne:
Le Moyne names one of New France's most illustrious families, whose deeds fill Canadian history. Founder Charles le Moyne was born at Dieppe in 1626 and died at Ville-Marie in 1683. He reached Canada in 1641 and spent four years in Huron country. Settling at Montreal, he became a prized interpreter through Indian languages and a defender through valour.

He fought Iroquois raiders single-handed and negotiated a five-year peace in 1653. He married Catherine Primot in 1654. Captured in 1665, he was released unwounded out of awe and fear of reprisal. Louis XIV ennobled him Sieur de Longueuil, and Intendant Talon granted him the vast Longueuil fief from Varennes to Laprairie. Father of fourteen, he sired seven sons famed as the Maccabees of New France, three dying in battle and four governing cities or provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leon-olle-lap:
Leon Olle-Laprune (1839-1898) was a French Catholic philosopher who spent his life teaching philosophy in the light of faith. After brilliant studies at the Ecole Normale Superieure from 1858 to 1861, he taught first in lycees. He then taught at the Ecole Normale from 1875, under the influence of Caro and Pere Gratry's Les Sources. His aim was a Catholic professorship of philosophy, as Ozanam's had been for history.

The press sometimes urged punishment of his clericalism, but his teaching repute shielded him. Only in 1881-82, after backing a demonstration for the expelled congregations, was he suspended by Jules Ferry. The first signer of his students' protest was the future socialist deputy Jean Jaures. His books include La Philosophie de Malebranche of 1870 and a Sorbonne thesis on moral certitude. They also include an Essai sur la morale d'Aristote of 1881 and La philosophie et le temps present of 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-goffi:
Leonard Goffine (1648-1719) was a Norbertine priest of the Eifel, born at Cologne or Broich, who entered the Abbey of Steinfeld at nineteen. After his novitiate and studies at the Norbertine college at Cologne, he was ordained priest. He was sent to assist at Dunwald and then Ellen, four years in each place. He was recalled to Steinfeld as novice master. The dearth of priests after the Lutheran troubles and the Thirty Years' War forced abbots and bishops to draw elsewhere.

Goffine then held Clarholz from 1680 to 1685, spent a short time at Niederehe, and served at Coesfeld to 1691. At Trier's archbishop's request he took Wehr (1691-94), then Rheinbollen (1694-96), then Oberstein from December 1696 until his death. He also attended Catholics at Weiersbach. Oberstein was mostly Protestant, and he bore much annoyance there. A contemporary sketch calls him a truly apostolic pastor, untiring in zeal, edifying all by word and example.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorraine:
Lorraine is the border land named for Lothair II. His strip of empire between France and Germany took his name after the Treaty of Verdun in 843. It ran from the North Sea toward the Rhone, plus Italy. It held Aachen, Charlemagne's capital, with Cologne and Trier as archbishoprics.

Neither fully German nor fully Roman, it was coveted by neighbours and torn by internal wars, its south left open while Meuse, Rhine, and sea fenced the other sides. Converted under Roman rule through Trier's missionaries, it built bishoprics at Metz, Toul, and Verdun by the fourth century, and its great archbishops soon became temporal lords as well as churchmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-rene-tu:
Louis Rene Tulasne was a French botanist famed for fungi, born at Azay-le-Rideau in 1815 and dead at Hyeres in 1885. He studied law at Poitiers, then botany, working with Saint-Hilaire on Brazil's flora until 1842, and served as assistant naturalist at Paris's Museum from 1842 to 1872.

Elected to the Academy in 1845, he traced the tangled life histories of small parasitic fungi under the microscope, founding modern mycology, the study of fungi. With his brother Charles he published Fungi hypogaei in 1851 and the three-volume Selecta fungorum carpologia of 1861 to 1865, famed for sixty-one plates. He left his library to the Catholic Institute of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucerne:
Lucerne is the chief town of its Swiss canton, grown from a small eighth-century Benedictine house to St. Leodegar where the Reuss leaves the Lake of the Four Cantons. That house belonged to Murbach Abbey in Alsace, and a charter of Lothair I in 840 first names the place.

Trade over the St. Gothard pass in the thirteenth century made Lucerne a mart. Citizens bought privilege after privilege from straitened abbots, winning a council, seal, and courts by 1252. Habsburg counts pressed their claims as overlords. Yet the town's drive for freedom, its alliance with the forest cantons, and its later Catholic stand in Swiss wars shape a long civic and church story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madame-de-sev:
Madame de Sevigne, Marie de Rabutin-Chantal, was a writer born at Paris 6 February 1626 and dead at Grignan 18 April 1696. Granddaughter of St. Jane Frances de Chantal, orphaned young, she learned Latin, Italian, and Spanish under Menage and Chapelain, married the Marquess de Sevigne at eighteen, and was widowed by duel after seven years.

Her life turned on her daughter, Countess de Grignan, wife of Provence's governor. The daughter's move south in 1671, her four returns north, and her mother's three visits south framed the famous letters. Widowed and courted by Turenne, Conti, and Bussy-Rabutin, she lived at court and the Hotel Carnavalet from 1677. She died at her sick daughter's bedside, her absorbing, unselfish maternal love the engine of her correspondence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maine:
Maine, the Pine Tree State, is covered here in full, land, laws, and church life near 1910. Geography opens the entry. Maine holds some 1,580 lakes, with Moosehead Lake at its centre. Vast forests, a cold climate, and steady growth frame the picture. Its people rose from 96,540 in 1790 to statehood in 1820.

Industries, farming, and government follow in turn. Its constitution mirrors the federal one. A people's veto by referendum dates from 1909. Seven executive councillors aid the governor, and eight justices sit on its supreme court. Long sections set out law on worship, oaths, blasphemy, holidays, confession, church property, clergy, marriage, schools, charities, liquor, prisons, and wills. History closes the piece, from Cabot's 1497 voyage and early colonies to Cheverus in 1797 and the Diocese of Portland in 1853.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marciane:
Marciane was a titular see of Lycia, under the metropolitan of Myra. It appears in the lists of bishoprics from the sixth century to the twelfth or thirteenth. No author mentions it besides those lists. Its site remains unknown.

Le Quien cites three of its bishops. Januarius attended the Council of Constantinople against Eutyches in 448. Augustine signed the synodal decree of Gennadius of Constantinople against simony in 459. Marcian signed a decretal letter of the Council of Constantinople against Severus and other heretics in 518, plus a report to Pope Hormisdas on the ordination of Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Beyond those three names, the see leaves almost no trace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marco-d-oggio:
Marco d'Oggione was a Milanese painter, born at Oggiono near Milan about 1470 and dead probably at Milan in 1549. He ranked among Leonardo da Vinci's chief pupils and copied his master's works again and again. He worked hard, yet his pictures lack warmth of feeling and purity of drawing.

A fine phrase sums his composition: strength of colour stands in for strength of feeling. He copied the Last Supper repeatedly, and a fine copy sits with the Royal Academy in England. Two signed pictures lead his output: St Michael at Brera and a Madonna in the Bonomi family gallery. More works appear at Berlin, Paris, St Petersburg, and Turin, the Russian one a clever Last Supper copy. Dates for his death range from Lanzi's 1530 to Milan writers' 1540, with 1549 now accepted. His skies, mountains, and distant views remain his best original passages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marguerin-de-:
Marguerin de la Bigne, also called Binius, was a French theologian and patrologist, born about 1546 at Bernieres-le-Patry in Normandy and dead about 1595. He studied at Caen College and the Sorbonne in Paris, where he took his doctorate. He became canon of Bayeux, his home diocese, and later dean of the church of Mans.

At Rouen's provincial council in 1581 he defended his chapter's rights against Bishop Bernadin de St Francois of Bayeux. He saw Protestant misuse of Father texts as a threat to Catholic interests and set out to gather and edit the Fathers' documents. His Sacra Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum of 1575 ran to eight volumes, plus one more in 1579. It held writings of some two hundred Fathers, many printed for the first time, with care for texts corrupted by heretics. It pioneered critical patristics, and he also edited Paris synodal statutes in 1578 and St Isidore in 1580.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-alphons:
Alphonse Ratisbonne was a converted Jew, born at Strasburg in 1814 and dead at Ain Karim in 1884. He came from a wealthy and prominent Alsatian Jewish family.

Nominally Jewish, he was in fact a scoffing unbeliever and, after his brother Theodor's conversion, a fierce foe of Catholicism. On a pleasure trip east he reached Rome, where on 20 January 1842 an apparition of the Blessed Virgin in Sant' Andrea delle Fratte converted him at once. He helped Theodor found the Sisters of Our Lady of Sion in 1843, was ordained in 1847, and joined the Jesuits. Leaving them with Pius IX's consent to convert Jews, he moved the sisters to Jerusalem in 1855. He built the Ecce Homo convent with school and girls' orphanage in 1856. Later he raised St John's convent at Ain Karim and a boys' orphanage near Jaffa Gate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-theodor:
Theodor Ratisbonne was a preacher, writer, and director of the Archconfraternity of Christian Mothers, born of Jewish parents at Strasburg in 1802 and dead at Paris in 1884. Raised in luxury and schooled at the Royal College, he led his community as a young man and was chosen to replace Samson Libermann after Libermann's conversion in 1824.

Conversions of three friends, Emile Dreyfus, Alfred Mayer, and Libermann, drove him to study Bible and church history. After two years of inward struggle he was baptised in 1826 and ordained in 1830.
