He worked in his home diocese until 1840, then became subdirector of Notre Dame des Victoires at Paris. In 1842 his brother Alphonse, a fierce freethinker, was converted at Rome and urged a home for Jewish children. Gregory XVI knighted Theodor and backed his work for Jewish conversion, and houses of Our Lady of Sion opened for Jewish boys and girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marin-mersenn:
Marin Mersenne was a French theologian, philosopher, and mathematician, born near Oize in 1588 and dead at Paris in 1648. He studied at Le Mans and the Jesuit College of La Fleche, where lifelong friendship with Descartes began. He joined the Minims at Nigeon in 1611 and taught philosophy at Nevers from 1614 to 1620.

His first books fought atheism and scepticism in theology, but later he gave himself almost wholly to science, running his own experiments and publishing mathematical works. His chief merit lay less in his own findings than in spurring others on, through interest, questions, and suggestions. Gassendi and Galileo were friends, but Descartes above all owed him guidance. Mersenne drew him from a loose life to serious study, then served in Paris as his correspondent, helper, spokesman, and defender against attacks on the Meditations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marmaduke-sto:
Marmaduke Stone was a Jesuit, born at Draycot in 1748 and dead at St Helens in 1834. Schooled at St Omers, he shared its historic move to Bruges in August 1762, joined the Society in 1767, and later taught at the Liege Academy. In 1790 he succeeded Father William Strickland as president, guiding English ex-Jesuits through over twenty stormy years.

His fellows, bound by vocation and uncancelled vows, could not reunite for government under the suppression brief, so he ruled only by appeal to conscience. On 14 July 1794 Liege College moved to Stonyhurst in good order, reopening that October, and Propaganda confirmed its Liege privileges in 1796. During the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars he worked for reunion with Russian Jesuits, whose corporate life Rome had recognised. On 19 May 1803 he was declared provincial, admitted others to vows for England, Ireland, and Maryland, and opened a Hodder novitiate that September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-of-th:
Martyrs of the Paris Commune were the secular priests and religious murdered in Paris in May 1871 for their sacred calling. They fall into three groups, by date and place of death. 

On 24 May the first group died inside La Roquette prison, headed by Archbishop Georges Darboy, frail in health and tried by prison hardship. With him died Abbe Duguerry of La Madeleine, Abbe Allard, who had served the wounded in the siege, and Jesuits Ducoudray and Clerc. On 25 May Dominican fathers of Arcueil College, led by founder-superior Captier with four friars and eight college laymen, were shot at the Barriere d'Italie after hunger and thirst at Bicetre fort. On 26 May over fifty prisoners were marched to Belleville, where eleven ecclesiastics, including Jesuit rector Olivaint, were massacred.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-jean-sto:
Mary Jean Stone was born at Brighton, Sussex, in 1853 and died at Battle, Sussex, in 1908. She learned French, German, and Italian at a Calvinist school in Paris and at Aschaffenburg in Germany. In Germany she met Catholicism and exchanged Protestantism for what she called the free atmosphere of the Catholic Church, received by Mainz Bishop Ketteler.

She also wrote Faithful unto Death of 1892 on Franciscan Reformation martyrs, Eleanor Leslie of 1898 on a Scottish convert, and Reformation and Renaissance studies of 1904. Studies from Court and Cloister of 1905, and The Church in English History of 1907, a higher textbook for teachers, followed. Her Cardinal Pole, begun for the St Nicholas Series, was cut short by death. She wrote often for the Dublin Review, Month, Blackwood's, and Cornhill, and contributed several articles to the Catholic Encyclopedia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurus-dantin:
Maurus Dantine, a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur born near Namur in 1688, died at Paris in 1746. He ranks among the founders of chronology as a branch of history. Like many Maurists, he joined the Appelants who in 1713 refused the bull Unigenitus and appealed to a general council. His chief merit lies in the careful plan he drew for a great work on checking historical dates.

Dantine built more exact chronological tables and a better method for dating charters, chronicles, and monuments since the birth of Christ. Illness forced him to hand the labour to others, chiefly Clemencet. He also studied languages deeply and published a translation of the Psalms from the Hebrew with notes in 1739. It drew such notice that a second edition followed that year and a third the next, and he helped prepare a new edition of a great lexicon with Dom Carpentier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mechline:
Mechline, or Malines in French, is the archdiocese covering the Belgian provinces of Antwerp and Brabant. Its present shape comes from the French Concordat of 1801. The province of Mechlin matches the Belgian kingdom, with suffragans at Tournai, Liege, Namur, Ghent, and Bruges, and under Napoleon it stretched to the Rhine. Before 1559 the city belonged to Cambrai's diocese, and its church weight came from the ancient chapter of St. Rombaut's collegiate church.

Paul IV's bull of 12 May 1559 built a new hierarchy in the Netherlands: three metropolitans, Mechlin, Cambrai, and Utrecht, with fifteen sees. Pius IV raised Mechlin's archbishop to primate in 1560 and 1561. Faith was preached with zeal there in the seventh and eighth centuries by St. Eligius, St. Amand, St. Lambert, and St. Hubert, then by Anglo-Saxons Willibrord and Rumold. The entry follows the see from mission field to primatial throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melbourne:
Melbourne, an archdiocese in the state of Victoria in south-eastern Australia, grew up along with the state itself. When its first bishop was consecrated in 1848, the town was still the Port Philip Settlement in Sydney's province. Father Patrick Bonaventure Geoghegan had looked after Port Philip from 1839, and Melbourne heard its first Mass on Pentecost Sunday, 15 May of that year. All told, the settlement held 11,738 souls in 1841, of whom 2,411 were Catholics.

James Alypius Goold, an Irishman and the first bishop, came overland from Sydney to Melbourne on 4 October 1848. In April 1850 he laid the first stone of St. Patrick's Cathedral, and within months Port Philip stood on its own as the colony of Victoria. Gold at Ballarat, Bendigo, and Castlemaine swelled the numbers, and the Catholic count climbed from 18,000 in 1851 to 88,000 by 1857, as exiles from Ireland found shelter there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melitene:
Melitene, home of an Armenian Catholic see and titular archbishopric, was founded, by Pliny's account, by Queen Semiramis near the Euphrates. Tacitus gives its earliest mention. A Roman camp stood there under Nero, and Trajan made it the frontier's chief stronghold. Its name likely comes from the river Melas, which joins the Euphrates. Under Marcus Aurelius the Twelfth Legion, the Fulminata, was stationed there, and to it belonged the forty martyrs of Sebaste.

Ptolemy and Strabo count it among Cappadocia's ten provinces. Justinian walled it and filled it with splendid monuments, all now gone. In 577 Rome beat Persia nearby, two years after Shah Chosroes burned the city. Mid-seventh century it returned to Byzantium, then fell to Arabs. Constantine Copronymus retook it in 751, moved its Christians to Thrace, and razed its walls. Caliph Al-Manzur restored it in 760, and Byzantines ruled again in the tenth century, taking it firmly in 965.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-messene:
Messene, a titular see under Corinth in Achaia, dates under that name only from the fourth century B.C. When Epaminondas crushed the Spartans at Leuctra, he called back the scattered Messenians and had them build, on Mount Ithome's slopes, a new capital called Messene in 370 B.C. Its fortified walls ran over five and a half miles and counted as the best in Greece. The surviving stretch justifies that fame.

Christianity took root there early, though few of its bishops are known. At the tenth century's start, Leo the Wise's Notitia lists Messene as an independent archbishopric, and the same holds for the fourteenth century's start. Since the diocese misses from the fifteenth century's Notitia, it may be assumed to have ceased by then. The little village of Mavromati, with 600 people, capital of the Deme of Ithome, now stands on ancient Messene's ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-eyquen:
Michel-Eyquem de Montaigne, a writer born at the chateau of Montaigne in Perigord on 28 February 1533, died there on 13 September 1592. His great-grandfather, a Bordeaux merchant in wines, salt fish, and more, had bought the Montaigne estate. His father served in the army, married Antoinette de Louppes, of Jewish origin, and spent two years as mayor of Bordeaux. 

At six and a half he entered the College of Guyenne at Bordeaux, staying seven years. He is believed to have studied logic and dialectics for two years at the Bordeaux Faculty of Arts under Marc-Antoine de Muret. Becoming counsellor at Perigord's Cour des Aides, he was soon absorbed with his colleagues into Bordeaux's Parlement. The new counsellor disliked his profession and was often absent. From 1561 to 1563 he attended court, and from 1559 he knew La Boetie, his chosen friend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mitylene:
Mitylene, a titulary archbishopric in the island of Lesbos, was inhabited first by the Pelasgians, then by the Aeolians. It was ruled in turn by the Persians, Athenians, Macedonians, Seleucids, and Romans. Included in the Eastern empire after Theodosius, it suffered much from invasions. The Scythians came in 376, the Slavs in 769, the Arabs in 821, 881, and 1035, and the Russians in 864 and 1027.

In 1204, after the Latin empire's foundation, the city became a French possession, only to be reconquered in 1248 by John Ducas Vatatzes. It belonged to the Genoese when Sultan Mahomet II conquered it in 1462. Its archbishops include figures of the Byzantine and Latin periods, and its long history mirrors Lesbos's passage among empires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-:
Obazine was a monastery in the Diocese of Tulle in France, begun about 1134 by Saint Stephen of Obazine. He and a fellow priest named Pierre took up the hermit's life. They drew followers to a site granted by Viscount Archambault. Bishop Eustorge of Tulle gave the venture his backing. The community grew until it needed daughter houses of its own.

At first the monks lived without a fixed rule. Stephen took the regular habit before 1142 and had Cistercians train his men in their way of life. He joined the abbey to Citeaux in 1147. Later abbots of note included Francois d'Escobleau, later Archbishop of Bordeaux, and Charles de la Roche-Aymon, later Cardinal Archbishop of Rennes. The Revolution seized the monastery in 1791, and its partly restored abbey church now serves as a parish church.

Saint Catherine's monastery stands on Mount Sinai at 4,854 feet, in a gorge below Jebel Musa, the mountain tradition links with the giving of the Law. A Byzantine house under the Rule of Saint Basil, it is famed for hospitality. Above all it is famed for its library, where the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus, a precious Bible manuscript, came to light.

Emperor Justinian raised a church there about 550, first called the Church of the Transfiguration. It gathered hermits who had lived scattered in cells and caves across the mountain. Monks still show the spot held to be the Burning Bush, in a small chapel entered barefoot where a lamp burns always. Orthodox Greeks revere the house both for the relics of Catherine of Alexandria it is believed to hold and for its ties to Scripture's great events.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monte-vergine:
Monte Vergine is an abbey in the province of Naples near Avellino. It commands views of the Mediterranean across the bays of Naples, Salerno and Gaeta and inland to the Abruzzi mountains. Once called Mons Sacer for a temple of Cybele that stood there, it also bears the name Mons Virgilianus. That name comes from a legend that Virgil retired there to study the Sibylline books.

Saint William of Vercelli raised a house of strict observance and lifelong abstinence on the hill in 1119. His successor gave it to the Benedictines in 1149 with Alexander III's approval. The house won favour from the kings of the Two Sicilies. At one time it counted a hundred monasteries of its branch in their lands. Laxity later threatened it until sixteenth-century reform restored its discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montefiascone:
Montefiascone stands nearly 2,000 feet above sea level on a tufa mass overlooking Lake Bolsena, famous for its wine. It is of Etruscan origin as Faliscodunum, perhaps the ancient Fanum Voltumnae. Gregory IX fortified it in 1235 against Frederick II, yet it surrendered to him in 1240 and never regained its earlier weight.

Its cathedral is the work of Sammicheli from 1519. Outside town stands the double basilica of San Flaviano, its lower church from 1030 and its upper from 1262 mixing pointed and round arches. There too lies the tomb of the drinker killed by Montefiascone wine, of Est, Est, Est fame, who was neither canon nor Fugger. Made a bishopric in 1369, it later joined Corneto, and it counts the poet Giambattista Casti among its sons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses-of-chor:
Moses of Chorene, perhaps Armenia's best known writer, is called by his countrymen the father of history and the father of scholars. He won fame also as poet, hymn writer and grammarian. A native of Chorene in Darou, he was sent young by Mesrop, founder of Armenian literature, to study at Edessa, Constantinople, Alexandria, Athens and Rome.

Returning home, he is said to have helped Mesrop between 407 and 433 in translating the Bible into Armenian. That places his birth near the end of the fourth century and his death near the end of the fifth. Besides treatises on rhetoric and geography, homilies and hymns still used in Armenian worship, his celebrated work is the History of Armenia Major. It is the chief surviving source for pre-Christian Armenian tradition, though it mixes legend and error with its history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nazarene:
Nazarene, as a name for Christ, occurs only once in the Douai Version, in Matthew 2:23, where the Vulgate reads Nazoraeus. Elsewhere Jesus Nazarenus is uniformly rendered Jesus of Nazareth. In Acts 24:5 Tertullus calls the Christians the sect of the Nazarenes. The name plainly refers to Nazareth, the Saviour's early home.

It is applied to him in the Gospels only by those outside his intimate friends' circle. In Acts, however, Saint Peter and Saint Paul use it, and the risen Lord himself uses it in Paul's account of his conversion. Matthew 2:23 says he shall be called a Nazarene, as the prophets said, yet no explicit Old Testament prediction says so. Some link the passage with netzer, flower, in Isaiah 11, or netzure, dregs, in Isaiah 49, but those readings seem far-fetched. The entry weighs whether Nazarite quality is meant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-none:
None, the ninth hour of prayer in the daily office, takes its name from the Roman day's third division, running from noon to about three. Greeks, Romans, and Jews split daylight into four three-hour parts, and the church borrowed the pattern, with Peter and John at prayer at the ninth hour in Acts.

Tertullian and Clement name Terce, Sext, and None as hours set apart by the late second century. At first they served private prayer, then, on station days and Sundays, public prayer. The entry follows None through monastic rules, fasting customs, and Roman and other liturgies to its modern form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odoric-of-por:
Odoric of Pordenone, a Franciscan friar born near Pordenone about 1286, traveled farther into Asia than almost any European of his age. Joining the order at Udine around 1300, he set out from Padua in April 1318, crossed the Black Sea, and crossed Persia by Tauris, Sultaniah, and Persepolis.

From Hormuz he reached India, gathered the bones of four martyred friars at Tana, sailed the Malabar and Coromandel coasts to Ceylon, and pressed on through the Nicobars toward China. His account of courts, customs, and wonders at the khan's court became a medieval bestseller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostracine:
Ostracine was a titular see and suffragan of Pelusium in Augustamnica Prima, on Egypt's eastern edge. Pliny sets the town sixty-five miles from Pelusium, and Ptolemy places it in Cassiotis, between Mount Cassius and Rhinocolura. Josephus records that Vespasian halted there with his army on the march from Egypt into Palestine. The unwalled town then drew its water from the Delta by canal and held a Roman garrison.

Hierocles, George of Cyprus, and other geographers always list it in Augustamnica. Le Quien names three bishops, Theoctistus, Serapion, and Abraham, who lived in the fourth and fifth centuries. A small town near the sea in the region, called Straki, probably stands where Ostracine stood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-gabriel-:
Paul Gabriel Antoine was a French Jesuit theologian born at Luneville on 10 January 1678 and dead at Pont-a-Mousson on 22 January 1743. At fifteen he sought the Society of Jesus and was received on 9 October 1693. After studies he taught humanities for years, first at Pont-a-Mousson, then at Colmar, and back at Pont-a-Mousson he held the chairs of philosophy and theology with marked success.

His Dogmatic Theology first appeared in 1723, and his Moral Theology in three volumes three years later. His Universal Theology, speculative and dogmatic, covering the whole scholastic field, won instant praise and stamped him among the age's first theologians, running nine editions in his life and ten after death. His Moral Theology, first printed at Nancy in 1726, ran sixty editions across countries, and Benedict XIV prescribed its use in the Propaganda College.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-auve:
Peter of Auvergne was a Paris philosopher and theologian who died after 1310. A canon of Paris and, by several accounts, a pupil of Aquinas, he was named university rector by the papal legate Simon of Brion during the nations' quarrel of 1279. He was elected to the post again in 1296. He is not, the entry argues, the Peter of Croc named canon of Clermont in a 1296 bull.

His published works continue Aquinas on the heavens and the world and comment on Aristotle's Meteorology, youth and age, length of life, and animal motion. No sound warrant backs the claim that he supplemented Aquinas's Summa. Manuscripts at the Bibliothèque Nationale and the Arsenal hold his six quodlibets, his Determinate Sophism, and questions on logic, Porphyry, metaphysics, politics, sleep, plants, and the soul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippine-ro:
Philippine Rose Duchesne founded the first American houses of the Society of the Sacred Heart, born at Grenoble in 1769. Daughter of an eminent lawyer and a Périer mother, she was schooled by Visitation nuns, joined their order, watched the Terror scatter it, and failed to restore Ste. Marie d'en Haut. In 1804 Mother Barat received her community into the Sacred Heart, and the childhood dream of distant missions took shape.

In 1818 she sailed with four companions to New Orleans, then up the Mississippi to St. Charles, Missouri, where cold, hunger, illness, opposition, and calumny only fired her zeal. Foundations followed at Florissant, Grand Coteau, New Orleans, St. Louis, and St. Michael, and Leo XII approved the society in 1826. At last she taught the Potawatomi at Sugar Creek, the desire of her life. She died at St. Charles in 1852, beatification already begun.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pie-pelicane-: Pie pelicane, Jesu Domine is the sixth quatrain of the hymn Adoro Te Devote. It is sometimes sung on its own at Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament. This brief Catholic Encyclopedia entry records that single fact: the verse's place inside the longer hymn, its Latin opening words, and its separate use in eucharistic devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-lagren:
Pierre Lagrené was a French Jesuit missionary who worked among the Indigenous peoples of Canada. He was born at Paris in 1659 and joined the order in 1677. He learned Huron at Lorette and served the Iroquois at Sault Saint Louis in two long postings around the turn of the century.

In Montreal he led the men's sodality, a lay devotional brotherhood, and gave it a firm organisation. He saw its chapel finished and blessed in 1710. Transferred to Quebec College in 1723 as prefect of schools, he also served as minister and sodality director there. Failing health ended his work in 1735, a year before his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-gianno:
Pietro Giannone, Italian historian, was born on 7 May 1676 at Ischitella in the province of Capitanata, Naples, and died at Turin on 27 March 1748. Taught first by his uncle, the lawyer Gaetano Argento, he took a doctorate of law at Naples and practised his father's profession. He gave all his leisure to history, and after twenty years of preparation published his Civil History of the Kingdom of Naples in 1723.

The work caused a sensation through its bitter anti-ecclesiastical bias and was repeatedly translated into English and German. It was put on the Index, its author excommunicated and forced to leave Naples. He went to Vienna, pensioned by Emperor Charles VI, and was readmitted to the Church. Later wanderings ended in arrest in Savoy, imprisonment at Ceva, and transfer to Turin, where he died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-constant:
Pope Constantine, Syrian-born son of John, took office 25 March 708 and died 9 April 715. The entry paints him as strikingly amiable. Rome starved through cruel famine in his reign's first half, then enjoyed rare plenty. Felix of Ravenna, whom he had consecrated archbishop, defied him until hardship drove Felix back to obedience.

Coenred of Mercia came as a pilgrim, and Offa of the East Saxons with him; both took the tonsure at Rome and turned monks. Egwin of Worcester travelled with them and gained privileges for Evesham, though every Evesham document carrying Constantine's name is fake. His hardest test was Justinian II's Quinisext Council of 692. Its 102 canons, touching clerical celibacy and Constantinople's freedom, had met refusal from every pope. Summoned east, Constantine met the highest honours at Constantinople.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-valentin:
Valentine was a Roman of the Via Lata district, though his birth date is unknown. He entered church service as a youth. The Liber Pontificalis praises his piety and pure morals, which won Paschal I's favour. Paschal gave him ordination at the Lateran palace and set him as archdeacon over Rome's diaconate. He kept that influential post under Eugene II.

After Eugene died on 27 August 827, clergy, nobles, and people unanimously elected Valentine. The election happened at the Lateran, and the company moved to Santa Maria Maggiore, where Valentine prayed. They led him to the Lateran basilica and set him on the papal throne. Probably the next Sunday he was consecrated at St Peter's and enthroned. Nothing survives about his brief reign. He died after forty days by the Liber Pontificalis, or barely a month by Einhard's Annals, about October 827.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portland-main:
Portland diocese, suffragan of Boston, was erected by Pius IX on 8 December 1854. At first it covered Maine and New Hampshire. In 1884 New Hampshire became its own diocese at Manchester, leaving Portland with all Maine: 29,895 square miles and 125,000 Catholics, a sixth of the population.

Maine saw the earliest Catholic colonization attempts in the north or east of the present United States. In 1604 Henry IV of France licensed Pierre du Gaust, Sieur de Monts, to colonize between latitudes forty and forty-six. He landed at Cape La Heve, explored toward the St Lawrence, found and named the St John River, and settled Ste-Croix Island, now De Monts Island. In the island chapel in July 1604, Nicholas Aubray offered the first Mass in New England. The entry continues through later missions, Irish immigrants, and Maine's Catholic growth, including Abenaki work passed to the Jesuits and Bapst's mission at Oldtown from 1848.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priene:
Priene stands as a titular see of Asia Minor under Ephesus. Its town dates from the age when Carians, Leleges, and Lycians alone ruled the land. Later Ionians held it, and it joined Ionia's twelve cities.   Set on Mount Mycale's south slope, it never grew great. By Augustus' time it stood forty stadia from the sea, since the Meander had silted its approach.

  After winning self rule, it stayed loyal to the Ionic league. The philosopher Bias was born there. The Notitiae episcopatuum keeps it under Ephesus until the thirteenth century. Four bishops are known by name: Theosebius, at Ephesus in 431; Isidore, living in 451; Paul, at Constantinople in 692; and Demetrius, in the twelfth century. Its fine ruins stand at Samsoon Kalessi, near Kelitesh village in the Smyrna vilayet, about two miles from the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-renaud-de-bea:
Renaud de Beaune, French bishop, was born at Tours in 1527 and died in Paris in 1606. Before entering the Church he served Francis of Valois, Duke of Touraine, as Chancellor, and sat as Councillor of Parliament. Court favour brought him many church offices. He became Bishop of Mende in 1568 and Archbishop of Bourges in 1581. Henry the Fourth made him grand almoner in 1591 and named him to Sens in 1595, though the pope confirmed that appointment only in 1602.

In 1600 he joined Henry the Fourth's commission to reform the University of Paris. Contemporaries ranked him among the greatest orators of his age. Posterity prized his work for the pacification of France above his oratory, and his influence helped bring that settlement about. His writings include a work on Catherine de Medici, a French Psalms translation, and a reform of the University of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-byrne:
Richard Byrne, brevet brigadier general in the United States Army, was born in County Cavan, Ireland, in 1832 and died at Washington on 10 June 1864. New York took him in 1844 as an emigrant; five years later he enlisted in the regular army, joining the Second Cavalry under Colonel E. V. Sumner. In that regiment he earned distinction in Indian fighting in Florida and Oregon.

At the Civil War's outbreak, on Sumner's recommendation, he was commissioned first lieutenant in the Fifth Cavalry, a new regiment authorized by Congress. After the campaigns of 1861 and 1862 with the regulars, Governor Andrew appointed him colonel of the Twenty-Eighth Massachusetts Volunteers, an Irish regiment he took command of on 18 October 1862. He died before his brevet appointment could officially be presented to him, and his remains were buried in Calvary Cemetery, New York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-langh:
Richard Langhorne, an English lawyer executed at Tyburn in 1679, was one of the victims of the Popish Plot scare. Born about 1635, the third son of a barrister of the Inner Temple, he entered that inn in 1646 and was called to the bar in 1654. He lived near Temple Bar, married a Protestant wife, and practised law quietly until the plot hysteria seized London.

Arrested in 1678, he was held eight months in solitary confinement at Newgate without prior examination. He was tried at the Old Bailey on the word of the informers Oates, Dugdale, Bedloe, and Prance. Offered pardon if he would confess guilt and reveal Jesuit property he knew of through his practice, he disclosed the property. He denied any conspiracy, and so went to the gallows. His last words spoke of readiness to be with his Jesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ripatransone:
Ripatransone is a diocese in Ascoli Piceno in central Italy, its city standing on five hills near ancient Cupra Marittima. Its modern name derives from Ripa trans Asonem, the bank beyond the Asone. A castle rose there in the early Middle Ages and was enlarged by the bishops of Fermo, who clashed more than once with the townspeople.

St Pius V made it an episcopal see in 1571, naming Cardinal Lucio Sasso as first bishop and drawing territory from Fermo, Ascoli, and Teramo. Noteworthy later bishops include Filippo Sega and Gaspare Sillingardi, who revived religious life in the town. Gian Carlo Gentili wrote the region's history, and Alessandro Spoglia was refused recognition by the government. The cathedral, by Gaspare Guerra, holds a marble altar with a triptych by Crivelli. Directly subject to Rome at first, the diocese has been suffragan to Fermo since 1680.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-blackb:
Robert Blackburne was an English Catholic imprisoned for fifty-three years without ever being brought to trial. A son of Richard Blackburne of Thistleton in Lancashire, from one of the county's oldest Catholic families, he was arrested in 1695. The charge was suspicion of connection with the so-called Lancashire Plot.

No trial ever followed. Parliament heard his case more than once, but no relief followed. He was neither tried nor released, and finally died in prison in 1748. The entry presents his fate as a stark example of imprisonment without justice in the penal years, a man held for over half a century on suspicion alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-mannyn:
Robert Mannyng of Brunne was an English poet of the early fourteenth century who wrote for readers who could not read French. From Bourne in Lincolnshire, he entered the Gilbertine house at Sempringham in 1288 and at some point was with Robert Bruce at Cambridge. By 1338 he lived in another priory of his order, still in Lincolnshire. His death date is unknown.

He wrote two poems, both free translations from French. Handlyng Synne renders the Manuel des Peschiez in stories on the commandments, the seven deadly sins, sacrilege, and the sacraments, with tales of his own drawn from English life. His Chronicle of England translates Wace's Geoffrey of Monmouth and then Peter de Langtoft, adding independent matter for Edward I's reign. Both poems matter because they speak to unlearned listeners, foreshadow the storytelling of the Canterbury Tales, and helped make East-Midland English the literary dialect. Furnivall edited both.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rule-of-st-au:
The title Rule of Saint Augustine has been applied to several documents. These are Letter 211, Sermons 355 and 356, part of a rule for clerks, a second rule, and a treatise on eremitical life. The last is by Blessed Aelred of Rievaulx, who died in 1166. The two preceding rules are of unknown authorship, so only Letter 211 and the sermons were Augustine's.

Letter 211 went to nuns in a monastery governed by Augustine's sister. Written to quiet troubles over naming a new superior, it also treats religious life's virtues and practices. These include charity, poverty, obedience, detachment, shared labour, common prayer, fasting, care of the sick, and silence. In his two sermons Augustine sought to dispel Hippo's suspicions of clergy living monastically with him. He showed bishop and priests in strict poverty, using money in common.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-engelbe:
Engelbert of Cologne was archbishop from 1216 to 1225, born at Berg about 1185. His father was Count of Berg, his mother Margaret of Gelderland. He studied at Cologne cathedral school. While still a boy, he was made provost of Cologne churches and St Mary's at Aachen. In 1199 he was elected Cologne cathedral provost. He led a worldly life, siding with his cousin Adolf, and was excommunicated and deposed in 1206.

After submission he was reinstated in 1208. In 1216 the chapter unanimously elected him archbishop. Tall and handsome, loving justice and peace, yet ambitious. He worked to repair his see. He guarded possessions and defended Berg, inherited in 1218. Though bearing himself as sovereign, he kept Church duties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-jean-de:
Saint Jean de Maurienne is the Savoy diocese covering the arrondissement of the same name in Haute Savoie, suffragan of Chambéry. Suppressed by the Concordat of 1802 and joined to Chambéry, it was cut off again in 1825 under Piedmontese rule. It became French territory with the rest of Savoy on 14 June 1860. Its pilgrimage fame began when Thecla of Valloires brought a finger of John the Baptist from the East to the church of Maurienne, then in the diocese of Turin.

King Gontran of Burgundy took the valleys of Susa and Maurienne from the Lombards in 574 and founded a bishopric near the shrine in 576, with Felmasius as first bishop. A letter of John VIII in 878 named Maurienne suffragan of Tarentaise, though the metropolitans of Vienne long claimed it and carried their point under Callistus II in 1120. Local tradition also counts martyred bishops Emilianus and Odilard among its early shepherds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-da:
John Damascene, born at Damascus about 676 and dead between 754 and 787, is known only through a tenth-century life by John, Patriarch of Jerusalem. The writer calls that life unsatisfactory history, thin on detail and heavy with legend. His father Mansur was a Christian who kept the caliph Abdul Malek's favour and served as his financial officer. Among captives from a raid on Italy, Mansur found a Sicilian monk named Cosmas, freed him, and made him tutor to his sons John and Cosmas.

Under Cosmas, John advanced so fast that his biographer compares him to Diophantus in algebra and Euclid in geometry, with progress in music, astronomy, and theology. On his father's death he became chief councillor of Damascus. When Leo the Isaurian issued his first edict against the veneration of images in 726, John was safe in the caliph's court. He defended the Christian usage and stirred resistance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sierra-leone:
Sierra Leone, a vicariate covering the English colony and the land from French Guinea to Liberia, centers on Freetown, in a territory of 30,000 square miles and 3,000,000 people. Its climate earned it the name White Man's Grave, with yellow fever endemic and malaria and hemoglobinuria rife. After the American Revolution, England bought land from native chiefs and settled freed and runaway slaves there, about 400 founding Freetown in 1787. It became a crown colony in 1808.

Protestants held exclusive control until Catholicism arrived in 1864, with Wesleyans leading among many sects. In the surrounding country the natives were pagans, and Islam spread as a dangerous rival to Catholicism. West African Catholic missions began in 1843 with Bishop Barron's Vicariate of the Two Guineas under the Holy Ghost Fathers. The entry follows Sierra Leone's mission from that founding through its bishops, schools, and stations to 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-le-moyn:
Simon Le Moyne, Jesuit missionary born at Beauvais in 1604, entered the Society in 1622 and sailed for Canada sixteen years later. With Chaumonot, Bressani, and future martyrs he laboured on the Huron mission. Second only to Chaumonot in command of the Huron-Iroquois tongue, he knew Indian character, customs, and traditions better than any of his peers. His death came in 1665 at Cap de la Madeleine near Three Rivers.

That mastery made him the natural ambassador for delicate and arduous occasions. He was the first European to reach the Onondagas, where his eloquence won their admiration and a plea for a missionary to teach them of the Great Spirit in 1654. His second mission took him to the fierce Mohawks, murderers of Father Jogues, who received him well, and on to Manhattan, where Governor Stuyvesant treated him courteously.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophene:
Sophene was an Armenian district and titular see whose tangled geography this entry works hard to sort out. Ancient sources place a Sophene in the north, well known to classical writers as a Roman province. They place a Sophenene further south, near Martyropolis and Amida. The entry argues the titular see belongs to the southern district.

Evidence runs from Justinian's letter to his commander Zetas, through George of Cyprus and the sixth-century lists of bishoprics. It ends with Le Quien's roll of bishops, including Arsaphus at Constantinople in 381 and Euphemius at Chalcedon. For readers untangling Armenia's shifting provinces, the entry is a careful piece of detective work built on texts rather than maps.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophie-jeanne:
Sophie-Jeanne Soymonof Swetchine was a Russian-born writer and convert whose Paris salon became a meeting place for French Catholic thought, and this entry follows her remarkable life. Born in Moscow in 1782 to a noble family, she received a careful education in everything except religion, became a maid of honour at fourteen, and married General Swetchine at seventeen.

Raised Orthodox, she came to the Catholic faith at thirty-three after years of trial, reading, and reflection, calling her faith the child of her sorrow. After her husband's disgrace at court, she left Russia for Paris. Where her letters and conversation made her a quiet but real force in the religious life of her adopted city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sorbonne:
The Sorbonne, strictly speaking, was the celebrated theological college of Paris, though common speech uses the name for the whole faculty of theology. This entry traces it to Robert de Sorbon, a distinguished professor and famous preacher who lived from 1201 to 1274 and saw a gap in the University of Paris.

Dominicans and Franciscans each ran a Paris college offering free lectures to outside students, while the university itself offered nothing comparable. Sorbon answered by founding a society of professors who would teach without charge, living by monastic rules except for vows. And the entry follows how that foundation grew into one of Europe's great names in theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ado-of-vie:
St. Ado of Vienne, born about 800 in the diocese of Sens and dead on 16 December 875, was a Benedictine scholar raised at Ferrieres under the celebrated humanist Abbot Lupus Servatus. This entry praises his brilliant talent and hard application, which won his masters' esteem, and his ready obedience, deep humility, and sincere piety, which foreshadowed holiness.

Though birth and brains entitled him to a worldly career, he took the Benedictine habit at Ferrieres, then taught sacred sciences at Prum at the new abbot Markward's request. Envious monks drove him out after Markward's death, and with his abbot's leave he moved on, the entry following a scholar whose learning never displaced his humility.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aidan-of-l:
St. Aidan of Lindisfarne was an Irish monk who became apostle of Northumbria, and this entry follows him from Scattery Island to Bamborough. Schooled under St. Senan at Iniscathay, placed as bishop of Clogher by Ware and Lynch, he resigned that see and became a monk at Iona about 630. Until his shining virtues won him election in 635 as first bishop of Lindisfarne.

Bede praises his rule and his Irish co-workers without stint, and King Oswald, himself schooled in Ireland, backed the mission until his death at Maserfield in 642. Aidan died at Bamborough on the last day of August 651, his body carried to Lindisfarne. And Bede's portrait of a pontiff full of passionate love of virtue and surpassing mildness closes the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anne:
St. Anne, Hebrew Hannah, grace, is the traditional name of the mother of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and this entry traces her story to apocryphal sources. Everything known of Anne and Joachim, Mary's parents, comes from the Gospel of the Nativity of Mary, the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew. And the Protoevangelium of James, whose earliest form dates to about 150. Though its claims can hardly be taken as certain on its sole authority.

In the East the Protoevangelium held great authority, read on Mary's feasts by Greeks, Syrians, Copts. And Arabians, while in the West the Fathers rejected it until Jacobus de Voragine wove its contents into the Golden Legend in the thirteenth century. From then on Anne's story spread through the Western Church, and the entry weighs tradition against evidence throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anne-line:
St. Anne Line was an English martyr, dead on 27 February 1601, and this entry follows a gentlewoman who paid for sheltering priests with her life. Daughter of William Heigham of Dunmow in Essex, a gentleman of means and ardent Calvinist, she and her brother were disowned and disinherited when they announced their conversion to Catholicism.

She married Roger Line, a convert like herself, who was soon arrested for attending Mass, briefly confined, then exiled to Flanders, where he died in 1594. When Father John Gerard set up a London refuge for priests, Mrs. Line took charge, and after Gerard's escape from the Tower in 1597 she moved house and made it a rallying point for local Catholics. Until priest-catchers broke in on Candlemas Day 1601 as Mass was about to begin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-benedict-o:
St. Benedict of Aniane was born about 745 to 750 and died at Cornelimunster on 11 February 821. This entry follows a man first called Witiza, son of the Goth Aigulf, count of Maguelone in southern France. He was educated at the Frankish court of Pepin and entered royal service. He took part in Charlemagne's Italian campaign of 773, then left royal service for religious life, and was received into the monastery of St. Sequanus, or Saint-Seine.

He gave himself most zealously to ascetic practices, and learned to value the Rule of St. Benedict as the best foundation for monastic life. Back home in 779, he set up a new monastic settlement on his own land near the little river Aniane. It soon grew into the monastery of Aniane, and became the model and centre for France's monastic reform under Louis the Pious. Benedict became the emperor's chief adviser.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernard-ar:
St. Bernard, or Barnard, was archbishop of Vienne in France, born in 778. He died at Vienne on 23 January 842. This entry follows a boy whose parents, living near Lyons with large possessions, gave him an excellent education. Obeying his father's wish, Bernard married and took service as a military officer under Charlemagne. Seven years as a soldier ended when his father and mother died and called him home.

He split his property three ways — for the Church, for the poor, and for his children — and withdrew to the Ambronay wilderness, site of a poor monastery. Bernard bought that monastery, enlarged it, and joined its inmates. Upon the abbot's death he was elected in 805 to fill the vacancy. In 810 he was chosen archbishop of Vienne to succeed Volfere, but only on the command of Pope Leo III and Charlemagne did he accept the honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-blane:
St. Blane, or Blaan, was bishop and confessor in Scotland, born on the island of Bute, date unknown. He died in 590, and his feast is kept on 10 August. This entry follows a nephew of St. Cathan, taught in Ireland by Sts. Comgall and Kenneth. He became a monk, moved to Scotland, and in time served as bishop among the Picts. Several miracles are told of him, including the restoration of a dead boy to life.

The Aberdeen Breviary gives those and other details of his life, which the Bollandists reject, however. Devotion to St. Blane was undoubtedly popular in Scotland from early times. His monastery became the site of Dunblane Cathedral. Dumfries had a church of St. Blane, and Kilblane another. The year of his death is variously given as 446, 590, and 1000, but 446 is evidently incorrect, and the entry weighs the rival dates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-mac:
St. Colman Mac Lenine was founder and patron of the See of Cloyne, born in Munster about 510. He died 24 November 601. This entry follows a man endowed with extraordinary poetic powers, styled by his contemporaries the Royal Bard of Munster. Ireland's Ardrigh gave him Cloyne, in today's County Cork, for his cathedral abbey in 560, and he worked there for over forty years across a wide diocese.

Some of his Irish poems survive, notably a metrical panegyric on St. Brendan, and Colgan notes a metrical life of St. Senan from him. His feast falls on 24 November, a day shared by another St. Colman, as St. Aengus records in his Felire, pairing Mac Lenine the most excellent with Colman of Duth-chuilleann.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eithene:
Eithene, remembered with her sister Sodelbia as daughters of Baite, belongs to the quieter corners of the Irish calendars. Daughters of Aidh, son of Caibre, king of Leinster in the mid-sixth century, they are commemorated on 20 March. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 reads their title not as their father's name, but as children of divine or ardent love.

A vision supports that reading: Christ as an infant rested in the two virgins' arms. In the Acts of Moling of Ferns, the saint visits the sisters at their home, Tech-Ingen-Baithe, the house of the daughters of Baite, near Swords in County Dublin. Eithene is also venerated at Killnais nearby. The entry is slight, but it preserves a household, a vision, and a place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eithne:
Eithne of the golden hair is remembered for a single scene beside a Roscommon brook, and this entry lets that scene carry her story. Daughter of Leoghaire, high king of Ireland when Patrick first came to Tara in 433, she was fostered near Cruachan, home of Connacht's kings, as royal children then were. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her commemoration to 11 January.

Her life centres on one morning at the Well of Clebach, where Patrick and his disciples camped on their way west. Rising at dawn to chant, the clerics met the king's daughters, and the brief encounter became her legend. No long career follows in the record. Instead the entry preserves a conversion moment: a princess, a well, and the new faith arriving at dawn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-euphrosyne:
Euphrosyne, who died about 470, belongs to the legends of Christian virgins who dressed as men to guard their vows. Only daughter of Paphnutius, a rich Alexandrian, she was promised to a wealthy youth. Having consecrated her life to God and seeing no other way to keep that vow, she put on male dress and entered a men's monastery near Alexandria as Smaragdus. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 takes her story from the Vitae Patrum.

For thirty-eight years she lived there, winning the abbot's notice by swift progress in ascetic life. When her grieving father sought comfort, the abbot gave him into Smaragdus's care, and the daughter counselled her own father unrecognized. Only while dying did she reveal herself. The entry preserves a tale of disguise, devotion, and a father's unknowing consolation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ine:
Ine, king of the West Saxons from 688 to 726, ruled a turbulent people as warrior and lawgiver with equal success. Son of the underking Cenred, he took the throne in 688, a year before Caedwalla's death, and held it thirty-seven years until his death in 728. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 credits him first with internal peace, then with a code of laws.

In his fifth year he drew up laws regulating justice and fixing the legal status of each class of subjects. Save Kent's laws, that code is the earliest surviving Anglo-Saxon legislation, and therefore of particular interest. With his realm settled, he marched against Withred of Kent, demanding weregild for Mul, Caedwalla's brother. Withred paid thirty thousand pounds of silver in full and admitted West-Saxon supremacy over English-held southern lands. The entry joins sword and statute book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-nepom:
John Nepomucene, vicar-general of Prague drowned in the Moldau in 1393, is a saint wrapped in an identity dispute. Born at Nepomuk about 1340, son of Welflin, a burger of Pomuk, he became Prague archdiocese's vicar-general. On 20 March 1393, by King Wenceslaus IV's command, he was thrown into the Moldau and drowned. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 sets out original sources before legend.

Documents, church records, and contemporary accounts agree on those facts unmistakably. What remains undecided, since the eighteenth century, is whether one John or two men of that name lived in Prague in the later fourteenth century and met precisely the same fate. The true cause of his violent death is likewise debated. The entry insists on sources first: a vicar-general, a king's command, a river, a date.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mary-de-ce:
Mary de Cervellione, a thirteenth-century Barcelona noblewoman known as Mary of Help, gave her life to ransoming Christian captives. Born about 1230 to a Spanish nobleman, she heard Bernard de Corbarie preach for slaves held by the Turks and resolved to aid them. In 1265 she joined a small group of devout women near the Mercedarian monastery at Barcelona and became their first superior.

Her community won leave to form a Third Order of Our Lady of Ransom and to wear the Mercedarian habit, adding a promise to pray for Christian slaves. Famed for charity to the needy, she was invoked after her death against shipwreck and is pictured holding a ship. Her cult won approval in 1692, and her feast is kept on 25 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-robert-bel:
Robert Bellarmine, a Jesuit cardinal and theologian, became the Catholic Church's chief controversialist against the Reformers. Born at Montepulciano on 4 October 1542, his mother was sister of the future Marcellus II. Schooled at the new Jesuit college in his town, he entered the Society in 1560, studied philosophy at the Roman College, and finished theology at Louvain.

Recalled to Rome in 1576, he took the new chair of Controversies, and his lectures grew into De Controversiis, a vast defence of Catholic doctrine. He served as rector of the Roman College, provincial of Naples, papal theologian, and cardinal from 1599. He advised moderation in the grace controversy and later ruled Capua as archbishop. He died on 17 September 1621, praised for learning and conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-roseline:
Roseline, a Carthusian prioress of Provence, overcame her father's opposition to enter a hard mountain order. Born at the château of Arcs in eastern Provence in 1263, she entered the Carthusians at Bertaud in the Dauphiné Alps, with her consecration in 1288. She later succeeded her aunt, Blessed Jeanne de Villeneuve, as prioress of Celle-Robaud near Fréjus.

Her brother Hélion, grand master of the Knights of St John, restored the monastery in 1320, and John XXII increased its revenue in 1323 and 1328. Roseline won leave to resign before her death on 17 January 1329. Visions, austerities, and power over demons are ascribed to her. Her cult was confirmed for Fréjus in 1851 and for the Carthusian order in 1857.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rusticus-o:
Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne in the fifth century, steered a Gothic-threatened diocese through siege, heresy, and division. Born at Marseilles or in Narbonnaise, he was the Rusticus to whom Jerome wrote about 411, urging him to imitate Exuperius of Toulouse. After study in Gaul and fame as a speaker at Rome, he chose the contemplative life at Lérins.

Ordained at Marseilles, he was consecrated bishop of Narbonne on 3 October 430 or 427. He could not halt Arianism spread by the Goths, and the siege of Narbonne with Catholic dissension drove him to offer his resignation to Leo, who refused it. He built Narbonne's church in 444 to 448 and backed Leo's letter against Nestorianism in 451. He died on 26 October 461.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-valentine:
Valentine is not one martyr but at least three, all named in early martyrologies for 14 February. One was a priest at Rome, another bishop of Interamna, modern Terni. Both appear to have died in the later third century. Both were laid to rest along the Flaminian Way, one farther from Rome than the other. A small church by the Flaminian Gate took the saint's name.

Acta survive for both, but they are late and of no historical value. A third Valentine suffered in Africa with companions, and nothing further is known of him. Popular customs of Valentine's Day, the entry argues, grew from a medieval belief in England and France that birds began to pair on 14 February, halfway through the second month. The piece separates martyrs from romance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-of:
William of Gellone, second count of Toulouse, defeated Saracen invaders and then became a monk in his own foundation. Born in 755 to Theoderic and Aldana, connected with Charlemagne's family, he grew up at the great emperor's court. Charlemagne sent him against Saracen raiders out of Spain, and he beat them at Orange.

In 804 he raised a Benedictine house, now St-Guilhem-le-Désert, in the valley of Gellone near Lodève, placing it under Benedict of Aniane, whose house stood nearby. Two years later he himself became a monk at Gellone, remaining until his death on 28 May about 812. He is the hero of the ninth-century Romance of William Short-Nose, but the entry prefers the near-contemporary biography written soon after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syene:
Syene was a titular see in Thebian Secunda, suffragan of Ptolemais, known in Egyptian as Souanou. It began as the marketplace of Elephantine island, whose town Abou served pharaohs as a principality capital and nome chief town. Across the Nile its suburb grew at the older town's cost, until the two counted as one, Souanou acting as port and working city.

Its quarries, with Rohannou's, were Egypt's chief source of red granite called syenite, cut into obelisks, temples, and colossi and shipped through the empire in Roman times. A pit there, wrongly thought to sit exactly under the equator, gave Eratosthenes his starting point for measuring the earth in 230 BC. Saracen rebuilding, Nubian raids, and a Turkish garrison from 1517 mark its later story, and it is now Assouan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synesius-of-c:
Synesius of Cyrene, bishop of Ptolemais and a Neoplatonist, died about 414, his birth date uncertain. A younger son of an ancient Cyrene family, he claimed descent from the city's mythical founders. He studied at Alexandria as a devoted pupil of Hypatia, to whom several letters are addressed. After army service he settled at home, studying, farming, hunting, and defending neighbours in trouble.

A mission to Constantinople broke that life. He carried a gold crown to the new emperor Arcadius and sought lighter taxes. He waited nearly three years for an audience before delivering his famous oration On Kingship. He left in 400, visited Athens to his disappointment, and married at Alexandria. Later pages treat his election as bishop and the debate over his religious views.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-martyrs-o:
Sixteen Carmelite nuns guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794 are honoured here, the first sufferers of the French Revolution on whom the Holy See passed judgment. Beatified on 27 May 1906, they knelt before the scaffold and chanted the Veni Creator as at a profession, then renewed aloud their baptismal and religious vows. The novice died first, the prioress last.

Absolute silence reigned through the executions. Heads and bodies went into a deep sand-pit at Picpus cemetery, some thirty feet square, holding 1,298 victims of the Revolution, so recovery of relics seems hopeless. Names, birthplaces, and profession dates of each sister follow, led by Prioress Madeleine-Claudine Ledoine, Mother Teresa of Saint Augustine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thibaut-de-ch:
Poet-king Thibaut IV of Champagne and Navarre, crusader and troubadour, is the prince portrayed here. Born at Troyes in 1201, he died on 8 July 1253, posthumous son of Thibaut III and Blanche, sister of Sancho VII of Navarre. He fought for his countship first in 1221 against his uncle of Brienne, then against his aunt Alice, Queen of Cyprus.

In Louis IX's minority he first backed nobles against Blanche of Castile, then broke with them, and the queen defended him when they attacked. Sancho VII died childless in 1234, and Thibaut took Navarre's crown. He led Gregory IX's crusade of 1239, landed at Acre on 1 September, lost battles, saw his troops crushed at Gaza, and left Syria on 1 September 1240. Four crusade songs rank among his best poems.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-august:
Thomas Augustine Arne, an English composer born in London in 1710, wrote the music for Rule Britannia and much else for the eighteenth-century stage. The son of Catholic parents, he was educated at Eton and apprenticed to a solicitor before turning to music. His masque Alfred, written with Thomson and Mallet for the Hanoverian anniversary, contains the famous patriotic song.

Arne worked at Drury Lane, Vauxhall, Ranelagh and Marylebone Gardens, and spent a fruitful stay in Ireland, where he produced the oratorio Abel and the operas Britannia and Comus. Oxford made him Doctor of Music in 1759, and Artaxerxes followed in 1762. He died in 1778 and was buried at St. Paul's, Covent Garden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-bra:
Thomas of Bradwardine, theologian known as Doctor Profundus, was born about 1290, by his own account at Chichester, and died in London in 1349. Educated at Merton College, Oxford, he acted as a university proctor in 1325 and built a name in theology. His lectures grew into the Summa Doctoris Profundi, or De Causa Dei, a great treatise on grace against Pelagius.

Chaucer ranks him with Augustine and Boethius. Called to London by Richard de Bury in 1335, he became chancellor of St. Paul's, chaplain to Edward III, and a commissioner for peace after Crecy and Neville's Cross. Elected Archbishop of Canterbury in 1348, he was passed over for John Ufford, who died of plague, and Bradwardine himself died soon after taking the see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-vane:
Thomas Vane, a convert whose dates of birth and death are unknown, wrote one of the best known accounts of conversion in seventeenth-century England. Educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he took a doctorate in divinity, he took Anglican orders. He became chaplain extraordinary to Charles I and rector of Crayford, then gave up both posts on becoming a Catholic.

With his wife he moved to Paris, where he practised as a physician and took a medical degree. There he wrote A Lost Sheep Returned Home, an account of his conversion. Its preface is dated August 1642, it appeared in 1643, and it ran through several editions, drawing an answer from Edward Chisenhall in 1653. He also wrote against the libel of Dr. Cosens on the Lateran Council and a work on wisdom and innocence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-throne:
A throne, in the language of church ceremonial, is the seat a bishop uses when he is not at the altar. Its Latin names are thronus, cathedra and sedes episcopalis. The Caeremoniale Episcoporum lays down where it stands. It goes at the head of the apse among the canons' stalls if the altar stands near the choir entrance. It goes on the Gospel side if the altar stands close to the apse wall.

The throne must be a fixed chair with a high back and arms, raised on three carpeted steps and covered in silk matching the bishop's vestments. Cloth of gold is barred unless the bishop is a cardinal. A canopy may crown it only if the altar also has one. In another diocese a bishop needs the local bishop's leave to use the throne, and must yield it to any cardinal present.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiro-prosper-:
Prosper of Aquitaine, called Tiro Prosper in some manuscripts, was a fifth-century writer on grace and free will. The first sure date in his life is his letter to Augustine in 428 or 429, written at Hilary's request about troubles over Augustine's teaching at Marseilles. That letter, with Hilary's own, opened the semi-Pelagian controversy, to which Augustine answered with treatises on predestination and perseverance.

Prosper then wrote a short treatise on grace, a poem of over a thousand lines, De Ingratis, against the semi-Pelagians, and epigrams against Augustine's critics. After Augustine's death in 430 he answered fifteen Gallic propositions charged against the master. His chronicle, in three editions running to 433, 445 and 455, is sometimes called the Consular Chronicle, distinct from the Imperial Chronicle wrongly ascribed to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-torone:
Torone was a titular see in Macedonia, subject to Thessalonica, and a Chalcidian colony from Euboea. It stood on the southwest coast of Sithonia, the middle peninsula of Chalcidice, between the Toronaic Gulf and the Gulf of Singitticus. Built on a hill in a fine position, it had a harbour called Kophos, or deaf, because no sea sound reached it, giving the proverb deafer than the port of Torone.

Thirty small cities stood under its rule, and it supplied Xerxes with men and ships. After the Persian War Athens ruled it, and Brasidas, Cleon, Agesipolis, Timotheus and Philip of Macedon each took it in turn. In 169 it beat off a Roman fleet, after which history falls silent. Pliny calls it a free city, its ruins still bear the name Toroni, and no bishop of the see is known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-udine:
Udine is the capital city of a province and archdiocese in Friuli, in northern Italy, set in mainly farming country. Its cathedral was begun in 1236 by Patriarch Bertoldo and altered several times, most recently in 1706 through the generosity of the Manin family. Their tombs adorn the choir. Inside are paintings by Pordenone, Tiepolo, and Matteo da Verona, statues by Torretto and others, and a baptistery font by Giovanni da Zuglio from 1480.

The entry moves on to Udine's other churches, from the ancient Santa Maria di Castello, reshaped in the sixteenth century, to houses holding tombs of the Barbaro patriarchs. It then sketches the archdiocese, its bishops, and its history under patriarchs of Aquileia, Venetian rule, and later regimes. The result is a compact guide to a regional capital where art, church history, and civic pride meet in stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Cologne was famed through the Middle Ages for cathedral and cloister schools and for scholars such as Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus. Yet no university existed there until late in the fourteenth century, when Urban VI, urged by the town council, issued the founding bull on 21 May 1388. The university opened the next year with twenty-one masters and 737 matriculated students.

Further privileges came from Boniface IX, Duke Wilhelm von Geldern, and Emperor Frederick III, while Gregory XII, Nicholas V, and Pius II showed it special favour. Pius sent his Bull of Retractation to its rector and university in 1463. The university was represented at the great councils, and the entry follows its faculties, its Thomist and Albertist schools, and its later decline and refounding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-upper-rhine:
The Upper Rhine ecclesiastical province gathers the Archdiocese of Freiburg with its suffragans Fulda, Mainz, Limburg, and Rottenburg. Its modern story begins with the secularization of the German church by the Imperial Delegates Enactment of 25 February 1803. Bishoprics, abbeys, and monasteries were handed over to compensate rulers who had yielded lands on the Rhine's left bank to France.

Part of the Archdiocese of Mainz survived for the primate Karl Theodore von Dalberg and moved to Ratisbon cathedral. Hanover, Brunswick, and Oldenburg also received church lands, yet none thought at first of founding new dioceses for their Catholic subjects. The entry follows the long negotiations that at last built the province, its concordats, and its bishops, a record of church rebuilding after revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentin-gron:
Valentin Gröne was a Catholic theologian born at Paderborn on 7 December 1817, who died at Irmgarteichen in Westphalia on 18 March 1882. After his studies he was ordained priest at Paderborn in July 1844, then took an advanced course in church history at Munich, where he earned his doctorate in theology in 1848. He served as chaplain at Bielefeld, Warstein, Brilon, and Scherfede.

On 14 October 1857 he became rector of the city high school at Fredeburg, moving later to Schmallenberg in the same post. On 24 September 1868 he was made pastor at Irmgarteichen, and later dean. His best-known works include Tetzel und Luther, a life and vindication of the indulgence preacher Johann Tetzel. The entry lists his writings and sketches a pastor-scholar of steady reputation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-ol:
Edward Oldcorne was a martyr born in 1561 who died in 1606. His father was Protestant and his mother Catholic. Trained as a doctor, he later chose the priesthood, went to the English College at Reims and then to Rome, where after ordination in 1587 he became a Jesuit. The next year he returned to England with Father John Gerard and worked chiefly in Worcester.

Arrested with Father Henry Garnet, he was taken to the Tower. No evidence linking him to the Gunpowder Plot could be found, and he was executed for his priesthood alone. Two of his letters survive at Stonyhurst, the second, written from prison, full of zeal and charity. His last combat came on 7 April at Red Hill, Worcester, where his faithful servant Ralph Ashby suffered with him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-nicholas-:
Nicholas Tichborne was a martyr born at Hartley Mauditt in Hampshire, who suffered at Tyburn in London on 24 August 1601. A recusant at large in 1592, he was jailed by 14 March 1597, when he gave evidence against various members of his family. Before 3 November 1598 he had gained his liberty and had freed his brother Thomas Tichborne, a prisoner in the Gatehouse at Westminster, by assaulting his keeper.

He must not be confused with the Nicholas Tichborne who died in Winchester jail in 1587. With him suffered Thomas Hackshot of Mursley in Buckinghamshire, condemned on the same charge of effecting the priest Thomas Tichborne's escape. During his long imprisonment in the Gatehouse, Hackshot bore diverse torments with great courage and fortitude, the entry notes, before both men suffered at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-ti:
Thomas Tichborne was a Hampshire priest executed at Tyburn in April 1602. Born at Hartley in 1567, he studied at Reims and Rome, where he was ordained in 1592, and returned to England two years later to work in his home county. He evaded arrest until 1597, when he was sent to the Gatehouse in London.

In autumn 1598 his brother Nicholas and Thomas Hackshot helped him escape, and both men were martyred soon after. Betrayed by an apostate priest named Atkinson, Tichborne was retried in 1602 with Robert Watkinson and James Duckett. He was executed on 20 April with Watkinson and Francis Page, a convert received into the Jesuits while a prisoner in Newgate. Tichborne was already in the last stages of consumption.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-we: Edwin Burton's Catholic Encyclopedia entry admits how little is known of Thomas Welbourne, martyred at York on 1 August 1605. A schoolmaster from Kitenbushel in Yorkshire, he and John Fulthering, a layman of the same county, were zealous Catholics who urged neighbours to embrace the faith. On that account, Bishop Challoner's early catalogues say, both were arraigned and condemned to suffer, as in high-treason cases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-s: John Wainewright's Catholic Encyclopedia entry recounts William Southerne, an English martyr who suffered at Newcastle-under-Lyme on 30 April 1618. He trained as a priest at the English College in Douai. He worked mainly around Baswich near Stafford, then held by a branch of the Fowler family. Arrested while saying Mass, he was committed to Stafford gaol. Condemned for priesthood and refusing the oath of allegiance, he waited six days in prison because no hangman could be found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-mor:
Walter of Mortagne was a twelfth-century scholastic philosopher and theologian, born at Mortagne in Flanders in the first decade of the twelfth century and dying at Laon in 1174. Educated at Tournai's schools, he taught at Paris's celebrated School of St Genevieve from 1136 to 1144, then went to Laon and became its bishop.

His principal works are a treatise on the Holy Trinity and six short works. Five of the short works were published in d'Achéry's Spicilegium of 1723 and the sixth in the Patrologia Latina. On universals, John of Salisbury reports, Walter led the Indifferentists, for whom the universal is in itself indifferent, becoming the predicate of an individual only by added status. Determinations or points of view: Socrates is an individual, a species, man, or a genus, animal, according to the status adopted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-berna:
William Bernard Ullathorne was an English Benedictine monk and bishop who built the early Australian mission into order. Born at Pocklington in Yorkshire in 1806, he died at Oscott in 1889. His father, a village tradesman descended from Saint Thomas More, and his convert mother moved the family to Scarborough when he was ten. Three and a half years at sea followed, and a chance Mass at Memel in the Baltic turned his mind to God's service.

He entered Downside as a novice in 1823, took the name Bernard, and took orders at Ushaw in 1831. Volunteering for Australia, he landed in February 1833 as vicar-general with full powers. Only three priests worked there, unsupervised and at odds, but his tact settled Sydney, Tasmania, and the Norfolk Island convict station. Later he gave evidence on transportation before a parliamentary commission and wrote a tract on the subject at the government's request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-byrne:
William Byrne was an Irish-born missionary priest who founded Saint Mary's College near Bardstown, Kentucky. Born in County Wicklow in 1780, he died at Bardstown on 5 June 1833. His father's death forced him to support a large family, and a pious uncle gave him only a plain elementary schooling. The bloody scenes of the 1798 rebellion near his home left a deep mark on his youth.

At twenty-five he emigrated to America, sought the Jesuits at Georgetown, then studied at Mount Saint Mary's, Emmitsburg, where he served as prefect. Ordained at Bardstown in 1819, among its first priests, he rode missions at Saint Mary's, Saint Charles, and Louisville. In spring 1821 he opened Saint Mary's College in an old stone farmhouse with about fifty boys. Fire twice struck the school, yet each time his drive rebuilt it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-malon:
William Malone was an Irish Jesuit missioner whose clash with Archbishop Ussher became a famous controversy. Born, on the best authorities, in 1585 to a Dublin merchant father, he died at Seville in 1655. He joined the Jesuits at Rome in 1606, studied in Rome and Portugal, and reached Ireland as a missioner in 1615. In 1635 Rome made him rector of the Irish College, and in 1647 he returned as superior of the Irish mission in its hardest years.

At Waterford in 1649 Malone wrote that his burden outweighed Mount Etna and wearied him of life. Parliamentarians took the town, captured him, and banished him; at Seville he again governed as rector of Saint Gregory's College. His one book grew from a brief thesis for Sir Piers Crosby, printed by Ussher in 1625 and answered by Malone at Douai in 1627. It argued that ancient consent stood for Roman religion and that Ussher had failed to answer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-au:
William of Auvergne was Bishop of Paris from 1228 and a pioneer in bringing Aristotle into Christian thought. Born at Aurillac toward the end of the twelfth century, he died at Paris in 1249. His birth date and early schooling are unknown. He reached Paris in the early thirteenth century, taught first in arts and then in theology about 1220, and kept keen interest in his university as bishop.

His works span practical theology, a treatise on the Trinity, and philosophy, including De Universo, De Anima, and a tract on the soul's immortality borrowed from Gundisalvi. Collected at Nuremberg in 1496 and reissued at Venice and Orléans, they mark the first stage toward Aristotle as dogma's base. Hampered by faulty translations and Arab commentaries, he still rescued Aristotle from Arab readings and fought the Cathar revival of Manichaeism. He denied the world's eternity, clearing ground for Alexander of Hales, Albert, and Aquinas.
common-sense-thomas-paine:
Thomas Paine published his 47-page pamphlet on January 10, 1776, when many American colonists still hoped to make peace with Britain. Paine argued the opposite: the colonies should declare independence. He wrote for ordinary readers rather than lawyers or members of an assembly.

Plain, blunt language carries his case against monarchy and hereditary rule, and against the idea that a distant king in Britain should govern America. V1 evidence notes it sold by the hundreds of thousands and pushed opinion toward revolution. Few short pamphlets have changed public debate so quickly, and its title states Paine's method exactly: appeal to what readers could see for themselves.
confiscation-an-outline:
William Greenwood wrote Confiscation: An Outline to put a radical scheme of political economy before ordinary voters in plain words. Greenwood complains that economists write a dismal science only for scholars, when in a republic the voter alone can enact change. He sets his scene in the America of the 1890s: one man with fifty million dollars, another without money for shoe repairs, and parties divided among silver, protection, and free trade.

Reviewing the Populists, Republicans, and Democrats, he finds none offering escape from poverty amid wealth. His outline argues for confiscation, the taking of unearned gains for the public, as the honest name for the remedy. The pamphlet is Georgist-era agitation at pamphlet length, earnest, statistical, and aimed at the ballot box.
cymbeline:
William Shakespeare's late romance Cymbeline plays out in ancient Britain, in this old-spelling text from the same electronic Shakespeare set. King Cymbeline's daughter Imogen has secretly married the poor gentleman Posthumus, whom the king banishes. In Rome, the villain Iachimo wagers he can seduce her and steals proof from her bedroom.

Iachimo inventories the mole on her left breast, cinque-spotted like cowslip drops, to convince Posthumus of her guilt. Lost princes, a wicked queen, Roman invasion, and Imogen disguised as a boy tangle until the final scene unties every knot. Shakespeare mixes tragedy, pastoral, and fairy tale here, and the result, long undervalued, now charms audiences with its improbable grace.
do-and-dare-a-brave-boy-s-fight-for-fort:
Do and Dare, a brave boy's fight for fortune by Horatio Alger Jr, opens at the post office in Wayneboro. Alger seats Herbert Carr beside his mother in their plain cottage and lets the boy wish aloud that they could keep the office. Herbert's father held it before them, glad of the work because a war wound had cost him an arm, leaving little he could do that needed two hands.

The accounts book on the table shows a modest income for the year past, yet men still scheme for the place. Word comes that a movement is afoot to install Ebenezer Graham instead. Later chapters promise Herbert's chance, a prodigal son, the loss of his place, and Eben's scheme. Alger's pattern holds: a small public trust, a greedy rival, and a boy whose honesty must find him a larger life than Wayneboro offers.
doctor-therne:
Doctor Therne, by H Rider Haggard, is a novel written as an argument about vaccination. Haggard dedicates it to the Jenner Society, named for the pioneer of smallpox vaccination, frankly admitting he never asked their permission. His author's note attacks a government that, in a single evening, surrendered to anti-vaccination agitation and threw away the findings of royal commissions and the medical profession alike.

The story opens with a diligence journey and a Mexican hacienda, then moves through Sir John Bell, a trial, and a chapter called Crossing the Rubicon. Jane meets Dr Merchison as a red headed man arrives and the shadow of pestilence falls. A final chapter named Harvest counts the cost. Haggard uses a doctor's career, and a community's sickness, to make his case that refusing vaccination is not a private choice but a public danger.
doctor-thorne:
Anthony Trollope published this Barsetshire novel in 1858, as the title page here records, and set it in the village of Greshamsbury. The Greshams are old county family, encumbered and proud. Dr. Thorne, the village doctor, lives with his niece Mary, whose birth is the parish's open secret and whose fortune depends on the will of the ruined railway baron Sir Roger Scatcherd.

Frank Gresham, the heir, loves Mary Thorne and is told to marry money. The contents map the siege: matrimonial prospects, sentence of exile, the doctor drinking his tea, and Miss Dunstable, the rich ointment heiress Frank is pushed toward. Sir Roger's will makes Mary a prize the county had scorned. Trollope keeps the love story plain and lets pride, debt, and one honest doctor carry the book.

dora-thorne:
Charlotte M. Brame, who wrote as Bertha M. Clay for much of her career, opens Dora Thorne with a father forbidding a marriage. Lord Earle tells his son Ronald, nineteen and in love, that Dora Thorne, the lodge-keeper's daughter, can never take his mother's place. Ronald answers that love levels caste and he will marry no one else.

Brame builds her popular melodrama on that clash between rank and affection. Dora is pretty, modest, and barely educated; the Earles are proud and rich; and the consequences of folly, as the first line warns, seldom end with the one who commits it. Brame wrote for the great story-paper audience of Victorian Britain, and Dora Thorne became one of her most reprinted tales of love across the class line.
down-the-ravine:
Charles Egbert Craddock's Down the Ravine opens under a new moon in the Cumberland Mountains. A red fox barks on a ledge, imprudent, for Tennessee pays a dollar for his scalp and ears. Young Birt Dicey's rifle flashes, and the fox dies on a cliff forty feet up. Birt will not leave a dollar lying there.

The climb, and what follows, entangle Birt in a feud over counterfeiters' hidden gold and his widowed mother's farm. Nate Griggs jeers at his ambition: all the foxes in a protracted meeting could not buy a horse. Craddock, the pen name of Mary Noailles Murfree, wrote Tennessee mountain life from its own speech. The dialect is dense, the scenery grand, and the boy's dollar starts a chain of danger, suspicion, and honour satisfied. Local colour fiction rarely came more authentic.
east-lynne:
Mrs Henry Wood wrote East Lynne, a bestselling sensation novel presented here in an 1883 New York edition from John B Alden. The story opens with William, Earl of Mount Severn, gouty and short of money in his town house. His beautiful daughter, Lady Isabel Vane, is his chief treasure. Lawyer Archibald Carlyle of West Lynne comes to buy the East Lynne estate.

Carlyle marries Isabel and brings her home as mistress of East Lynne. Barbara Hare, who loves Carlyle herself, watches from the sidelines.
